Hypotonia in an Infant

brain, anterior horn cell, neuromuscular junction or muscle · strength and reflexes · genetic confirmation · Down syndrome careIs the infant floppy but strong, or weak with absent reflexes, and which test confirms the level?

Source case Pt — infant with low tone, Aquifer Pediatrics 29; the case works from the hypotonia differential to Down syndrome, its confirmation and its health supervision · Q — decide whether the low tone comes from the brain or from the motor unit, confirm the chromosomal cause, then plan the child’s care for the first years
The approach

Hypotonia is a finding, not a diagnosis. Localize where it starts. Causes in the brain include Down syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, congenital hypothyroidism and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. Other levels are the anterior horn cell (spinal muscular atrophy), the neuromuscular junction (infant botulism) and the muscle (congenital myotonic dystrophy, congenital myopathies). A central cause produces an infant who is floppy but strong for the tone, often dysmorphic or sleepy, with normal or brisk reflexes. A peripheral cause produces a weak, alert infant with low or absent reflexes. Check breathing and feeding first. Send the confirmatory test, usually genetic, once the level is known.

Down syndrome (trisomy 21) What it is — the commonest chromosomal cause of intellectual disability, about 1 in 700 US births · Who — any couple; risk climbs from the mid-30s, but most affected infants have mothers under 35 because younger women have more pregnancies · Mechanism — extra chromosome 21 material: free trisomy (most likely at any maternal age), an unbalanced translocation (relatively likelier with a younger mother), or mosaicism, with features from classic to almost none · Features — hypotonia, upslanting fissures, epicanthal folds, flat midface, small ears, loose nuchal skin; Brushfield spots, single palmar crease, clinodactyly, sandal gap; intellectual disability usually mild (intelligence quotient (IQ) 50 to 70) or moderate (35 to 50) · Diagnosis — prenatal serum analytes, nuchal ultrasound and cell-free DNA estimate risk; CVS (chorionic villus sampling) or amniocentesis diagnose; after birth a lymphocyte karyotype · Treatment — early intervention at diagnosis; an IEP (individualized education program) at school entry, with parents as advocates · Complications — heart disease in about half, some silent; duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease; hypothyroidism at any age; hearing and vision loss; transient myeloproliferative disorder and leukemia; atlantoaxial instability · Follow-up — the grid below · Return for — neck pain, head tilt, a change in walking, new weakness or wetting; pallor, bruising or fever; poor feeding or weight gain

Scenario bank
  1. 1-day-old boy, floppy since birth and slow to feed; upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, a flat midface, small ears, loose skin at the back of the neck, a single transverse palmar crease and a wide gap between the first and second toes; strength and reflexes are preserved; the parents ask whether a future child could be affected → Lymphocyte karyotype → Down syndrome; only the karyotype shows free trisomy, a translocation or mosaicism, which sets the recurrence risk
  2. 5-week-old girl who slips through the examiner's hands when held under the arms; she lifts her arms and legs against gravity and kicks vigorously; knee reflexes are 3+; no fasciculations; flat midface and upslanting palpebral fissures → Brain → Central hypotonia: strong for the tone, reflexes preserved; chromosomal cause likely
  3. 3-month-old girl, born at term after a normal pregnancy, whose parents are first cousins; over 6 weeks she has stopped kicking and now lies with her legs flopped outward; alert and follows faces; fine quivering movements of the tongue; knee and ankle reflexes absent; the chest sinks as the belly rises with each breath; no ptosis, pupils react briskly, stools normal → Spinal muscular atrophy → Anterior horn cell loss; autosomal recessive, so consanguinity raises the risk
  4. 3-month-old with progressive symmetric weakness of the limbs, absent reflexes, tongue fasciculations and paradoxical breathing; face and eye movements normal; alert and social → SMN1 deletion testing → Spinal muscular atrophy; CK is normal or near normal
  5. Newborn boy, pregnancy with polyhydramnios and reduced fetal movement, intubated at birth for weak breathing; weak face with a tented upper lip, poor suck, bilateral clubfeet and low reflexes; his mother has a long thin face and cannot quickly let go after a handshake → Congenital myotonic dystrophy → Muscle; DMPK CTG repeat expanded, passed from the mother
  6. 2-day-old boy, profoundly floppy since birth with a suck too weak to feed without a tube; almond-shaped eyes, a small penis and bilateral undescended testes; palpebral fissures and palmar creases normal; standard karyotype normal → DNA methylation analysis → Prader-Willi syndrome; methylation detects deletion, uniparental disomy and imprinting defects
  7. 5-week-old girl born at home with no newborn screen; increasingly sleepy, feeds poorly, constipated, still jaundiced; large tongue, umbilical hernia, wide posterior fontanelle; tone low, face otherwise typical, reflexes present → TSH and free T4 → Congenital hypothyroidism; start levothyroxine without waiting for imaging
  8. Newborn girl with trisomy 21 confirmed on karyotype, floppy but feeding with support; the parents ask which tests she will need in the coming weeks → Brain MRI → No consistent finding in Down syndrome; not indicated
  9. Newborn boy with the features of Down syndrome born to a 24 yo mother; karyotype shows 46 chromosomes with the extra chromosome 21 material joined to chromosome 14 → Karyotype of both parents → Translocation Down syndrome; a balanced carrier parent changes the recurrence risk
  10. 2-week-old with Down syndrome, feeding well and gaining weight; no murmur; pulse oximetry 98% in the right hand and in a foot → Echocardiogram now → Heart disease in about half, some silent; echo in the first month
  11. 3 yo boy with Down syndrome at a well visit; normal newborn screen, growing along his curve, no symptoms, normal examination → TSH level → Hypothyroidism can develop after a normal newborn screen
  12. 7 yo girl with Down syndrome and 3 weeks of neck pain, holding her head tilted, falling more often and new daytime wetting; brisk knee reflexes, sustained ankle clonus and upgoing toes → Atlantoaxial instability → Cord compression at C1-C2; urgent cervical spine imaging and neurosurgery
  13. 3-day-old with Down syndrome, feeding well and afebrile; liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin; white count 45,000 with 30% blasts, hemoglobin and platelets normal → Transient abnormal myelopoiesis → Transient myeloproliferative disorder; usually resolves on its own, but later leukemia risk calls for CBC follow-up
  14. 6 yo boy with intellectual disability, poor eye contact and hand flapping; long face, large protruding ears, lax finger joints and flat feet; his mother's brother also has intellectual disability; a karyotype last year was normal → FMR1 CGG repeat analysis → Fragile X syndrome; over 200 repeats; the mother carries at least a premutation
  15. 7-week-old boy, well until 3 days ago, now constipated with a weak cry, drooping eyelids, a poor suck and weakness spreading from the face to the arms; afebrile; the team plans empiric antibiotics while cultures are pending → Gentamicin → Infant botulism; aminoglycosides worsen neuromuscular blockade; botulism immune globulin
  16. 2-month-old girl with Down syndrome, lifting her head briefly and smiling socially; the parents ask what they should do now for her development → Early intervention referral → Referral at diagnosis, before any delay appears; an IEP follows at school entry
Pairs with Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers the trisomy feature map and the prenatal screen. Ask: are the hands clenched or open, and is the tone up or down? Part I Congenital Hypothyroidism covers the floppy infant found on the newborn screen. Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers the malformation syndromes without an aneuploidy. Part I Cerebral Palsy covers hypoxic-ischemic injury and its imaging. Part I The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant covers duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease in Down syndrome. Part II Abnormal Growth in a Child covers Turner syndrome in the short girl. Part I Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth covers the early intervention referral for delay.
Transferable rule For a floppy infant, first decide whether the problem is in the brain or the motor unit. An infant who is strong for the tone with normal reflexes has a central cause, often chromosomal. A weak infant with absent reflexes has a peripheral cause. Then send the genetic test for that level.
Unchecked attributeLow tone read as weakness without testing strength and reflexes, which is the step that separates central from peripheral causes.
Salient decoyA mother under 35 argues against Down syndrome, yet most affected infants are born to younger mothers.
Mirror twinPrader-Willi syndrome is as floppy as Down syndrome from birth but has almond-shaped eyes, small genitals and a normal karyotype.
Test-overrides-findingsA positive FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization) taken as the final answer, when only the karyotype shows a translocation that changes the parents’ recurrence risk.

Anaphylaxis

organ-system criteria · hypotension not required · mast cell mechanism · bradykinin angioedema · delayed drug reactionsHow many organ systems are involved, and how soon after the exposure?

Source vignette Pt — 12 yo M, 30 minutes of burning, swollen eyes, a scratchy, tight throat and crampy abdominal pain; seen earlier the same day for several days of sore throat and started on amoxicillin; no known drug allergies · Exam — T 37.2, BP 116/68, HR 92; bilateral periorbital swelling, mild conjunctival redness, scattered wheals on the trunk · Q — the pathogenesis of his symptoms; options spanned Epstein-Barr virus infection, immune complex formation, impaired bradykinin degradation, mast cell activation and systemic vasculitis
The decision point

Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis based on the number of organ systems involved and the time since exposure; hypotension is not required. Within minutes to hours of a likely allergen, skin or mucosal findings plus one more system (respiratory, gastrointestinal or cardiovascular) meet criteria. This boy has wheals and periorbital swelling (skin), throat tightness (respiratory) and cramps (gut) 30 minutes after amoxicillin. He therefore has anaphylaxis despite a normal blood pressure. The mechanism is IgE-mediated mast cell and basophil degranulation releasing histamine, prostaglandins and leukotrienes. A history of no known drug allergies does not argue against it. An earlier exposure sensitized him without a reaction, and re-exposure triggers the release.

The exception is angioedema without hives. Swelling of the lips, tongue, face or bowel wall with no wheals and no itch from an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor or hereditary angioedema is bradykinin-mediated. It builds over hours and responds poorly to epinephrine and antihistamines. Rashes that arrive days into a drug or an infection are delayed reactions, not anaphylaxis.

Defining criteria Anaphylaxis is likely with acute onset (minutes to hours) and any 1 of: · 1 — skin or mucosal involvement (hives, flushing, swollen lips, tongue or eyes) plus respiratory compromise or hypotension · 2 — 2 or more systems after a likely allergen: skin or mucosa, respiratory, cardiovascular, persistent gastrointestinal symptoms · 3 — hypotension alone after a known allergen for that patient
Anaphylaxis and its mimics — the differential
DiagnosisTiming after exposureMechanismThe NBME tell
AnaphylaxisMinutes to a few hoursIgE-mediated mast cell activation (type I)Skin plus a second system: wheeze, stridor, throat tightness, vomiting or cramps, hypotension
Acute urticaria aloneMinutes to hoursMast cell activation, often IgEHives and itch with no second system; normal airway, gut and blood pressure
Bradykinin angioedema (ACE inhibitor, hereditary angioedema)Hours; ACE inhibitor reactions can start months or years into therapyImpaired bradykinin degradation (ACE inhibitor); C1 inhibitor deficiency (hereditary, low C4)Lip, tongue or bowel-wall swelling with no hives or itch; little response to epinephrine or antihistamines
Serum sickness-like reaction5 to 14 days into a drugDelayed drug hypersensitivity; true serum sickness is immune complexUrticarial rash with fever, arthralgia and nodes
Epstein-Barr virus with an aminopenicillinDays into amoxicillinVirus-driven drug rash, not IgEMaculopapular rash with fever, exudative pharyngitis, posterior nodes, left upper quadrant pain
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritisDays to weeks after pharyngitisImmune complex (type III)Edema building over days with hypertension and cola-colored urine
Systemic vasculitis (IgA vasculitis)DaysImmune complex vessel inflammationPalpable purpura, fever, arthralgia, colicky abdominal pain
Vasovagal syncopeSeconds, with pain or fear (needles)Vagal surgeBradycardia, pallor and sweating; no hives, no wheeze
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo M, 30 minutes of burning, swollen eyes, a scratchy, tight throat and crampy abdominal pain; earlier today diagnosed with pharyngitis after several days of sore throat and started on amoxicillin; no known drug allergies; T 37.2, BP 116/68, HR 92; bilateral periorbital swelling, mild conjunctival redness, scattered wheals on the trunk → Mast cell activation → anaphylaxis: skin, respiratory and gastrointestinal involvement within 30 minutes of amoxicillin, after sensitization by an earlier course; intramuscular (IM) epinephrine
  2. 7 yo F at a birthday party, 10 minutes after eating a cookie made with peanut butter, develops hives on the face and trunk, wheezing and 2 episodes of vomiting; no previous reactions to food; T 37.0, BP 98/60, HR 128, RR 30, SpO2 94% on room air; diffuse expiratory wheezes → Intramuscular epinephrine → anaphylaxis by skin plus respiratory and gastrointestinal involvement; blood pressure need not fall
  3. 9 yo M, itchy raised wheals on the trunk and arms 1 hour after eating strawberries for the first time this season; no lip or tongue swelling, throat symptoms, cough, vomiting or abdominal pain; BP 104/66, HR 90, SpO2 99%; lungs clear; blanching urticarial plaques → Oral cetirizine → acute urticaria alone: one system, so criteria for anaphylaxis are not met
  4. 15 yo M treated in the emergency department for hives, throat tightness and wheezing 20 minutes after eating cashews, his first reaction to food; one dose of intramuscular epinephrine was given, and after 6 hours of observation he is asymptomatic with normal vital signs and clear lungs → Epinephrine autoinjector prescription → anaphylaxis, observed for a biphasic reaction; discharge with self-injectable epinephrine, an action plan, avoidance and allergy referral
  5. 58 yo M with hypertension and diabetes, 6 hours of progressive swelling of the lips and tongue; no itching, hives, wheezing or abdominal pain; takes lisinopril, which he started 2 years ago, and metformin; no new foods or medications; swelling did not improve after intramuscular epinephrine and diphenhydramine → Impaired bradykinin degradation → ACE inhibitor angioedema: no urticaria and little response to epinephrine; stop the ACE inhibitor permanently
  6. 16 yo F with recurrent episodes over 3 years of painless, nonpruritic swelling of the hands, face and once the throat, each lasting 2 to 3 days, and separate episodes of colicky abdominal pain with vomiting; no hives; takes no medications; her mother has similar episodes; antihistamines and epinephrine have not helped; examination between episodes is normal → Serum C4 level → hereditary angioedema from C1 inhibitor deficiency; low C4, bradykinin-mediated, so epinephrine disappoints
  7. 17 yo F, 5 days of fever, sore throat and fatigue, treated with amoxicillin for presumed strep pharyngitis; 4 days later, a diffuse, mildly itchy maculopapular rash on the trunk and limbs; T 38.4, BP 112/70; tonsillar exudates, tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, left upper quadrant tenderness; no wheals, no lip swelling, lungs clear → Infectious mononucleosis → an aminopenicillin rash during Epstein-Barr virus infection; not an IgE-mediated penicillin allergy
  8. 34 yo F with a known severe shellfish allergy becomes lightheaded 15 minutes after eating a dish she later learns contained shrimp; no rash, flushing, lip swelling, wheeze or vomiting; BP 76/44, HR 132, warm extremities; lungs clear → Anaphylaxis → hypotension alone after a known allergen meets criteria; give IM epinephrine
  9. 22 yo F with recurrent episodes since adolescence of painless, nonpruritic swelling of the lips and one hand lasting 2 to 3 days, the latest starting the day after a dental extraction; separate bouts of colicky abdominal pain with vomiting; no hives; takes a combined oral contraceptive and no other medications; her father has similar episodes; epinephrine and diphenhydramine in the emergency department did not help; serum C4 low → C1 inhibitor deficiency → hereditary angioedema: bradykinin-mediated swelling without urticaria; confirm with C1 inhibitor level and function
  10. 19 yo M with known hereditary angioedema, 4 hours of progressive swelling of the face and tongue with a hoarse voice after a facial injury in a basketball game; no stridor; SpO2 98% on room air; no hives; no improvement after intramuscular epinephrine and intravenous diphenhydramine → Intravenous C1 inhibitor concentrate → acute hereditary angioedema attack with laryngeal involvement: give specific therapy and be ready to secure the airway
  11. 45 yo F with hereditary angioedema, low C4 and a family history, now with blood pressure 152/96 on three separate visits; no diabetes or kidney disease → Lisinopril → ACE inhibitors block bradykinin breakdown and provoke attacks
Management First — IM epinephrine in the anterolateral thigh, 0.01 mg/kg of the 1 mg/mL solution (max 0.5 mg adult, 0.3 mg child); lie the patient flat with legs raised · Repeat — every 5 to 15 minutes if symptoms persist; persistent hypotension gets isotonic fluid boluses and then an epinephrine infusion; glucagon if the patient takes a beta-blocker · Adjuncts only — H1 and H2 antihistamines for itch and hives, albuterol for residual wheeze, glucocorticoids; none of them treats airway obstruction or shock, and none replaces or delays epinephrine · Observe — for a biphasic reaction, symptoms returning hours later without re-exposure; 1 symptom-free hour may be reasonable without severe risk features; extended observation up to 6 hours or longer, including admission, may be appropriate at higher risk · Discharge — epinephrine autoinjector with training and an action plan, avoidance of the trigger, and allergy referral
Hereditary angioedema Mechanism — autosomal dominant C1 inhibitor deficiency; unchecked kallikrein makes excess bradykinin · The tell — recurrent nonpitting swelling of the face, lips, limbs or bowel wall (colicky abdominal attacks) with no urticaria and no itch, often with a family history · Triggers — dental work, trauma, stress, estrogen (oral contraceptives, pregnancy) · Avoid — ACE inhibitors, which block bradykinin breakdown and worsen attacks · Tests — screen with C4 (low), confirm with C1 inhibitor level and function · Acute attack — secure the airway if the larynx is involved; give C1 inhibitor concentrate, icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor blocker) or ecallantide (kallikrein inhibitor); epinephrine, antihistamines and steroids do not work
Pearls Waiting for hypotension is a deadly delay; in children hypotension is a late sign. Throat tightness or wheeze with hives is enough to give epinephrine · Diagnosis is clinical; a serum tryptase drawn early can support mast cell activation afterward but never delays treatment · Bradykinin swelling is the one angioedema in which epinephrine works poorly. Stop the ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor for life, and check C4 when swelling recurs without a drug · Most childhood anaphylaxis is from food (peanut, tree nuts, milk, egg); insect stings and drugs such as beta-lactams follow
Pairs with Part II Fever and Rash in a Child covers the serum sickness-like reaction: did the hives start 5 to 14 days into the drug, with joint pain? Part I Transfusion Reactions covers anaphylaxis during transfusion: is the recipient IgA deficient? Aquifer Shock in Children covers anaphylactic shock as a distributive subtype: is perfusion abnormal? Part I Stool Changes in a Well Infant covers FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome), the non-IgE mimic: is it hours of vomiting without hives? Part I Childhood Vaccine Schedule and Contraindications covers anaphylaxis after a vaccine dose as a contraindication. Aquifer Child with Puffy Eyes places the acute allergic reaction among the other causes of swollen eyelids: is it one eye or both, and does the urine contain protein?
Transferable rule Skin or mucosal involvement plus any second system within minutes to hours of an exposure is anaphylaxis. Treat it with IM (intramuscular) epinephrine first. Swelling with no hives points to bradykinin. A rash that arrives days later points to a delayed drug or immune complex reaction.
Unchecked attributeImpaired bradykinin degradation: the swollen eyes suggest angioedema, but bradykinin swelling has no wheals or itch; he has wheals on the trunk plus throat and gut symptoms, which is mast cell release.
Unchecked attributeImmune complex formation: the sore throat invites poststreptococcal disease or serum sickness, but immune complexes take days to form; this began 30 minutes after the drug.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpstein-Barr virus infection: mononucleosis really does cause a rash after amoxicillin, but that rash is maculopapular, comes days later and brings fever and nodes; he is afebrile with wheals.
Salient decoySystemic vasculitis: crampy abdominal pain recalls IgA vasculitis, but vasculitis develops over days with fever and palpable purpura, not wheals within minutes.

Urinary Incontinence

stress, urge, overflow, fistula · the postvoid residual splits the differential · cough stress test · drug pairingsWhat is the postvoid residual, and which diagnosis does that number make impossible?

Source vignette Pt — woman with urinary leakage; no pelvic surgery, obstetric injury, malignancy or radiation · Labs — postvoid residual 800 mL · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned overflow, stress and urge incontinence and vesicovaginal fistula
The decision point

Postvoid residual 800 mL. Retention of 800 mL points to overflow incontinence. The PVR (postvoid residual) splits the entire differential before any symptom is weighed.

Fistula is not merely unsupported but mechanically impossible. A bladder draining continuously through a fistula cannot hold 800 mL. Two further findings exclude it. Fistula requires pelvic surgery, obstetric injury, malignancy, or radiation, and all are absent. Fistula shows urine pooling in the vagina, but the examination shows no abnormalities.

A positive cough stress test A positive cough stress test normally means stress incontinence. However, a chronically overdistended bladder leaks with any rise in intra-abdominal pressure, so the test loses specificity once the PVR (postvoid residual) is high. A positive test can fail to mean what it usually means, just as a negative test can fail to exclude. In each case, context sets a test's operating characteristics.
Urinary incontinence types
TypeMechanismPresentationPVRTreatment
StressUrethral hypermobility / sphincter deficiencyLeaks with cough, sneeze, liftingLowPelvic floor → pessary → midurethral sling

FunctionalCognitive or mobility barrierCan't reach the toilet; tract normalNormalScheduled toileting
FistulaAbnormal communicationContinuous leakage, vaginal urine poolingNormal/lowDye test, cystoscopy → repair
The causal chain & a drug pairing T1DM (type 1 diabetes mellitus) since age 6 causes diabetic autonomic neuropathy. The neuropathy causes detrusor underactivity and retention. Retention causes overflow leakage and the recurrent UTIs (urinary tract infections) from stasis. Oxybutynin treats urge incontinence and would worsen overflow. The same drug causes fecal impaction. Gut motility down, bladder emptying down: when oxybutynin appears on an elderly or diabetic patient's medication list, check both.

  3. 72 yo M, hesitancy and weak stream, PVR 350, enlarged prostate → Overflow incontinence from outlet obstruction → α-blocker ± 5-α-reductase inhibitor
  4. 28 yo F, continuous leakage two weeks after a difficult delivery, vaginal urine pooling → Vesicovaginal fistula
  5. 84 yo F with dementia, wets before reaching the bathroom, tract normal → Functional incontinence
  6. 68 yo F on oxybutynin with rising PVR and retention → Anticholinergic-induced retention → stop the drug
  7. 45 yo F, urgency and frequency with dysuria, pyuria and nitrites → Urinary tract infection → not chronic incontinence
  8. 40 yo F with multiple sclerosis, mixed retention and urgency → Neurogenic bladder → urodynamics
  9. 32 yo F, T1DM, PVR 800 → Screen for autonomic neuropathy → gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension and resting tachycardia
Boundary conditions A high PVR (postvoid residual) suggests that overflow is present, not that it is the only mechanism; mixed incontinence is common. A positive cough test may reflect a real coexisting stress component. A PVR is only interpretable when measured after a normal void. PVR thresholds in adults: under 50 mL argues against overflow; over 200 mL suggests overflow as a main contributor.
Transferable rule When a quantitative measure of organ function is given, check whether each candidate diagnosis is compatible with that number before weighing symptoms. Exclude a diagnosis the physiology forbids without arguing from symptoms.

Isolation Precautions

particle size · droplet, airborne or contact · gear and room · when it ends · neutropenic precautionsHow big is the particle, and who is being protected from whom?

Source vignette Pt — 8 mo M with fever and lethargy; BP 70/40; antibiotics started and admitted to the pediatric ICU (intensive care unit) · Labs — CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) Gram stain: gram-negative diplococci · Q — which isolation precautions to institute; options spanned airborne, contact, droplet, neutropenic and standard
The decision point

Choose the precaution by how the organism travels. Droplets are 5 microns or larger and fall within 3 to 6 feet, so a surgical mask within that range is enough. Droplet organisms include N. meningitidis, H. influenzae type b, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, influenza, adenovirus (plus contact for pneumonia) and pertussis. Airborne particles are under 5 microns and stay suspended, so they need an N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room. Airborne organisms include tuberculosis, measles, varicella and SARS (severe acute respiratory syndrome). Contact organisms spread by hands and surfaces and need a gown and gloves. They include MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), VRE (vancomycin-resistant enterococci), C. difficile, E. coli O157:H7 (diapered or incontinent), scabies and RSV (respiratory syncytial virus). Gram-negative diplococci in the CSF are meningococcus. This infant therefore needs droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective antibiotics.

Standard precautions apply to every patient, so they are never the added precaution. Neutropenic precautions protect the patient from the environment rather than others from the patient.

Defining criteria Droplet — particles 5 microns or larger, fall within 3 to 6 feet · Airborne — particles under 5 microns, remain suspended and travel on air currents · Contact — spread by direct touch or contaminated surfaces · Neutropenic (protective) — shields an immunocompromised patient, usually severe neutropenia (ANC (absolute neutrophil count) under 500)
Isolation precautions — the differential
PrecautionOrganismsGear and roomEnds when
StandardEvery patientHand hygiene; gloves, gown, mask or eye protection when contact with blood or body fluids is expectedNever; always in effect
DropletN. meningitidis, Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b), Mycoplasma, influenza, adenovirus (plus contact for pneumonia), pertussis, mumps, rubellaSurgical mask within 3 to 6 feet; private roomMeningococcus and Hib: 24 hours of effective antibiotics; pertussis: 5 days of effective antibiotics
AirborneTuberculosis, measles, SARS (plus droplet and contact)N95 respirator and a negative-pressure single room; nonimmune staff stay out of measles roomsTB (tuberculosis): improving clinically on therapy with 3 consecutive negative sputum AFB (acid-fast bacilli) smears; measles: 4 days after rash onset (duration of illness if immunocompromised)
Airborne plus contactVaricella, disseminated zosterN95 and negative-pressure room, plus gown and glovesAll lesions crusted
ContactMRSA, VRE, C. difficile, E. coli O157:H7 (diapered or incontinent), scabies, RSVGown and gloves; dedicated equipment; soap and water for C. difficile because alcohol does not kill sporesDuration of illness for C. difficile and RSV; scabies: 24 hours after effective therapy starts
NeutropenicProtects a patient with severe neutropenia (chemotherapy, stem cell transplant)Hand hygiene, private room with filtered air; no fresh flowers, plants or animals; no rectal thermometers, enemas or suppositoriesNeutrophil count recovers
Scenario bank
  1. 8 mo M with fever and lethargy; BP 70/40; lumbar puncture shows gram-negative diplococci on CSF Gram stain; intravenous antibiotics have been started, and he is being admitted to the pediatric ICU → Droplet precautions → Neisseria meningitidis: surgical mask within 3 to 6 feet until 24 hours of effective antibiotics
  2. 2 yo M, unvaccinated, 4 days of fever to 40 C, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, then a maculopapular rash that began at the hairline and spread to the trunk; small gray-white spots on the buccal mucosa; admitted for dehydration → Airborne precautions → measles: N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room
  3. 4 mo F admitted with 3 days of cough, rhinorrhea and increased work of breathing, SpO2 88% on room air; diffuse crackles and wheezes; nasal swab positive for respiratory syncytial virus → Contact precautions → RSV spreads mainly by hands and contaminated surfaces: gown and gloves
  4. 48 yo M with 2 months of cough, night sweats and weight loss, admitted with an upper lobe cavity on chest radiograph; sputum smear positive for acid-fast bacilli; four-drug therapy and airborne isolation were started 3 days ago → Three negative sputum AFB smears → active pulmonary TB: airborne isolation ends when the patient is improving clinically on effective therapy and three consecutive sputum smears are negative
  5. 3 yo F admitted with cellulitis of the thigh complicating chickenpox that began 3 days ago; several vesicles on the trunk and scalp have not yet crusted; T 38.9 → Airborne and contact precautions → varicella: N95, negative-pressure room, gown and gloves until every lesion has crusted
  6. 6 yo F with acute lymphoblastic leukemia admitted during induction chemotherapy; afebrile; absolute neutrophil count 200/mm3; placed in a private room under neutropenic precautions → Rectal temperature measurement → neutropenic precautions protect the patient: no rectal thermometers, enemas or suppositories, no fresh flowers or plants
  7. 8 yo M on clindamycin for an abscess develops 6 watery stools a day and cramping; stool PCR (polymerase chain reaction) positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin; admitted for dehydration → Contact precautions with soap-and-water hand washing → alcohol-based rubs do not kill C. difficile spores
Management Meningococcal disease — droplet precautions for the first 24 hours of effective antibiotics, plus chemoprophylaxis (rifampin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone) for close contacts: household, day care, and anyone exposed to oral secretions; staff need it only after unprotected exposure such as intubation without a mask · Suspected TB or measles — airborne isolation before the workup or treatment; a patient who must leave the room wears a surgical mask
Pearls Adenovirus pneumonia needs droplet plus contact precautions; RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) needs contact precautions · For C. difficile, the hand-hygiene method matters: alcohol rub fails against spores · The 24-hour rule applies to meningococcus and Hib. TB isolation ends with clinical improvement and 3 consecutive negative smears, and varicella isolation ends with crusting · A patient with a rash and fever of unknown cause gets airborne and contact precautions until measles and varicella are excluded
Pairs with Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) grid, the organism by age and chemoprophylaxis: who counts as a close contact? Part II Fever and Rash in a Child covers measles and varicella, including postexposure prophylaxis: is the contact immune, and how long since exposure? Part I Tuberculosis covers the latent-versus-active distinction: is the radiograph abnormal or are there symptoms? Part II Scabies covers the contact-spread rash whose treatment includes the household.
Transferable rule Pick the precaution by the particle and the route. Large droplets that fall within 6 feet need a surgical mask. Small particles that hang in the air need an N95 and a negative-pressure room. Organisms on skin, stool or surfaces need a gown and gloves. Neutropenic precautions protect the patient rather than the staff.
Unchecked attributeAirborne precautions: the right idea, a respiratory route, with the wrong particle size; meningococcus travels in large droplets that fall within 3 to 6 feet, and airborne isolation is for TB, measles and varicella.
Salient decoyContact precautions: a septic, possibly petechial infant in the ICU feels like a gown-and-gloves patient, but meningococcus spreads by respiratory droplets, not by skin or surfaces.
True-fact-wrong-slotStandard precautions: they apply to every patient, including this one, but they are the baseline, not the transmission-based precaution the organism requires.
Unchecked attributeNeutropenic precautions: the direction is reversed; they protect an immunocompromised patient, and this infant is the source of infection.

edits.html:
Abnormal Growth in a Child

short stature and growth velocity · faltering weight · normal variants, endocrine, nutritional and genetic causesIs velocity normal, which parameter fell first, and what is the bone age?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Velocity matters more than the percentile. A low, steady channel is a normal variant; height crossing 2 or more major percentile lines downward is growth failure.

Then ask which parameter fell first:

  • Weight first, length and head preserved: inadequate intake (up to 80%, mostly psychosocial), malabsorption or increased demand.
  • Height first, weight preserved or rising: endocrine (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, glucocorticoid excess).
  • All three from birth: genetic, congenital infection or intrauterine insult.

Bone age comes first among tests: delayed means growth potential remains; advanced means sex steroid exposure.

Choose a rare organic cause over inadequate intake only when a symptom, sign or admission supports it.

Diagnosis
Defining criteria Short stature – height at or below the 2nd percentile for age and sex · Faltering weight – weight below the 2nd percentile, or crossing 2 or more major percentile lines downward · Not pathologic – catch-up growth in a preterm infant; shifts toward genetic potential in the first 2 years · Midparental height – average of the parents' heights, plus 6.5 cm for a boy or minus 6.5 cm for a girl
Short stature: the differential
CauseVelocityWeightBone ageThe tell
Familial or idiopathicNormal, low channelProportionateNormalShort parents; puberty on time
Constitutional delayNormal, low channelProportionateDelayedLate puberty; a parent who bloomed late; normal adult height
Hypothyroidism (usually Hashimoto)FallsPreservedDelayedFatigue, bradycardia, constipation, cold intolerance, goiter; no breasts but pubic hair
Growth hormone deficiencyFallsPreserved, chubbyDelayedLow IGF-1; neonatal hypoglycemia or micropenis; midline defects, cranial irradiation, sellar mass
Glucocorticoid excessFallsRisesDelayedOral steroids for asthma or nephrotic syndrome; central obesity, striae, hypertension
Malnutrition, celiac, IBD (inflammatory bowel disease), chronic illnessFalls after weightFalls firstDelayedPoor intake, diarrhea, abdominal pain, iron deficiency, raised ESR
Turner syndromeSlows through childhoodProportionateNormal to mildly delayedAny short girl, even without features; webbed neck, broad chest, absent breasts with pubic hair
Skeletal dysplasia (achondroplasia), Down syndromeLow from early childhoodDysplasia: short limbsNot the deciding testDysmorphic features: genetic diagnosis before endocrine tests
Precocious puberty or adrenal tumorAccelerated: tall now, short adultProportionateAdvancedEarly breasts or testes, or virilization (clitoromegaly, acne, voice change)
Faltering weight: the organic causes Cystic fibrosis – steatorrhea, recurrent respiratory infection, abnormal newborn screen · Congenital heart disease – sweating and tachypnea with feeds, murmur, hepatomegaly; limits feeding and activity · Metabolic disease – hypoglycemia, acidosis, regression, prior admissions · Renal tubular acidosis or chronic kidney disease – polyuria and polydipsia, length also low; normal anion gap acidosis, low potassium, urine pH above 5.5 in distal renal tubular acidosis · Psychosocial – food insecurity, feeding technique, neglect, caregiver depression · Head circumference – spared longest; a fallen head means prolonged severe deprivation or a non-nutritional cause
Breasts versus pubic hair Breasts – need gonadotropins and ovarian estrogen · Pubic hair – needs only adrenal androgens · Tanner 1 breasts with pubic hair – hypothyroidism (suppressed gonadotropins, delayed bone age, bradycardia) or Turner syndrome (ovarian failure, high FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone)); Hashimoto is common in Turner, so both can coexist
Management and treatment
By diagnosis Normal variants – reassurance and serial heights; no hormone treatment · Inadequate intake – caloric supplementation with serial weights; catch-up growth is the treatment and the confirmation · Hypothyroidism – levothyroxine; catch-up growth and puberty resume · Growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome – growth hormone through an endocrinologist · Glucocorticoid excess – lowest effective dose; inhaled rather than oral steroids for asthma
Practice
  1. 14-year-old girl, increasingly tired, in bed right after dinner height down ≥2 major percentiles to the 2nd weight near 50th Picky, 3 meals BP 110/70 mm Hg · HR 52/min · breasts Tanner 1, pubic hair Tanner 4 · bone age markedly delayed → Acquired hypothyroidism → falling velocity with weight preserved, a delayed bone age, fatigue and bradycardia: acquired hypothyroidism; suppressed gonadotropins keep the breasts at Tanner 1 while adrenal androgens drive pubic hair; check TSH and free T4, then levothyroxine
  2. 7-year-old boy is seen for slowing growth height fell from the 50th to the 10th percentile over 2 years weight stayed at the 50th No headaches, visual change, abdominal pain or diarrhea Vital signs normal · prepubertal · neurologic exam normal → Bone age radiograph → pathologic velocity with weight preserved suggests an endocrine cause; bone age comes first, then TSH, free T4 and IGF-1
  3. 9-year-old boy has height at the 3rd percentile same channel since age 2 weight at the 3rd percentile, also steady since age 2 Mother 152 cm, father 163 cm Well, examination normal · prepubertal genitalia · bone age equal to chronologic age → Familial short stature → normal velocity and normal bone age with short parents is familial short stature: adult height will match midparental height; not faltering growth
  4. 14-year-old boy has height at the 3rd percentile growing about 5 cm a year, same channel since early childhood testes prepubertal His father's growth spurt came at 16; no chronic symptoms Afebrile · examination normal · bone age 11.5 years → Reassurance and serial height measurements → normal velocity, delayed bone age and late puberty with a late-blooming parent is constitutional delay: reassurance and serial heights; catch-up follows
  5. 11-year-old girl's height is below the 2nd percentile velocity slowing over 3 years weight 25th percentile Mother 165 cm, father 178 cm Breasts Tanner 1, sparse pubic hair · no dysmorphic features · thyroid tests, blood count, ESR and celiac serology normal → Karyotype → Turner syndrome is possible in any short girl, even without dysmorphic features: karyotype
  6. 8-year-old boy's weight fell from the 50th to 5th percentile in 18 months height fell from the 50th to 25th in 6 months intermittent abdominal pain, bloating, loose stools Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, ferritin low · bone age delayed → Tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody → weight falling before height points to malabsorption: tissue transglutaminase IgA for celiac disease, sent with total IgA
  7. 9-year-old boy with severe asthma: 6 prednisone courses this year height fell from the 50th to the 10th over 2 years weight rose from the 75th to 95th Takes it between courses Round face, purple abdominal striae · BP 95th percentile → Glucocorticoid excess → height falling while weight rises on repeated oral steroids is glucocorticoid excess (iatrogenic Cushing syndrome); use the lowest dose and inhaled steroids
  8. 15-month-old boy, 4.3 kg at term birth, mother with gestational diabetes length drifted from the 90th to the 25th over year 1, then held 3 months Mother 157 cm, father 168 cm Weight-for-length 50th percentile · milestones met · examination normal → Reassurance and routine growth monitoring → a percentile shift toward genetic potential in the first 2 years is normal: reassurance and routine growth monitoring
  9. 4-year-old boy has height below the 1st percentile since infancy growing steadily along that channel short arms and legs relative to the trunk Large head, frontal bossing, flat nasal bridge Afebrile · development and intelligence normal → Achondroplasia → a dysmorphic, disproportionate child goes down the genetic branch first: achondroplasia
  10. 15-month-old boy has weight at the 2nd percentile length at the 30th, head circumference at the 40th active, keeps up with peers, eats well at daycare Never hospitalized Afebrile · examination normal → Inadequate caloric intake from psychosocial causes → weight alone low with length and head preserved is inadequate intake, most often psychosocial; heart disease would limit feeding and activity
  11. 15-month-old boy is evaluated for poor weight gain weight low; length and head circumference preserved no diarrhea, cough or sweating with feeds Lives with his mother, who works nights Afebrile · examination normal → Detailed diet history and observed feeding → in a well child with a normal exam, broad testing has very low yield: a detailed diet history and observed feeding come first
  12. 4-year-old girl has height at the 3rd percentile weight at the 40th percentile height crossed down from the 25th over 2 years Eats well; no diarrhea Afebrile · examination normal · bone age delayed → Growth hormone deficiency or hypothyroidism → a short child heavy for height has an endocrine cause until shown otherwise: height falls more than weight, the inverse of malnutrition
  13. 8-month-old boy has weight, length and head circumference below the 2nd percentile small for all three since birth microcephaly and dysmorphic features Born small for gestational age at term Afebrile · feeding well, observed intake adequate → Genetic or intrauterine cause → all three parameters low from the outset is symmetric restriction: a genetic or intrauterine cause
  14. 6-month-old girl has poor weight gain bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools two admissions for pneumonia Feeds eagerly, never satisfied T 37.2 °C · respiratory rate 40/min · crackles at both bases · weight below the 2nd percentile → Sweat chloride testing → malabsorption with recurrent lung infection is cystic fibrosis: sweat chloride
  15. 3-month-old boy has poor weight gain sweats and breathes fast during feeds harsh holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border Tires before finishing a bottle respiratory rate 62/min · liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin → Echocardiography → sweating and tachypnea with feeds and a murmur point to congenital heart disease raising caloric demand: echocardiography
  16. 14-month-old girl has poor weight gain drinks constantly and wets many diapers length also at the 3rd percentile No vomiting or diarrhea; eats well Afebrile · BP normal · examination otherwise normal · weight below the 2nd percentile → Serum electrolytes with a venous blood gas → polyuria with length also low points to renal tubular acidosis: electrolytes with a venous blood gas for a normal anion gap acidosis
  17. 15-month-old boy is seen 4 weeks after starting caloric supplementation had isolated low weight, normal length and head now gaining well with family support Eating eagerly at home and daycare Afebrile · weight up 600 g → Continue outpatient management with close follow-up → catch-up growth on adequate calories confirms inadequate intake and is the treatment: continue outpatient care with close follow-up
Pairs with Puberty: is the bone age delayed in a late bloomer? Primary Amenorrhea: the Turner branch; is there a uterus, and is the FSH high? Brain Tumors in a Child: growth failure from a craniopharyngioma; headache, papilledema, a visual field defect? Puberty: the advanced bone age; central or peripheral? Follow-Up of the Preterm Infant: proportionate parameters, normal growth Feeding an Infant or Toddler: the refusal pattern, not calories
Transferable rule

Judge a growth problem by velocity first, then by which parameter fell first, then by bone age. When one common cause competes with several rare ones, the rare one needs a symptom, sign or admission behind it.

Wilson Disease

copper and ATP7B · liver plus brain, eye or red cells · ceruloplasmin, slit lamp, urine copper · chelation or transplantDoes unexplained liver disease come with brain, eye or red-cell findings, and is the ceruloplasmin low?

Source vignette Pt — adolescent with liver disease (hepatitis, possibly progressing to cirrhosis) plus neuropsychiatric change: tremor, slurred speech and altered behavior · Exam — Kayser-Fleischer rings at the corneal margin · Labs — elevated transaminases · Q — the most likely underlying mechanism of the disease
The decision point

Think of Wilson disease in any patient with unexplained liver disease. Think of it especially when liver disease comes with neuropsychiatric signs (tremor, dysarthria, dystonia, depression, personality change, psychosis), Kayser-Fleischer rings, or a Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia. Screen with serum ceruloplasmin (low) and a slit-lamp exam. A high 24-hour urine copper confirms the diagnosis, and liver biopsy copper settles cases where the tests disagree.

Wilson disease is autosomal recessive loss of ATP7B, the hepatocyte transporter that loads copper onto ceruloplasmin and excretes the excess into bile. Copper builds up in the liver (hepatitis, cirrhosis, sometimes acute liver failure). It then spills into the blood and deposits in the basal ganglia, the cornea and red cells. Ceruloplasmin is low because it is unstable without its copper. In patients with liver disease alone, Kayser-Fleischer rings are often absent. Ceruloplasmin can also read normal in these patients because it rises with inflammation. The urine copper or the liver biopsy then makes the diagnosis.

Unexplained liver disease: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellWhy less likely here
Wilson diseaseAutosomal recessive; child, teen or young adult; hepatitis, cirrhosis or acute liver failure, with movement or psychiatric changeKayser-Fleischer rings, low ceruloplasmin, Coombs-negative hemolysisThe key: the only one that adds brain, eye and red-cell findings to the liver
Autoimmune hepatitisYoung woman, often with another autoimmune disease; acute or chronic hepatitisAntinuclear antibody (ANA) and anti-smooth muscle antibody (anti-LKM1 in children), high IgGNo neurologic signs or corneal rings; Wilson can mimic it, so check ceruloplasmin
Hereditary hemochromatosisAutosomal recessive HFE; iron builds for decades, so middle-aged men and women after menopauseHigh transferrin saturation and ferritin; diabetes, bronze skin, arthropathy, cardiomyopathy, hypogonadismToo young; iron does not cause tremor or corneal rings
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiencyMisfolded protein retained in hepatocytes; neonatal cholestasis in infants, cirrhosis in adults, early basal emphysemaLow serum alpha-1 antitrypsin; lung disease in a young smokerIts second organ is the lung, not the brain or eye
Viral hepatitisMost common cause; risk factors for hepatitis B or C, or an acute illness with hepatitis APositive serologiesNo neuropsychiatric signs or corneal rings; hemolysis is not a feature
MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease)Obesity, diabetes, dyslipidemia; mild alanine aminotransferase (ALT)-predominant riseMetabolic syndrome with a hyperechoic liver; a diagnosis of exclusionNothing outside the liver
Antipsychotic-induced parkinsonismTremor, rigidity or dystonia after starting a dopamine blockerMovement signs follow the drug; liver tests normalDoes not explain the liver disease
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Liver tests: aspartate aminotransferase (AST), ALT, bilirubin, international normalized ratio (INR)FirstHepatocellular rise, from mild to acute liver failureLiver injury; the pattern alone does not name the cause
Hepatitis serologies, iron studies, ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody, alpha-1 antitrypsin levelFirstNormalExcludes the common mimics
Serum ceruloplasminScreenLow, below the lower limit of normal (usually about 20 mg/dL)Wilson disease; a normal value does not exclude it in active hepatitis, because ceruloplasmin is an acute-phase reactant
Slit-lamp examinationNextKayser-Fleischer ringsCorneal copper; almost always present with neurologic disease, often absent with liver disease alone
24-hour urine copperConfirmsHigh, typically over 100 mcg per day when symptomatic; over 40 mcg/day may indicate it in children or asymptomatic patientsCopper overflow from an overloaded liver; also used to monitor chelation
Liver biopsy with copper measurementBy branchHigh hepatic copperWhen ceruloplasmin, urine copper and the slit-lamp exam disagree
Complete blood count (CBC), reticulocytes, direct Coombs testSupportsAnemia, high reticulocytes, Coombs negativeCopper damages red cells; with acute liver failure, fulminant Wilson disease
Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)SupportsBasal ganglia signal changeNeurologic involvement; not needed for the diagnosis
Scenario bank
  1. 16 yo M with several months of fatigue and mild jaundice, a new hand tremor, slurred speech and irritability with falling grades; elevated AST and ALT; golden-brown rings at the corneal margins on slit-lamp exam → Defective copper transport in hepatocytes → Wilson disease: ATP7B failure blocks biliary copper excretion and copper loading onto ceruloplasmin, so copper deposits in the liver, basal ganglia and cornea
  2. 19 yo F with 3 months of fatigue and a fine hand tremor; ALT 240, AST 190, bilirubin normal; hepatitis B and C serologies negative; ferritin and transferrin saturation normal; ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody negative; normal body mass index and no alcohol use → Serum ceruloplasmin → screen for Wilson disease in a young patient with unexplained hepatitis and a tremor; slit-lamp exam and 24-hour urine copper follow
  3. 17 yo F with Hashimoto thyroiditis and 6 weeks of fatigue, joint aches and jaundice; ALT 850, AST 700; serum IgG high; ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody positive; ceruloplasmin normal; no Kayser-Fleischer rings; normal neurologic exam → Autoimmune hepatitis → corticosteroids, with azathioprine to spare steroids
  4. 21 yo M with 1 year of hand tremor and dysarthria; compensated cirrhosis on imaging, INR 1.3, no ascites or encephalopathy; ceruloplasmin low, 24-hour urine copper high, Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam → Oral penicillamine → symptomatic Wilson disease: lifelong chelation (penicillamine or trientine), zinc later for maintenance
  5. 18 yo F with 1 week of jaundice, now confused; INR 3.2; hemoglobin 7.8 with high reticulocytes and a negative direct Coombs test; Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam; no acetaminophen ingestion → Urgent liver transplantation → fulminant Wilson disease: acute liver failure with Coombs-negative hemolysis does not recover with chelation alone
  6. 14 yo M, asymptomatic, whose 17-year-old sister was just diagnosed with Wilson disease; normal growth and development; normal physical and neurologic exam → Serum ceruloplasmin and liver tests → siblings carry a 1 in 4 risk; add a slit-lamp exam and 24-hour urine copper, and treat presymptomatic disease with zinc
  7. 24 yo M with Wilson disease treated with penicillamine for 3 years; tremor resolved, liver tests now normal, urine copper at target; asks about coming off medication → Stopping copper-lowering therapy → treatment is lifelong; stopping can precipitate acute liver failure
Management Symptomatic disease — copper chelation with penicillamine or trientine, lifelong, with a low-copper diet (avoid shellfish, organ meats, nuts, chocolate and mushrooms) · Maintenance or presymptomatic disease — zinc, which blocks intestinal copper absorption · Fulminant liver failure — urgent liver transplantation, which corrects the liver defect · Family — screen first-degree relatives, siblings above all (a 1 in 4 chance of disease, since it is autosomal recessive), with ceruloplasmin, liver tests and a slit-lamp exam · Never stop — stopping therapy can precipitate acute liver failure
Pearls Psychiatric change or falling school performance can precede the liver findings. A young patient with new psychiatric illness and abnormal liver tests needs a ceruloplasmin · Acute liver failure with a Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia in a teen or young adult is fulminant Wilson disease. It needs a transplant center, not chelation alone · A presumed autoimmune hepatitis in a young patient should have ceruloplasmin checked before steroids · Serum total copper is usually low; urine copper is high
Pairs with Part I Fatty Liver Disease lists Wilson disease among the exclusions: is there tremor or Kayser-Fleischer rings, and is the ceruloplasmin low? Part I Abnormal Liver Tests places Wilson in the hepatocellular pattern: are the transaminases, not the alkaline phosphatase, leading? Part II Hemolytic Anemia covers the other Coombs-negative hemolysis of the young: are there spherocytes and an affected parent, or liver disease with corneal rings? Part I Tick-Borne Illness holds the acute mimic: did confusion with transaminitis arrive over hours with fever and a rash, or over months with a tremor?
Transferable rule When unexplained liver disease comes with a finding outside the liver, identify the organ. Brain, cornea or red cells point to copper, and the lung points to alpha-1 antitrypsin. The pancreas, skin, joints and heart in an older patient point to iron.
Class-vs-memberIncreased intestinal iron absorption: the right class, an inherited metal overload of the liver, but the wrong metal; HFE hemochromatosis presents in middle age with diabetes, skin and joint findings, never tremor or corneal rings.
Unchecked attributeHepatocyte retention of a misfolded protease inhibitor: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is an inherited liver disease of the young, but its second organ is the lung; it does not explain neuropsychiatric signs or Kayser-Fleischer rings.

Cervical Cancer Screening

age gates, coverage clocks, abnormal results and special populations · eligibility depends on age, not on individual riskIs she eligible yet, which clock is running, and what does the result call for?

SchedulePracticeResults and special populations
Bottom line

Screening starts at 21 whatever the sexual history: risk factors adjust intensity within the eligible window but rarely move the floor. Each negative test then starts its own interval, the test type sets its length, and screening is due when the longest valid coverage expires.

  • Age-21 floor: no screening under 21, regardless of sexual debut, partners, sexually transmitted infection (STI) history or human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination.
  • Why the floor ignores risk: HPV infection in adolescents is near-universal and clears in about 90% within 2 years; progression takes more than a decade, so cancer under 21 is rare. Early screening finds transient infection and leads to excisions by loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) that raise preterm-birth risk: harm without benefit.
  • Coverage clock: negative cytology covers 3 years from that date; a negative test that includes HPV covers 5.
  • Primary HPV testing: an HPV test alone. Co-testing: cytology plus HPV.
  • Self-collection: patient-collected HPV testing should be offered as an option at 30 to 65 at average risk, per the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), accepted December 2025; the American Cancer Society (ACS) repeats a negative self-collected test in 3 years.
  • Adequate prior screening: 3 consecutive negative cytology results or 2 consecutive negative co-tests within 10 years before stopping, the most recent within 5 years.
Schedule
Cervical screening schedule (average risk)
AgeTestInterval
Under 21None, whatever the sexual historyNot applicable
21 to 29Cytology aloneEvery 3 years
30 to 65Primary HPV, preferred by HRSA; clinician- or patient-collectedEvery 5 years
30 to 65, alternativesCo-testing; cytology alone5 years; 3 years
Older than 65Stop after adequate prior screening, if not otherwise at high risk and no CIN2 (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2) or worse in 25 yearsNot applicable
Primary HPV start age: exam answer versus clinical practice Exam answer: the US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) 2018 statement, still final (the 2024 draft is not), keeps cytology alone at 21 to 29 and offers primary HPV from 30, as question banks do. Answer 30 on the exam.
Clinical practice: the ACS starts screening at 25, not 21, and recommends primary HPV every 5 years through 65, with co-testing every 5 years or cytology every 3 if primary HPV testing is not available; the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) keeps the start at 21 and advises that primary HPV every 5 years can be considered for average-risk patients aged 25 to 29.
Practice
  1. 20-year-old woman asks whether she needs a Pap test Sexual debut at 15; five lifetime male partners Uses condoms inconsistently; no symptoms normal external genitalia T 36.7 °C · BP 114/70 mm Hg → No screening → she is below the floor: screening is not recommended under 21, and her debut, partners and condom use raise HPV exposure but none lowers the starting age. Cytology now or co-testing now would find transient infection that clears in about 90% within 2 years, and the excisions that follow raise preterm-birth risk
  2. 18-year-old woman seen to start care 2 weeks after a positive HIV test Sexually active since 15; two lifetime partners Uses condoms inconsistently pelvic examination normal T 36.8 °C · BP 112/70 mm Hg → Begin at 21 as usual → HIV does not lower the start age: invasive cancer incidence with HIV under 25 is exceedingly low, so screening starts at 21, per the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). From 21, cytology yearly, then every 3 years after 3 consecutive normal results, for life. Screening now follows the older Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) 2021 rule (1 year after sexual debut); 25 is the American Cancer Society start for average risk, not HIV
  3. 20-year-old woman has had postcoital bleeding for 2 months Sexually active; not yet screened because of her age exophytic friable mass on the cervix Afebrile · BP 116/70 mm Hg · urine pregnancy test negative → Biopsy the lesion → a visible lesion is biopsied at any age, including under 21: that is diagnosis, not screening, so the age floor does not apply. Cytology is a screening test, not the diagnosis of a visible lesion, and reassurance ignores the lesion
  4. 21-year-old woman comes for her first well-woman visit Has never been sexually active Asks whether she can wait until she has a partner No symptoms; no medical problems normal external genitalia T 36.6 °C · BP 108/66 mm Hg → Cytology now → the US Preventive Services Task Force rule is age-based, not activity-based: it applies to anyone with a cervix regardless of sexual history, so cytology every 3 years starts at 21. Starting at 25 is the American Cancer Society guideline, not the exam answer
  5. 28-year-old woman asks when her next Pap test is due Cytology 2 years ago was normal; HPV testing was not done No symptoms; no abnormal results ever Afebrile · BP 118/76 mm Hg → Return in 1 year → from 21 to 29 the schedule is cytology alone every 3 years, counted from the last negative test, so she is due in 1 year. A 3-year wait restarts the clock from today, and co-testing belongs to the 30 to 65 options
  6. 26-year-old woman's routine cytology shows atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US) Reflex HPV test on the same sample is negative No previous abnormal results; no symptoms Afebrile · BP 112/68 mm Hg → Resume routine screening → HPV-negative ASC-US with an unknown history can return at 3 years (ASCCP), which at 26 is her routine cytology interval. Colposcopy is for HPV-positive ASC-US, and the negative HPV test already removes the reason for an early repeat
  7. 24-year-old woman's routine cytology shows atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US) Previous cytology at 21 was normal No symptoms; one male partner normal cervix on speculum exam Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg → Repeat cytology in 1 year → under 25, repeat cytology at 1 year is preferred for ASC-US, per the American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology (ASCCP); reflex HPV testing is acceptable, and a negative result resumes routine screening. Colposcopy is indicated only if the first 1-year repeat shows a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL), atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL (ASC-H), atypical glandular cells (AGC) or AIS, or the second shows ASC-US or worse; immediate colposcopy over-treats lesions that usually clear, and a 3-year wait skips the 1-year recheck
  8. 34-year-old woman asks when her next screening test is due Co-test 3 years ago: cytology negative, HPV negative No symptoms; no abnormal results ever normal speculum exam Afebrile · HR 72/min · BP 120/78 mm Hg → Return in 2 years → a negative test that includes HPV covers 5 years from that date, so the 5-year clock governs and she is due in 2 years. Returning now applies the 3-year cytology clock, and 3 more years restarts the clock from today
  9. 34-year-old woman has routine co-testing Cytology: negative for intraepithelial lesion High-risk HPV positive; genotyping shows HPV 16 Prior screening normal; no symptoms normal cervix on speculum exam Afebrile · BP 116/74 mm Hg → Colposcopy → HPV 16 or 18 escalates even with negative cytology: colposcopy is recommended now. A 1-year repeat is for HPV positivity without 16 or 18, and 5 years is for a fully negative co-test
  10. 33-year-old woman has routine co-testing Cytology: negative for intraepithelial lesion High-risk HPV positive; genotyping negative for HPV 16 and 18 Previous screening unknown; no symptoms normal cervix on exam Afebrile · BP 114/72 mm Hg → Repeat co-test in 1 year → HPV positive with NILM (negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy) cytology and an unknown history: repeat HPV-based testing in 1 year (ASCCP). Colposcopy now is for HPV 16 or 18, and 5 years ignores the positive HPV test
  11. 33-year-old woman has co-testing at a new clinic Cytology negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy HPV positive; genotyping shows HPV 18 Last screened 6 years ago, normal T 36.7 °C · BP 110/72 mm Hg → Colposcopy → the genotype escalates: HPV 18 with negative cytology goes to colposcopy now, as HPV 16 does (ASCCP). Repeat co-testing in 1 year is for HPV positive, not 16 or 18; 5 years is for a fully negative co-test
  12. 26-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation has her first prenatal visit Last cytology, 2 years ago, was negative No HPV test was done with it No symptoms; no abnormal results ever T 36.9 °C · BP 110/70 mm Hg → Return in 1 year → pregnancy does not change the schedule: pregnant patients are screened at the same intervals as those who are not. Negative cytology covers 3 years from that date, so she returns in 1 year. Waiting 3 years from today stretches the interval, and co-testing is a 30 to 65 option on the exam (the American Cancer Society allows HPV-based testing, including co-testing, from 25, but her cytology still covers her until next year)
  13. 38-year-old woman's routine cytology shows atypical glandular cells (AGC) Regular menses; no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding Not pregnant; no previous abnormal results normal cervix on speculum exam Afebrile · BP 122/78 mm Hg · urine pregnancy test negative → Colposcopy with endocervical and endometrial sampling → every subcategory of AGC gets colposcopy regardless of the HPV result, with endocervical sampling; at 35 or older endometrial sampling is added. Repeat cytology and HPV testing alone both leave a glandular lesion unsampled
  14. 67-year-old woman asks whether she still needs Pap tests Three consecutive negative cytology results, at 58, 61 and 64 No history of cervical precancer or abnormal results Afebrile · BP 128/80 mm Hg → Stop screening → older than 65 with adequate prior screening (3 consecutive negative cytology results within 10 years, the most recent within 5) and no high-grade history, she stops. Once the exit criteria are met, the USPSTF recommends against further screening, so neither co-testing every 5 years nor a final test at 70
  15. 34-year-old woman's routine cytology shows a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) Not pregnant; no previous abnormal results No symptoms normal-appearing cervix on speculum exam T 36.8 °C · BP 118/74 mm Hg · urine pregnancy test negative → Colposcopy, or immediate excision → nonpregnant and 25 or older, she may have colposcopy with biopsy or excision without prior biopsy (see-and-treat LEEP); excision is preferred when the immediate CIN3+ risk is 60% or more, and both are acceptable from 25% to under 60%. Repeat cytology delays a high-grade result, and reflex HPV is the triage for ASC-US
  16. 67-year-old woman asks whether she can stop Pap tests Excision for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2, 10 years ago Every test since treatment negative No symptoms; postmenopausal Afebrile · BP 132/82 mm Hg → Keep screening → after treatment for CIN2+ (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse), surveillance with HPV testing or co-testing every 3 years runs at least 25 years, even past 65; 15 years remain. The age-65 exit applies only to women not otherwise at high risk
  17. 42-year-old woman had a total hysterectomy for fibroids 1 year ago Cervix removed; pathology benign No history of cervical precancer; screening always normal No symptoms healed vaginal cuff on exam Afebrile · BP 124/80 mm Hg → Stop screening → with the cervix removed for benign disease and no high-grade lesion in her history, screening stops. Vaginal cuff testing continues only after CIN2, CIN3 or adenocarcinoma in situ diagnosed within the previous 20 years (CDC), or after cervical cancer; a retained cervix keeps the usual schedule
Abnormal results and special populations
Abnormal result management by age (ASCCP 2019, risk-based)
ResultAge 25 or olderAge 21 to 24
ASC-USReflex HPV: positive, colposcopy; negative, can return at 3 yearsRepeat cytology in 1 year (preferred); reflex HPV acceptable
LSILColposcopy if HPV positive or untested; HPV negative, repeat in 1 yearRepeat cytology in 1 year
ASC-H (atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL)Colposcopy regardless of HPVColposcopy
HSIL (high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion)Colposcopy or excision without biopsy (see-and-treat LEEP)Colposcopy only
AGC (atypical glandular cells)Colposcopy + ECC; endometrial sampling at 35 or older, or younger with abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), chronic anovulation or obesitySame
Cytology negative, HPV 16 or 18Colposcopy nowNot applicable
Colposcopy outcomes SCJ not fully visualized: endocervical curettage. CIN1: observation is preferred. CIN2: treat, unless her concerns about treatment's effect on future pregnancy outweigh concerns about cancer. CIN3: treat; observation is unacceptable. Adenocarcinoma in situ: diagnostic excision with an intact specimen and interpretable margins, classically cold knife conization, since a LEEP can fragment the margins. Invasive cancer: staging, not LEEP. After treatment: surveillance for at least 25 years.
Special populations: where the schedule changes
  • HIV: start at 21 as usual, or at diagnosis if older; cytology yearly, and after 3 normal annual results every 3 years; from 30, cytology alone or co-testing, not primary HPV alone; continue for life, never stopping at 65 (Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) guideline, updated 2024, reviewed 2026).
  • Older rule: the CDC 2021 STI guideline still screens 1 year after sexual debut, no later than 21; current HHS guidance (start at 21) sets the answer.
  • Other immunosuppression: solid organ transplant, end-stage renal disease, hematopoietic stem cell transplant or systemic lupus erythematosus, on immunosuppressants or not; inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis or multiple sclerosis on immunosuppressants. Follow the HIV schedule, which starts at 21, for life, stopping by shared decision-making (American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology (ASCCP) review, 2025).
  • In-utero diethylstilbestrol (DES): an annual examination has generally been advised; its benefit over routine screening is now unclear.
  • Treated CIN2+: HPV testing or co-testing every 3 years for at least 25 years, including past 65.
  • Hysterectomy, cervix removed for benign disease: stop entirely. Cervix retained (supracervical): keep screening. After CIN2+, adenocarcinoma in situ or cervical cancer: keep screening the vaginal cuff (CDC: CIN2, CIN3 or adenocarcinoma in situ within the previous 20 years; HHS: annual cuff cytology in HIV).
  • HPV-vaccinated: same intervals. Pregnant: same intervals; colposcopy is safe, but ECC and endometrial biopsy are contraindicated, and CIN2 or CIN3 treatment waits until after delivery unless invasive cancer appears.
Common wrong answers Her risk history (salient decoy): makes no screening feel negligent, but it does not lower the floor. Colposcopy (sequencing trap): it is for an abnormal result, and she has none. HPV vaccination counseling (true-fact-wrong-slot): at 20 she is within catch-up vaccination, which runs through 26, so it is indicated, but it does not answer the screening question. A female partner: does not lower risk; HPV transmits between women, and screening is identical. Obesity: with AGC under 35 it is a listed indication for endometrial sampling, even without abnormal bleeding.
Pairs with Adolescent Vaccines. Ask “Is she eligible yet?” before “Is she at risk?”
Transferable rule

Screening guidelines are population rules with age gates. Individual risk factors adjust intensity within the eligible window; they rarely move the floor. Check eligibility before you calculate risk.
