Cervicitis and Pelvic Inflammatory Disease

chlamydia and gonorrhea at the cervix, then ascent to the upper tract · treat on the exam finding, before the test returns; the threshold is low by designIs there cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness, is she pregnant, and does she meet an admission criterion?

DiagnosisPracticeManagement
Bottom line

Both are clinical diagnoses, usually treated at the visit. Send nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) for both organisms at the same time, but do not wait for it in pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), or in cervicitis when she is at increased risk. The aim is to interrupt transmission and prevent the sequelae: PID, ectopic pregnancy, infertility and chronic pelvic pain.

  • Cervicitis: two major signs, a mucopurulent discharge and a friable cervix that bleeds easily on swab contact. Most prevalent under 25; frequently asymptomatic, or an abnormal discharge and intermenstrual bleeding.
  • Presumptive cervicitis treatment: for women at increased risk, if follow-up cannot be ensured, or if NAAT is not possible; deferring until results is an option at lower risk. Doxycycline covers C trachomatis; ceftriaxone, considered when she is at risk for gonorrhea or lives in a community where gonorrhea prevalence is high, covers N gonorrhoeae.
  • Increased risk includes: under 25, a new partner, or a partner with concurrent partners or a sexually transmitted infection (STI).
  • PID: a presumptive clinical diagnosis with a deliberately low threshold.
  • Minimum criteria for PID: a sexually active young woman or other woman at risk, pelvic or lower abdominal pain, no other identified cause, and any one of cervical motion tenderness (CMT), uterine tenderness or adnexal tenderness.
  • Additional criteria: oral temperature above 38.3 °C, mucopurulent cervical discharge or friability, abundant white blood cells on saline microscopy, a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein, documented gonococcal or chlamydial infection. They support the diagnosis and raise its specificity.
  • Absent CMT does not reassure in cervicitis: CMT marks ascent, and early or low-burden infection lacks it.
  • Pregnancy: azithromycin replaces doxycycline; PID in pregnancy means admission.

The threshold is low because treatment prevents the sequelae and delay causes them. Managing the alternatives (ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, ovarian cyst, torsion) is not impaired by starting antimicrobials: treating early carries no diagnostic penalty, treating late a permanent one.

Diagnosis
Pelvic pain or discharge in a young woman: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe tell
Cervicitis (chlamydia, gonorrhea)Age under 25, high-risk sexual behavior; asymptomatic most commonly; the two organisms often coinfectMucopurulent discharge, friable cervix; no CMT needed
PIDAscending gonococcal, chlamydial or vaginal-flora infectionCMT with mucopurulent discharge
Ectopic pregnancy, can't missAmenorrhea then unilateral painPositive human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) with an empty uterus; a pregnancy test is always mandatory
Tubo-ovarian abscessA complication of PID rather than a separate diseasePalpable or sonographic adnexal mass; admit
Ovarian torsionSudden severe unilateral pain with an ovarian massNausea and vomiting, usually afebrile, absent or reduced Doppler flow, though preserved flow does not exclude it when suspicion is high
AppendicitisPeriumbilical pain that migratesMcBurney point tenderness, no cervical findings
PyelonephritisAscending urinary infectionCostovertebral angle tenderness with pyuria
Chlamydial urethritisDysuria that reads as cystitisLeukocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative, with cervical discharge
Screening The USPSTF (US Preventive Services Task Force) recommends screening every sexually active woman under 25 for chlamydia and gonorrhea, and older women at increased risk, annually by Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidance, with NAAT for both organisms, even with no discharge and a normal exam. Most infections are silent, and treating them prevents PID and its sequelae.
Practice
  1. 17-year-old girl has had sudden pelvic pain since yesterday Sexually active; no other cause found cervical motion tenderness purulent cervical discharge no adnexal mass on bimanual exam T 39 °C · HR 104/min · urine pregnancy test negative → Start empiric antibiotics now → pelvic pain with cervical motion tenderness and no other cause meets the minimum criteria, so presumptive treatment starts now. The purulent discharge and an oral temperature above 38.3 °C add specificity, and above 38.5 °C she meets an admission criterion. A pelvic ultrasound is normal in uncomplicated disease and delays treatment; the amplification test is positive in only about half, so neither result could change today's decision
  2. 22-year-old woman has 1 week of vaginal discharge New male partner 2 months ago mucopurulent discharge at the cervical os cervix bleeds on contact with the swab no cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness Afebrile · urine pregnancy test negative → Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline → mucopurulent discharge and a cervix that bleeds easily on swab contact are the two major signs. Under 25 with a new partner she is at increased risk, so presumptive treatment for both organisms is given at the visit while the nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) is pending: doxycycline for chlamydia, and ceftriaxone for gonorrhea, considered when she is at risk or lives in a high-prevalence community. Sexually active and under 25, she is in the group screened annually for gonorrhea (CDC). Azithromycin plus doxycycline covers chlamydia twice and leaves gonorrhea untreated
  3. 23-year-old woman has 3 days of lower abdominal pain Mucopurulent vaginal discharge for 2 weeks No pregnancy or delivery in the past year uterine and adnexal tenderness cervical motion tenderness T 38.4 °C · HR 96/min · urine pregnancy test negative → Pelvic inflammatory disease → pelvic pain with cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness and no other cause meets the minimum criteria: the infection has ascended from the cervix. Cervicitis alone lacks that tenderness, and postpartum endometritis needs a recent delivery
  4. 24-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation has a positive screening test for chlamydia First pregnancy; no symptoms Same test negative for gonorrhea normal pelvic exam Afebrile · BP 110/68 mm Hg → Azithromycin → azithromycin 1 g orally once is the recommended regimen in pregnancy; doxycycline is not the recommended regimen in pregnancy and is contraindicated in the second and third trimesters because of tooth discoloration, and ceftriaxone alone treats gonorrhea, not chlamydia. A test of cure about 4 weeks after treatment is recommended in pregnancy
  5. 19-year-old woman has 4 days of pelvic pain and fever Sexually active; urine pregnancy test negative cervical motion and left adnexal tenderness 6-cm tubo-ovarian abscess on transvaginal ultrasound T 38.9 °C · HR 108/min · BP 118/72 mm Hg → Admit for intravenous antibiotics → a tubo-ovarian abscess is a hospitalization criterion, and more than 24 hours of inpatient observation is recommended: intravenous antibiotics first, with drainage if the abscess fails medical therapy. Outpatient oral therapy is for women without an admission criterion, and laparotomy is not the first step
  6. 21-year-old woman has 4 days of dysuria Sexually active with a new partner no costovertebral angle tenderness mucopurulent cervical discharge on speculum exam Afebrile · urinalysis: leukocyte esterase positive · nitrite negative → Chlamydial urethritis with cervicitis → leukocyte esterase without nitrite in a sexually active woman should prompt a pelvic exam for chlamydia: atypicals do not reduce nitrate, and the cervical discharge reframes the urinary tract infection. Send a NAAT; a urine culture often shows no growth. Cystitis lacks the discharge, and pyelonephritis brings costovertebral angle tenderness
  7. 24-year-old woman has 2 days of lower abdominal pain Copper intrauterine device placed 2 years ago cervical motion and uterine tenderness no adnexal mass on ultrasound T 37.9 °C · HR 90/min · urine pregnancy test negative → Treat and leave the device in place → the intrauterine device does not need to be removed: treat with close clinical follow-up, and consider removal only if there is no improvement within 48 to 72 hours. All contraceptive methods can be continued during treatment
  8. 25-year-old woman has fever and lower abdominal pain 3 days after vaginal delivery Membranes ruptured 24 hours before delivery uterine tenderness foul-smelling lochia T 38.7 °C · HR 104/min · BP 116/70 mm Hg → Clindamycin plus gentamicin → fever with uterine tenderness days after delivery, after prolonged rupture of membranes, is polymicrobial ascent from the lower genital or gastrointestinal tract; first-line treatment is intravenous clindamycin plus gentamicin, not an STI regimen. Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline treats gonorrhea and chlamydia, and TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) is not a regimen for gonorrhea, chlamydia or PID
  9. 22-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation has 2 days of pelvic pain Intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound mucopurulent cervical discharge cervical motion and adnexal tenderness T 38.1 °C · HR 98/min → Hospitalize for intravenous antibiotics → pregnancy is itself a hospitalization criterion: suspected ascending infection in pregnancy carries a high risk of maternal morbidity and preterm delivery, so she is admitted for intravenous antimicrobials in consultation with an infectious disease specialist. Outpatient therapy is wrong whatever the regimen because pregnancy mandates admission, and azithromycin alone also leaves gonorrhea untreated
  10. 17-year-old girl has 2 days of right upper quadrant pain that worsens with deep breaths Treated last week for lower abdominal pain with cervical motion tenderness gallbladder normal on ultrasound T 38.2 °C · HR 96/min · chest radiograph normal → Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome → the pelvic infection reached the liver capsule: perihepatitis with violin-string adhesions, which gives right upper quadrant pleuritic pain. Cholecystitis would show on the gallbladder ultrasound, and a lower lobe pneumonia on the chest radiograph
  11. 18-year-old woman has worsening pelvic pain 72 hours after starting outpatient therapy Ceftriaxone injection, then oral doxycycline and metronidazole persistent cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness T 38.6 °C · HR 106/min · urine pregnancy test negative → Admit for intravenous therapy and reassess the diagnosis → no clinical improvement within 72 hours of outpatient intramuscular or oral therapy calls for hospitalization, assessment of the antimicrobial regimen and additional diagnostics, including consideration of diagnostic laparoscopy for an alternative diagnosis. Extending the oral course or adding azithromycin keeps a failing outpatient plan
  12. 19-year-old woman has a positive screening test for chlamydia No symptoms; routine screening at her annual visit Same test negative for gonorrhea normal pelvic exam Afebrile · urine pregnancy test negative → Doxycycline alone → confirmed chlamydia alone in a nonpregnant patient is treated with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days; ceftriaxone is not needed once gonorrhea has been tested for and excluded. Treat partners from the previous 60 days, and retest her about 3 months after treatment; a test of cure is not advised
  13. 20-year-old woman has 4 days of lower abdominal pain Starting outpatient treatment today; no other cause found Last sexual intercourse 3 weeks ago, with her only partner cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness T 37.9 °C · urine pregnancy test negative → Evaluate, test and treat the partner now → pelvic pain with cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness and no other cause is presumptive PID, so anyone who had sexual contact with her during the 60 days before symptom onset is evaluated, tested and presumptively treated for chlamydia and gonorrhea, regardless of the cause or pathogens found; if her last intercourse was more than 60 days ago, the most recent partner is treated
  14. 16-year-old girl has sudden severe right pelvic pain that began 3 hours ago Vomited twice tender right adnexal mass ultrasound: enlarged, edematous right ovary with reduced Doppler flow Afebrile · HR 112/min · urine pregnancy test negative → Ovarian torsion → sudden severe unilateral pain with vomiting, an adnexal mass and no fever: Doppler ultrasound may show absent or reduced flow, though complete loss of flow is not necessary and preserved flow does not exclude it when suspicion is high; then laparoscopy. Pelvic inflammatory disease findings include cervical motion, uterine and bilateral adnexal tenderness, and ovarian edema, enlargement and abnormal flow are among the most sensitive ultrasound findings of torsion
  15. 17-year-old girl is starting treatment today for pelvic pain with cervical motion tenderness Cervical NAAT for gonorrhea and chlamydia sent No earlier testing for sexually transmitted infections T 38.0 °C · urine pregnancy test negative → HIV and syphilis → every woman with this diagnosis is tested for gonorrhea, chlamydia, HIV and syphilis, and a woman with chlamydial or gonococcal infection is retested 3 months after treatment. Hepatitis C testing alone misses the infections recommended here
How NBME framed it: question 1

16-year-old girl seen with her mother for a routine health maintenance visit Previously healthy; takes no medications; immunizations current Periods come every 28 to 35 days, irregularly; last one 3 weeks ago No tobacco, alcohol or illicit drugs One male partner for the past year; no condom use Family history: breast cancer in her mother at age 40 height 163 cm · weight 65 kg · body mass index 25 kg/m² · vital signs normal breasts: no masses, no nipple discharge external genitalia normal; no vaginal discharge sexual maturity rating 5 for breasts and pubic hair

Most appropriate screening test now?

Competing answers
  • Mammography: her mother's breast cancer at 40 is the planted cue; but routine mammography starts at 40, not in adolescence.
  • Fasting serum glucose: a body mass index of 25; but that alone does not meet the adolescent diabetes screening bar, which needs overweight plus risk factors such as insulin resistance.
  • Hemoglobin concentration: irregular menses are the planted cue; but routine iron deficiency anemia screening is not a US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation.

Down to two: a Pap smear or chlamydia and gonorrhea NAAT. NAAT for both organisms: every sexually active woman under 25 is screened, even with no discharge and a normal exam, because most infections are silent and the two often coinfect. Cervical cytology starts at 21 whatever the sexual history. Each decoy carried a planted cue, and the key named the test in full.

Management
Regimens and follow-up (CDC 2021)
SituationRegimenThen
Cervicitis, presumptiveDoxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days; consider adding ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once if she is at risk for gonorrhea or in a high-prevalence community (1 g at 150 kg or more)Treat partners for the infection identified or suspected. If an organism is identified: partners from the previous 60 days, and retest her at 3 months
Chlamydia alone, confirmedDoxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 daysNo test of cure if not pregnant; retest about 3 months after treatment
Chlamydia in pregnancyAzithromycin 1 g orally once; amoxicillin 500 mg 3 times daily for 7 days is the alternativeTest of cure about 4 weeks after treatment
GonorrheaCeftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once (1 g at 150 kg or more); doxycycline as above if chlamydia is not excludedTest of cure only for pharyngeal infection, at 7 to 14 days; retest at 3 months
PID, outpatientCeftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once, plus doxycycline 100 mg and metronidazole 500 mg, each orally twice daily for 14 daysNo improvement within 72 hours: hospitalize, reassess the regimen and the diagnosis, consider diagnostic laparoscopy
PID, inpatientCeftriaxone 1 g intravenously (IV) every 24 hours with doxycycline 100 mg and metronidazole 500 mg, each orally or IV every 12 hours; or cefotetan 2 g IV every 12 hours, or cefoxitin 2 g IV every 6 hours, with doxycycline; doxycycline orally when possible, because IV infusion is painfulOral doxycycline and metronidazole usually within 24 to 48 hours of improvement, completing 14 days; an abscess failing medical therapy is drained
When to admit By provider judgment and any of: a surgical emergency such as appendicitis cannot be excluded, tubo-ovarian abscess (more than 24 hours of inpatient observation), pregnancy, severe illness, nausea and vomiting or an oral temperature above 38.5 °C, inability to follow or tolerate an oral regimen, or no response to oral therapy. Adolescence is not itself a criterion; the same thresholds apply as for adults. All contraceptive methods can be continued, and an intrauterine device does not need removal; consider removing it if there is no improvement within 48 to 72 hours.
Partners and retesting Treat partners. For PID, everyone with sexual contact in the 60 days before symptom onset is evaluated, tested and presumptively treated for chlamydia and gonorrhea, whatever her results; if her last intercourse was more than 60 days ago, the most recent partner is treated. Partners abstain until both are treated. Retest a woman with chlamydial or gonococcal infection 3 months after treatment, whether or not partners were treated.
Pearls The low threshold is the guideline, not a shortcut: clinical diagnosis carries a positive predictive value of only 65 to 90% for salpingitis, and that is accepted deliberately. Only about half of acute PID has a positive gonorrhea or chlamydia test, so a negative test never excludes it. Metronidazole joined the routine outpatient regimen in 2021 for anaerobic coverage; older item banks may key ceftriaxone plus doxycycline alone. Quinolones are no longer recommended because of gonococcal resistance. Fitz-Hugh-Curtis is PID that reached the liver capsule, with right upper quadrant pleuritic pain. Sterile pyuria in a sexually active woman (leukocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative) should prompt a pelvic exam for chlamydia.
Common wrong answers Azithromycin plus doxycycline: looks like dual therapy, but both cover the same organism; it doubles atypical coverage and leaves N gonorrhoeae untreated, the classic wrong pairing. TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole): not a regimen for gonorrhea, chlamydia or PID; gonococcus is multidrug-resistant, and United States strains are not adequately susceptible to penicillin, tetracycline and older macrolides, with fluoroquinolones dropped in 2007 for resistance. A negative nitrite: it cannot rule out infection that nitrite was never sensitive for, because atypicals do not reduce nitrate. Pelvic ultrasound first: normal in uncomplicated PID; it delays the only intervention that prevents sequelae. Urine culture: right class of test, wrong compartment. Contraception: appropriate care, but prevention rather than treatment of an established infection. A Pap smear for a sexually active 16-year-old: cervical cytology starts at 21 whatever the sexual history.
Pairs with Part II Cervical Cancer Screening: is she 21 or older, or is she due only for chlamydia and gonorrhea screening? Part I Ectopic Pregnancy must always be considered with PID: both present as acute pelvic pain in a reproductive-age woman, and one test settles the fork. Ask: what is the pregnancy test?
Transferable rule

When a diagnosis is clinical or presumptive and the sequelae are irreversible, treat at the visit and send the tests at the same time; the confirmatory test is documentation rather than management. Ask what the pending test could change today, and treat if the answer is nothing.

Obstructive Lung Disease

asthma vs COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) by spirometry · alpha-1 antitrypsin · what lowers COPD mortality · long-term oxygenIs the obstruction reversible, and does the intervention change survival or only symptoms?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Reversibility is a measurement: spirometry before and after a bronchodilator separates asthma from COPD; relief after albuterol does not.

  • Asthma: FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) rises 12% or more and 200 mL or more; the ratio often normalizes.
  • COPD: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC (forced vital capacity) below 0.70; obstruction persists despite some improvement.
  • Asthma-COPD overlap: long-standing asthma, smoking, fixed obstruction; include an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS).

In COPD, rank interventions by outcome. These lower mortality:

  • Smoking cessation: first-line while the patient still smokes.
  • Long-term oxygen: for resting hypoxemia that meets the criteria below.
  • Others: annual influenza vaccination; lung volume reduction surgery in severe upper-lobe emphysema with low exercise capacity; nocturnal noninvasive ventilation for chronic daytime hypercapnia.

Bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, macrolides and roflumilast reduce symptoms or exacerbations, with no survival benefit shown as single agents; on low-certainty evidence, triple inhaled therapy (a long-acting beta-agonist, a long-acting muscarinic antagonist and an inhaled corticosteroid) may reduce mortality compared with the two bronchodilators alone. Pulmonary rehabilitation improves dyspnea, fatigue and quality of life.

Diagnosis
Defining criteria Asthma – onset in childhood or early adulthood; episodic, variable, trigger-driven, often atopic; reversible obstruction · COPD – progressive, usually after 40 and years of smoking; post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 · Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency – emphysema in the young or minimal smoker, panlobular and worst at the bases; liver disease from misfolded protein: neonatal cholestasis, later cirrhosis
Management and treatment
Long-term oxygen: who qualifies
ThresholdApplies whenThen
PaO2 (arterial oxygen pressure) 55 mm Hg or less, or SaO2 (arterial oxygen saturation) 88% or lessAt rest; not for exertional or nocturnal hypoxemia aloneOxygen 15 hours a day or more, titrated to SaO2 90 to 94%
PaO2 59 mm Hg or less, or SaO2 89% or lessWith cor pulmonale or secondary polycythemia (hematocrit over 55%)Oxygen; reversing hypoxic vasoconstriction protects the right heart
By diagnosis Asthma – inhaled corticosteroid, with or without a long-acting beta-agonist · COPD – long-acting muscarinic antagonist and beta-agonist; add an inhaled corticosteroid for frequent exacerbations with eosinophils of 300/μL or more · Secondary polycythemia – treat the hypoxemia, not the number; phlebotomy only for symptomatic hyperviscosity, typically hematocrit over 65% · Polycythemia vera – all three cell lines up, low erythropoietin, a JAK2 (Janus kinase 2) mutation
Practice
  1. 68-year-old man with COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) is seen for follow-up former smoker, quit 2 years ago already on a long-acting bronchodilator pair No ankle edema PaO2 52 mm Hg at rest on room air · hematocrit 46% → Long-term oxygen therapy → a resting PaO2 of 55 mm Hg or less meets the standard criterion: long-term oxygen, which lowers mortality; adding an inhaled corticosteroid has only low-certainty mortality evidence
  2. 68-year-old man with COPD still smokes a pack a day two exacerbations this year asks which single step most improves survival No oxygen requirement SaO2 93% at rest · FEV1 48% of predicted → Smoking cessation → smoking cessation gives the largest mortality benefit available; oxygen is for resting hypoxemia, which he lacks
  3. 68-year-old man with COPD asks what else reduces mortality stopped smoking 3 years ago already completed pulmonary rehabilitation and is vaccinated Dyspnea on one flight of stairs SaO2 87% at rest on room air · hematocrit 49% → Long-term oxygen if hypoxemic → with cessation already done, long-term oxygen for resting hypoxemia is a remaining intervention that lowers mortality; bronchodilators and roflumilast treat symptoms
  4. 68-year-old man with COPD is referred to pulmonary rehabilitation asks what it will achieve breathless walking to the mailbox Stopped smoking last year SaO2 92% at rest · FEV1 45% of predicted → Improved symptoms and quality of life → rehabilitation improves dyspnea, fatigue and quality of life; it does not raise lung function
  5. 68-year-old man with stable COPD has ankle edema from cor pulmonale jugular venous distension, loud pulmonic second sound ruddy, plethoric face PaO2 57 mm Hg at rest · SaO2 89% · hematocrit 57% · white cells and platelets normal → Start long-term oxygen → cor pulmonale or a hematocrit over 55% lowers the gate to PaO2 59 mm Hg or SaO2 89%: start oxygen now
  6. 68-year-old man with COPD has had 3 exacerbations this year on a long-acting bronchodilator pair for 2 years inhaler technique and adherence checked Former smoker SaO2 93% at rest · blood eosinophils 340/μL → Add an inhaled corticosteroid → eosinophils of 300/μL or more with frequent exacerbations: adding an inhaled corticosteroid reduces exacerbations
  7. 24-year-old woman has 6 months of episodic wheeze and cough worse with exercise and cold air symptom-free between episodes Spirometry today is normal Afebrile · SaO2 98% · lungs clear on exam → Methacholine challenge → suspected asthma with normal spirometry: methacholine challenge; a negative test rules out asthma
  8. 62-year-old man has 3 years of progressive exertional dyspnea 40 pack-years of smoking daily cough with sputum No childhood wheeze or allergies Afebrile · post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.62 · FEV1 up 6% after albuterol → COPD → a post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70 with little reversibility is COPD: a long-acting muscarinic antagonist and beta-agonist
  9. 30-year-old woman has episodic wheeze and chest tightness each spring eczema as a child; hay fever never smoked Symptom-free between episodes Afebrile · pre-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.66 · post 0.78, FEV1 up 18% and 350 mL → Asthma → a 12% and 200 mL rise with a normalized ratio is reversible obstruction: asthma, treated with an inhaled corticosteroid
  10. 40-year-old man has 2 years of progressive exertional dyspnea minimal smoking history: 5 pack-years, quit at 25 CT: emphysema worst in the lower lobes Mildly raised liver enzymes Afebrile · post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.58 → Alpha-1 antitrypsin level → emphysema under about 45, little smoking, lower lobes, and liver involvement: alpha-1 antitrypsin level
  11. 34-year-old woman with asthma has worsening control despite high-dose inhalers coughs up brown mucus plugs most mornings CT: central bronchiectasis Aspergillus precipitins positive; skin test to Aspergillus positive Afebrile · eosinophils 1,400/μL · IgE 2,600 international units per mL → Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis → refractory asthma with brown plugs and central bronchiectasis is allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA): oral steroids and itraconazole
  12. 70-year-old woman with COPD has had 2 hospitalized exacerbations this year on a long-acting bronchodilator pair uses her inhalers correctly Quit smoking 10 years ago SaO2 92% at rest · blood eosinophils 360/μL → Add ICS → frequent exacerbations with eosinophils of 300/μL or more: add an inhaled corticosteroid
  13. 29-year-old man has 3 months of dry cough worse at night and when he runs in cold air no heartburn; takes no medications Never smoked; no postnasal drip Afebrile · spirometry normal · chest x-ray normal → Cough-variant asthma → isolated cough worse at night and with cold air and normal spirometry is cough-variant asthma
  14. 55-year-old woman, a long-standing asthmatic who smokes, is breathless breathless on most days for a year, not only in attacks obstruction no longer fully reverses Prior inhaled corticosteroid response Afebrile · post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.64 · FEV1 up 9% → Asthma-COPD overlap → long-standing asthma with smoking and fixed obstruction is asthma-COPD overlap; the regimen must include an inhaled corticosteroid
  15. 60-year-old man, a smoker, has chronic airflow obstruction productive cough for years and progressive dyspnea barrel chest The team must decide between emphysema and chronic bronchitis as the main process Afebrile · post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.60 → DLCO → the diffusing capacity (DLCO) is low in emphysema, normal in chronic bronchitis, and normal or high in asthma
  16. 15-year-old boy has had a wet cough since infancy recurrent sinusitis and two pneumonias digital clubbing; weight below the 5th percentile Never smoked; eats well but stays thin Afebrile · SaO2 94% · chest x-ray: hyperinflation → Cystic fibrosis → clubbing with a lifelong wet cough and poor growth points to cystic fibrosis: sweat chloride test; clubbing is not a feature of COPD or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
How NBME framed it: question 1

16-year-old girl in the emergency department with 3 days of cough with thick yellowish sputum and 1 day of shortness of breath No fever. Asthma on albuterol and inhaled corticosteroids, hospitalized 10 times between ages 8 and 10 Smokes 1.5 packs a day for 4 years T 37 °C · pulse 102/min · respirations 42/min · BP 108/80 mm Hg mild clubbing; increased anteroposterior chest diameter; occasional end-expiratory wheezes chest x-ray: severe bilateral hyperinflation, nothing else

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Congenital lobar emphysema: emphysema and hyperinflation; but it overinflates one lobe, not both lungs diffusely, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is more common.
  • Kartagener syndrome: thick sputum and clubbing; but there is no situs inversus, chronic sinusitis or lifelong wet cough.
  • Pulmonary sequestration: a congenital lung lesion; but it gives recurrent pneumonia in one region, and this film shows only hyperinflation.
  • Sarcoidosis: chronic lung disease in the young; but there is no hilar adenopathy or infiltrate.

Down to two: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency or Kartagener syndrome. Emphysema this young, with barrel chest and diffuse hyperinflation, points to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: unopposed neutrophil elastase, panlobular and basal; misfolded protein in the liver causes cirrhosis. The common answer (severe asthma in a smoker) is not offered, the childhood asthma admissions pull toward it, and the clubbing is a planted pull toward Kartagener syndrome. Confirm with a serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level.

Pairs with Asthma covers severity and step therapy once asthma is confirmed. Recurrent Respiratory Infection and Structural Lung Disease covers ABPA and the structural lung. Ask: which test measures the defining variable?
Transferable rule

When two choices test the same variable, pick the one that yields a number. An association is not a discriminator, and an intervention is ranked by the outcome the question names.

Congenital Heart Disease

cyanotic lesions · left-to-right shunts · their timing: weeks for shunts, days for the ductusWhen did it declare, and which structure makes the murmur?

WorkupCyanotic lesionsShuntsPractice
Bottom line

Sort by when it declares (birth, infancy, spells) and the murmur (present or absent, and its source).

  • A murmur needs a pressure gradient: when one appears or fades, the gradient changed.
  • Left-to-right shunts declare over weeks, as pulmonary vascular resistance falls.
  • Ductal-dependent lesions declare over days, as the ductus closes.
  • Silent cyanosis: total anomalous pulmonary venous return or hypoplastic left heart syndrome.
  • Tet spell: the outflow obstruction is partly dynamic; crying or dehydration can tighten it (the trigger is not fully understood), or a drop in systemic vascular resistance (SVR) lets more blood shunt right to left; squatting or knee-chest raises SVR and aborts it.
Workup
Cyanotic lesions
Mechanism, then the tell
LesionMechanismThe tell
Total anomalous pulmonary venous returnPulmonary veins drain to the right heartBirth; no murmur, at most soft pulmonic flow
Hypoplastic left heart syndromeTiny left ventricle, absent mitral and aortic valves; lives on the ductus and atrial defectBirth; no murmur
Tricuspid atresiaNo right atrium to right ventricle path; atrial defect plus a ventricular defect or ductusBirth; ventricular defect or ductal murmur, or both
Truncus arteriosusOne arterial trunk over a ventricular septal defectTypically infancy, not birth; holosystolic murmur
Tetralogy of FallotOutflow narrowing pushes blood right to left across a large ventricular septal defectHarsh systolic, left upper sternal border; fades in a spell
Ebstein anomalyTricuspid valve displaced apically; atrialized right ventricleTricuspid regurgitation, widely split S1 (first heart sound), sail sound; severe: birth
Tetralogy PROVe – Pulmonic stenosis (right ventricular (RV) outflow obstruction), RV hypertrophy, Overriding aorta, VSD (ventricular septal defect) · Murmur – from the narrowed outflow tract; the defect is too large to make one · Spectrum – severe narrowing, cyanotic at birth; milder, spells in infancy · 5 Ts – Truncus, Transposition, Tricuspid atresia, Tetralogy, Total anomalous pulmonary venous return
Left-to-right shunts and the transitional clock
Acyanotic lesions
LesionThe tellThen
Ventricular septal defectHolosystolic, lower sternal border; louder means smallerDiurese and feed; close if failure persists
Atrial septal defectFixed split S2 (second heart sound), soft pulmonic flow murmurOften silent into childhood; no cyanosis
Patent ductus arteriosusContinuous machine-like, bounding pulses, wide pulse pressurePreterm: indomethacin or ibuprofen closes it; murmur disappears
Coarctation of the aortaArm-leg pressure gap, weak femoral pulsesDays: PGE1 reopens the ductus
Prostaglandin opens, indomethacin closes Ductal-dependent – coarctation, pulmonary atresia, transposition, hypoplastic left heart decompensate as the ductus closes: reopen it · Preterm ductus – shunting into the lungs is the problem: close it · Softening murmur – in an unrepaired large shunt, a warning, not an improvement
Practice
  1. 5-week-old boy, born at term, had a normal 2-week visit now feeds poorly and breathes fast new holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border Murmur absent on the newborn examination Afebrile · respiratory rate 70/min · acyanotic → Pulmonary vascular resistance has fallen → at birth pulmonary vascular resistance is near systemic, so almost nothing crosses the defect; as it falls, the gradient opens, the murmur appears at 2 to 4 weeks, and the same overcirculation causes the tachypnea and poor feeding. The ductus was already closed by the normal 2-week visit, and its closure removes a continuous murmur rather than creating a holosystolic one; rising pulmonary pressure would soften the murmur
  2. 1-day-old boy has been cyanotic since birth no murmur echocardiogram shows the pulmonary veins draining to the right atrium Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy Afebrile · oxygen saturation 80% on room air · HR 160/min → Total anomalous pulmonary venous return → pulmonary veins draining to the right heart give cyanosis at birth with no murmur, at most a soft pulmonic flow murmur; tetralogy has a harsh outflow murmur, and truncus arteriosus has a holosystolic murmur with cyanosis typically arriving in infancy
  3. 6-week-old boy was diagnosed with a large ventricular septal defect at 2 weeks poor weight gain liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin Feeds tire him Afebrile · respiratory rate 70/min → Diuretics, afterload reduction and caloric fortification → heart failure from a left-to-right shunt arrives at 4 to 6 weeks; failure to thrive is the infant form of exercise intolerance. Diurese and feed first, and close the defect if failure persists: observation leaves the failure untreated, and surgery comes after medical therapy fails
  4. 4-month-old boy has episodes of deep cyanosis while crying episodes resolve when he is held with knees to chest harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border Afebrile · oxygen saturation 84% between episodes → Tetralogy of Fallot → right ventricular outflow tract obstruction drives right-to-left flow across a large ventricular septal defect, and knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance to reverse it; truncus arteriosus gives a holosystolic murmur without spells, and total anomalous pulmonary venous return has no murmur
  5. 1-day-old girl has a normal examination before discharge fails her pulse oximetry screen at 24 hours Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy; feeding well Afebrile · HR 140/min · BP 70/42 mm Hg → Echocardiography → a failed screen means possible critical congenital heart disease, and only echocardiography names the anatomy; a chest radiograph only supports, and repeating a failed screen delays the study
  6. 1-day-old girl has been cyanotic since birth no murmur echocardiogram shows a severely underdeveloped left ventricle Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy Afebrile · oxygen saturation 82% on room air · HR 166/min → Prostaglandin E1 infusion → the ductus and the atrial defect are the only route to the systemic circulation, so the shunts must stay open: prostaglandin E1 keeps the ductus open; indomethacin closes it, and oxygen alone leaves it to close over days
  7. 3-week-old girl is seen for a weight check fixed splitting of S2 soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border Thriving and gaining weight Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% on room air → Atrial septal defect → a fixed split S2 with a soft pulmonic flow murmur and no cyanosis is an atrial septal defect; the atrial gradient stays low, so it is often silent into childhood. A ventricular septal defect is holosystolic at the lower sternal border, and a patent ductus is continuous and machine-like
  8. 2-month-old boy was diagnosed with tetralogy of Fallot at birth deeply cyanotic while crying improves when his mother holds his knees to his chest Afebrile · oxygen saturation 62% while crying, 84% after → Increased systemic vascular resistance reduces right-to-left shunting → knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance, which reverses the right-to-left shunt; the lever is systemic vascular resistance, not venous return or the coronary circulation
  9. 2-month-old girl is evaluated for a murmur holosystolic tricuspid regurgitation murmur at the left lower sternal border widely split S1 early systolic sail sound Feeding and growing well Afebrile · oxygen saturation 92% on room air → Ebstein anomaly → apical displacement of the tricuspid valve atrializes the right ventricle and makes the regurgitation murmur, the widely split S1 and the sail sound; tricuspid atresia has no right atrium to right ventricle path, and pulmonic stenosis makes an outflow murmur
  10. 4-month-old girl was diagnosed with a large ventricular septal defect at 1 month never repaired murmur has softened now desaturates with crying Parents say the quieter murmur means it is closing Afebrile · oxygen saturation 88% at rest → Urgent cardiology referral → a softening murmur in an unrepaired large shunt is a warning, not an improvement: it can mean pulmonary vascular resistance is rising and the shunt is starting to reverse, the road to Eisenmenger syndrome; refer urgently while repair is still possible. Reassurance reads it as closure; an afterload reducer with a 3-month recheck treats overcirculation that is already reversing and delays repair
  11. 1-day-old boy has been cyanotic since birth holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border ECG shows left axis deviation with small right ventricular forces No spells with crying Afebrile · oxygen saturation 78% on room air → Tricuspid atresia → with no right atrium to right ventricle path, flow depends on the atrial defect plus a ventricular defect or ductus, whose murmur is heard; left axis deviation with small right ventricular forces is its ECG. Tetralogy has right ventricular hypertrophy and an outflow murmur. Ebstein, cyanotic at birth when severe, also gives a regurgitation murmur, but adds a widely split S1, a sail sound and a massive box-shaped heart; left axis with small right ventricular forces is the tricuspid atresia ECG
  12. 2-day-old boy is pale and mottled weak femoral pulses right arm blood pressure 30 mm Hg above the leg In shock on arrival Afebrile · BP 86/50 mm Hg in the right arm · HR 190/min → Start prostaglandin E1 → coarctation declares in days, as the ductus closes: prostaglandin E1 reopens it. Diuretics and a fluid bolus leave the closing ductus untouched
  13. 2-month-old boy has cyanosis that began in recent weeks holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border echocardiogram shows a single arterial trunk over a large defect in the ventricular septum Afebrile · oxygen saturation 86% → Truncus arteriosus → a single shared arterial trunk over a ventricular septal defect gives cyanosis characteristically in infancy, not at birth, with a holosystolic murmur; tetralogy has a harsh outflow murmur and spells, and total anomalous pulmonary venous return has no murmur
  14. 3-month-old girl was diagnosed with a ventricular septal defect at 2 weeks loud grade 4/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border echocardiogram shows a small defect Afebrile · weight at the 50th percentile → A small defect produces high-velocity turbulent flow → a small defect makes high-velocity turbulent flow; large defects are quieter and shunt more, so murmur intensity runs opposite to severity. A loud murmur reflects a high gradient, not a high right ventricular pressure, which would soften it
  15. 3-month-old girl has episodes of deeper cyanosis with crying episodes resolve when she is calm harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border Afebrile · baseline oxygen saturation 86% → Echocardiography → echocardiography confirms the ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta and narrowed outflow tract; a chest radiograph (boot-shaped heart) and an ECG only support
  16. 3-day-old preterm boy born at 28 weeks continuous murmur below the left clavicle bounding pulses widened pulse pressure Murmur first heard today on rounds Afebrile · BP 58/24 mm Hg · respiratory rate 64/min → Indomethacin or ibuprofen → a hemodynamically significant preterm ductus (bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, tachypnea) shunting into the lungs is the problem, so close it with indomethacin or ibuprofen; prostaglandin E1 keeps a ductus open, and observation alone leaves the shunt in place
  17. 1-day-old boy with Down syndrome has mild cyanosis with feeds fixed split S2 grade 3/6 systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border Born at term after an uncomplicated delivery Afebrile · oxygen saturation 90% during feeds → Complete atrioventricular canal defect → an atrial sign (fixed split S2) and a lower-sternal-border murmur, with cyanosis, in Down syndrome: echocardiography defines it. An isolated ventricular or atrial septal defect shunts left to right and causes no cyanosis. On day 1 pulmonary vascular resistance is still near systemic, so little crosses left to right yet
  18. 3-day-old girl has cyanosis unimproved on 100% oxygen single S2 now weak pulses with poor perfusion Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy; feeding poorly today Afebrile · oxygen saturation 70% on 100% oxygen · HR 190/min → Start prostaglandin E1 and obtain echocardiography → unchanged saturation on 100% oxygen is a fixed shunt, not lung disease; weak pulses mean the ductus is closing, so instability licenses prostaglandin E1 before the picture; waiting for echocardiography or adding oxygen lets it close
  19. 3-month-old girl was diagnosed with tetralogy of Fallot at birth harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border echocardiogram shows a large ventricular septal defect and an overriding aorta Afebrile · oxygen saturation 88% → Flow through the narrowed RV outflow tract → the ventricular septal defect is real anatomy but too large to generate a murmur; the murmur comes from the narrowed right ventricular (RV) outflow tract, and the overriding aorta adds none
  20. 6-week-old boy has fed poorly for 1 week tachypneic and acyanotic holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border Murmur absent on the newborn examination; born at term Afebrile · respiratory rate 68/min · oxygen saturation 98% → Ventricular septal defect → a holosystolic lower-sternal-border murmur in an acyanotic infant is a ventricular septal defect, appearing as pulmonary vascular resistance falls; an atrial septal defect gives a fixed split S2 and is often silent into childhood, and a patent ductus is continuous
How NBME framed it: question 1

3-month-old boy brought to the emergency department with 3 days of pallor, low-grade fever, vomiting, occasional diarrhea and poor feeding Mildly dehydrated and cyanotic; perfusion and muscle tone normal T 37.8 °C · pulse 165/min · respirations 35/min · BP 80/48 mm Hg · oxygen saturation 85% on room air harsh grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur over the whole precordium cries and becomes agitated as an intravenous catheter is attempted saturation then drops to 60% and the murmur is barely audible Supplemental oxygen is given

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Atrial septal defect: a common defect with a systolic murmur; but it shunts left to right with a fixed split S2 and causes no cyanosis.
  • Coarctation of the aorta: a can't-miss lesion in an ill infant; but it gives arm hypertension, weak leg pulses and lower leg pressures, not cyanotic spells.
  • Ventricular septal defect: a harsh murmur in an infant; but an isolated defect is holosystolic and acyanotic; a murmur that fades as cyanosis develops over months can mean rising resistance reversing the shunt, the road to Eisenmenger syndrome, not an acute spell with crying.

Down to two: tetralogy of Fallot or pulmonary stenosis. Tetralogy of Fallot: isolated pulmonary stenosis makes a similar outflow murmur, but with no ventricular septal defect it causes no cyanotic spells with crying. Crying tightens the outflow obstruction (the trigger is not fully understood), pulmonary flow drops, and less flow makes a softer murmur. The stem reads like a febrile stomach illness; the witnessed spell names the lesion, and the oxygen given treats the number, not the shunt.

Common wrong answers Give oxygen in a spell: the shunt is anatomic; SVR, not inspired oxygen, is the lever. Flow across the ventricular septal defect: real anatomy, wrong source of the tetralogy murmur. Ductal closure: removes a continuous murmur, cannot create a holosystolic one. Rising pulmonary pressure: the opposite direction; it would soften the murmur.
Pairs with Part I Heart Murmurs in a Child: central cyanosis and a single or fixed S2 are pathologic; ask, cyanosis at birth, and is there a murmur? Part I Cyanosis in the Newborn: the sort to finish first. Part II Heart Murmurs in an Adult: murmur shape and location. Part II Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant: lung versus heart.
Transferable rule

Time it, then hear it: when did cyanosis or the murmur arrive, and which structure makes the sound? A murmur that appears or fades means the gradient changed, not the heart.

22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome

the syndrome is given; find the missing piece · CATCH · which syndrome has which finding · read the last sentence firstWhich component did the vignette leave out, and which bedside sign in the exam shows it?

Source vignette Pt — 3 h old F, 38 wk by cesarean for nonreassuring tones, Apgars 8 and 8, moved to the nursery for a dusky appearance; cyanotic and tremulous, with low-set ears, micrognathia and a cleft palate · Labs — pulse oximetry 72% in the right hand and the leg, unchanged after 10 minutes of 100% oxygen by hood · Imaging — chest radiograph shows an absent thymus; echocardiography shows truncus arteriosus · Q — which condition this patient most likely has; options spanned anemia, duodenal atresia, horseshoe kidney, hypocalcemia, hypoglycemia, myelomeningocele and neutropenia
The decision point

The vignette already gives the diagnosis. Conotruncal defect plus absent thymus plus cleft palate plus low-set ears and micrognathia is 22q11.2 deletion. Every answer option is a condition, not a syndrome. CATCH lists the components: Cardiac outflow anomaly, Anomalous face, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia from parathyroid hypoplasia. Four of the five are printed in the vignette; the missing one is hypocalcemia. The clue is in the physical examination: tremulous is neonatal hypocalcemia. This matters because these infants are at real risk of tetany, seizures and arrhythmia.

Defining criteria CATCH-22 — Cardiac outflow tract anomaly such as truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot or interrupted aortic arch; Anomalous face with prominent nasal bridge, low-set ears and micrognathia; Thymic hypoplasia or aplasia reducing T-cell immunity; Cleft palate; and Hypoparathyroidism producing hypocalcemia · DiGeorge versus velocardiofacial syndrome — both are 22q11.2 phenotypes; DiGeorge requires thymic involvement, with a CD3+ T-cell count under 500/mm3, while velocardiofacial requires facial abnormalities · Pathogenesis — loss of genes controlling third and fourth pharyngeal pouch derivation and neural crest migration, which is why the thymus, parathyroids, palate, face and cardiac outflow tract fail together
Pertinent positives & negatives Absent thymus on chest radiograph — third and fourth pouch failure; the most specific finding in the stem and the reason this is DiGeorge rather than isolated truncus · Truncus arteriosus — a conotruncal defect, the cardiac C · Cleft palate, low-set ears, micrognathia — the C and the A; with the thymus, four of five CATCH letters are printed · Tremulous — neonatal hypocalcemia before it becomes tetany · Saturation 72% in right hand and leg — no differential cyanosis, which excludes severe coarctation and interrupted arch physiology, and with them Turner syndrome · Refractory to 100% oxygen for 10 minutes — a fixed right-to-left shunt, confirming cyanotic structural heart disease rather than lung disease · Apgars 8 and 8, uncomplicated pregnancy, primigravida — no asphyxia and no maternal diabetes, closing the usual setups for hypoglycemia · No abdominal or spinal findings — nothing pointing at duodenal atresia or a neural tube defect
The dysmorphic neonate with a heart defect — which syndrome has which finding
SyndromeIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge)Pouch 3 and 4 failure; conotruncal defect, hypoplastic thymus and parathyroidsAbsent thymus plus conotruncal defect plus cleft palate; hypocalcemia is the fourth member— (the answer)
Down syndrome (trisomy 21)Commonest aneuploidy; AV septal defect, hypotoniaDuodenal atresia with a double bubble, single palmar crease, upslanting fissuresThymus present; no gastrointestinal malformation described
Turner syndrome (45,X)Female, short stature, gonadal dysgenesisHorseshoe kidney, coarctation, webbed neck, wide-spaced nipplesEqual pre- and postductal saturations; no renal or neck findings
CHARGE associationColoboma, choanal atresia, ear anomaliesColoboma and choanal atresia alongside the heart defectNo eye or nasal findings; thymic loss is not its signature
Infant of a diabetic motherMacrosomia, transposition, septal hypertrophyHypoglycemia in the first hours with a high birth weightPregnancy uncomplicated in a primigravida, no macrosomia
Management, in one line Once 22q11.2 is suspected, send an ionized calcium and get an echocardiogram. Confirm the deletion with chromosomal microarray or FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization). Treat symptomatic hypocalcemia with intravenous calcium. Until normal T-cell immunity is confirmed, these infants get irradiated blood products and no live vaccines.
Decision spine Read the last sentence first. — It asks for a condition, not a diagnosis · Name the syndrome from the cluster. — Conotruncal defect plus absent thymus plus cleft palate is 22q11.2 · Recite CATCH and cross off what is printed. — Cardiac, face, thymus and cleft are all given, so H is missing · Look for its bedside tell. — Tremulous means hypocalcemia · Assign each remaining option to its own syndrome. — Horseshoe kidney to Turner, duodenal atresia to Down, hypoglycemia to the infant of a diabetic mother, myelomeningocele to folate · Check the cell line. — DiGeorge takes lymphocytes, not neutrophils or red cells
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Pulse oximetry on 100% oxygenFirstSaturation unchanged, equal in hand and legFixed intracardiac shunt: cyanotic heart disease
EchocardiographyNextConotruncal defect: truncus, tetralogy or interrupted archRaises suspicion for 22q11.2 deletion
Chest radiographSupportsAbsent thymic shadowThymic hypoplasia or aplasia
Ionized calciumNextLowParathyroid hypoplasia; IV calcium if tremulous or seizing
Chromosomal microarray or FISH for 22q11.2ConfirmsMicrodeletion at 22q11.222q11.2 deletion syndrome
T-cell subsetsStagingCD3 count under 500/mm3DiGeorge immune phenotype: irradiated blood, no live vaccines
Standard karyotypeSkipNormal; the deletion is too small to seeUse microarray or FISH instead
Scenario bank
  1. 3 h old F, cyanosis refractory to 100% oxygen, saturation 72% in right hand and leg, low-set ears, micrognathia, cleft palate, absent thymus on chest film, truncus arteriosus on echocardiography, tremulous on examination → Hypocalcemia → parathyroid hypoplasia in 22q11.2 deletion
  2. Term neonate with truncus arteriosus, cleft palate and an absent thymic shadow on chest radiograph → Chromosomal microarray for the 22q11.2 deletion → a standard karyotype does not resolve a microdeletion
  3. Neonate with known 22q11.2 deletion who develops a generalized seizure; ionized calcium is low → Intravenous calcium gluconate → hypocalcemic seizure from parathyroid hypoplasia
  4. 4 mo old with 22q11.2 deletion and a CD3+ T-cell count of 210/mm3, presenting for routine immunizations → The live attenuated rotavirus vaccine → live vaccines are withheld until CD3 and CD4 exceed 500/mm3 and CD8 exceeds 200/mm3 with a normal mitogen response
  5. Newborn with a double-bubble sign on abdominal radiograph, a single transverse palmar crease and an atrioventricular septal defect → Down syndrome → duodenal atresia
  6. Newborn girl with coarctation of the aorta, a webbed neck, wide-spaced nipples and a horseshoe kidney → Turner syndrome → 45,X
  7. Why the thymus, parathyroids, palate and cardiac outflow tract fail together in this syndrome → Failed third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development with abnormal neural crest migration → one embryologic field, four organs
  8. 6 yo with 22q11.2 deletion, recurrent sinopulmonary infections and poor responses to polysaccharide vaccines → T-cell subsets with quantitative immunoglobulins → humoral failure follows defective T-cell help
Decoy note Tremulous is the bedside sign of both neonatal hypoglycemia and neonatal hypocalcemia. An uncomplicated pregnancy in a primigravida with Apgars of 8 closes off the hypoglycemia route. The equal right-hand and leg saturations read as an incidental vital sign, but they exclude differential cyanosis, and with it coarctation and Turner syndrome.
Pearls Syndrome with a missing component: when a vignette describes most of a syndrome, recite the mnemonic and cross off what is printed. Answer with the remainder; CATCH, JONES and CREST are tested this way · Hypocalcemia and hypoglycemia share a neonatal presentation of jitteriness, tremor and seizure, and the pregnancy history separates them · Differential cyanosis means ductal or arch pathology; equal pre- and postductal saturations mean a fixed intracardiac shunt, which is what truncus produces · DiGeorge takes lymphocytes, so an option of neutropenia or anemia tests which lineage the thymus governs · Until normal T-cell immunity is confirmed, these infants need irradiated blood and no live vaccines · The same deletion has two names: thymic involvement makes it DiGeorge, and facial abnormality makes it velocardiofacial
Pairs with Part I Congenital Heart Disease covers truncus arteriosus within the cyanosis differential, and the oxygen-refractory shunt logic that leads to it. Antibody Deficiencies covers the downstream question of which immunodeficiency the absent thymus produces. Ask: is the thymic shadow present, and does the face carry a syndrome? Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth places this syndrome beside CHARGE, VACTERL, trisomy 13 and Fanconi anemia. There, the deciding finding is the one on the fewest lists.
Transferable rule Read the last sentence before the vignette. When a vignette assembles a recognizable syndrome, the diagnosis is given, and the question asks for the component it left out. That component usually has a one-word bedside sign in the physical examination.
True-fact-wrong-slotHorseshoe kidney: a real and memorable syndrome pairing, but it belongs to Turner, and the equal limb saturations already exclude Turner's coarctation.
True-fact-wrong-slotDuodenal atresia: congenital heart disease with low-set ears reads as Down syndrome, but that is where duodenal atresia belongs and Down has no thymic aplasia.
Unchecked attributeNeutropenia: DiGeorge genuinely causes a cytopenia, but the lineage is lymphocytes; red cell and neutrophil counts are unaffected.
Mirror twinHypoglycemia: a tremulous neonate is the classic hypoglycemia cue and also the hypocalcemia cue, but this pregnancy was uncomplicated with normal Apgars.

Hereditary Polyposis Syndromes

adenomas or hamartomas: count the polyps, find the pigment · when a known carrier is scoped and operated on · lip macules that redirect an anemia workupHow many polyps, is there an adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) mutation, and where exactly is the pigment?

Which syndromeScreen and operatePigment plus anemiaPractice
Bottom line
  • Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP): an autosomal dominant APC mutation; hundreds to thousands of colonic adenomas, and colon cancer in nearly 100% before age 40.
  • Screening gate: annual sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy from puberty, age 10 to 12, not the first-degree-relative or average-risk schedule.
  • Colectomy gate: prophylactic proctocolectomy in the teens to early 20s, or at any age with gastrointestinal bleeding, polyps over 1 cm, innumerable polyps or high-grade dysplasia.
  • Upper tract: upper endoscopy for duodenal and ampullary adenomas, continued after colectomy.
  • Gardner syndrome: FAP plus osteomas and desmoid tumors.
  • Turcot syndrome: FAP plus central nervous system (CNS) tumors.
  • Peutz-Jeghers syndrome: autosomal dominant, a tumor-suppressor mutation, with mucocutaneous pigmented macules and two or more gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps.
  • Peutz-Jeghers macules: lips, buccal mucosa, palms and soles.
Which syndrome
Hereditary colon cancer syndromes: the differential
SyndromeIllness scriptThe tell
FAPAPC, autosomal dominant; adenomas carpet the colon from adolescenceHundreds of polyps; scope from puberty, colectomy in the teens to 20s
Gardner syndromeFAP variantPolyposis plus osteomas and desmoid tumors
Turcot syndromeFAP variantPolyposis plus CNS tumors
Lynch syndrome, or hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC)Mismatch-repair mutation; few polyps, early right-sided cancer; endometrial and other cancers in the familyEarly colon cancer with few polyps and an endometrial cancer in the pedigree
Peutz-Jeghers syndromeHamartomatous polyps that intussuscept or bleedMucocutaneous pigmentation of lips and buccal mucosa
Exceptions Sporadic family history – a first-degree relative with sporadic colon cancer follows a different schedule: colonoscopy at 40, or 10 years before the relative's cancer; earlier than average-risk screening, but not annual scoping from puberty · Lynch pedigree – few polyps and endometrial cancer in the family follow a third schedule
FAP: when to scope, when to operate
The ladder Testing unavailable – screen the child as affected · Why puberty – adenomas appear in adolescence and cancer follows within decades · Polyposis develops – plan surgery; any colectomy trigger means operating now, at any age, rather than in the teens to early 20s · The operation – proctocolectomy, or colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis; a retained rectum keeps its own endoscopic surveillance · After colectomy – upper endoscopy continues, because the duodenum and ampulla remain at risk
Peutz-Jeghers: pigment plus anemia
Pigmentation plus anemia: where the pigment is decides
DiagnosisThe pigmentThe anemiaWhat to do
Peutz-JeghersDiscrete brown macules on lips, buccal mucosa, palms and solesMicrocytic, from occult polyp bleedingUpper and lower endoscopy; genetic testing
Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)Diffuse, worst on pressure and sun-exposed areasUsually normocytic if presentACTH stimulation test
Lead poisoningBlue gingival line at the tooth marginMicrocytic with basophilic stipplingBlood lead level
Menstrual iron deficiencyNoneMicrocytic, from heavy or prolonged mensesIron; hormonal control if bleeding is heavy
Marrow failure or malignancyNoneUsually normocytic, with other cytopeniasBone marrow evaluation
Gates Not automatically menstrual – microcytic anemia in an adolescent girl: check the mouth, palms and family history · Polyp complications – obstruction or intussusception, anemia from bleeding, rectal prolapse · Intussusception – in an older child it has a lead point until proven otherwise; a hamartoma can be one; perioral pigmentation with intussusception in a child is the classic presentation · Normal platelets and leukocytes – argue against marrow failure
Cancer and family Cancer risk – gastrointestinal, pancreatic, breast and genital tract (ovary, cervix) cancers, plus testicular Sertoli cell tumors, so surveillance is lifelong · Why broader – the syndrome is an inherited STK11 variant, and its risk reaches past the gut: pancreas, breast, ovary, cervix, and Sertoli cell tumors of the testis; colorectal and gastric cancers can arise from adenomas common in Peutz-Jeghers · Faded macules – the macules can fade in adulthood but the polyp risk persists, so a normal skin examination in a parent does not exclude the family history
Practice
  1. 12-year-old boy is seen for a well visit His father has familial adenomatous polyposis genetic testing shows the family APC mutation Asymptomatic; no rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL · abdomen soft and nontender → Annual sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy starting now → the screening gate opens at puberty, age 10 to 12, so a known APC carrier starts annual sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy now. Colonoscopy at 40 is the sporadic family-history schedule and does not apply to a carrier; prophylactic colectomy is planned for the teens to early 20s, or sooner only for bleeding, polyps over 1 cm, innumerable polyps or high-grade dysplasia, and none is present
  2. 13-year-old girl has 2 months of fatigue Regular menses lasting 6 days; no medications pale conjunctivae; brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 70 fL · platelets and leukocytes normal → Upper and lower endoscopy → six-day menses with a microcytic anemia suggest menstrual iron deficiency, but brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa mark Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, so the anemia is occult bleeding from hamartomatous polyps: scope above and below. Iron with an oral contraceptive treats the anemia but leaves the syndrome undiagnosed; lead gives a blue gingival line, not mucosal macules
  3. 28-year-old man has a firm mass in the abdominal wall biopsy shows a desmoid tumor radiograph shows a mandibular osteoma colonoscopy shows hundreds of colonic adenomas No headaches or neurologic deficits Afebrile · hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL → Gardner syndrome → polyposis plus osteomas and desmoid tumors is Gardner syndrome, an FAP variant managed on the same pathway with the same colectomy rules. Turcot syndrome adds central nervous system tumors, and there are no neurologic findings; Peutz-Jeghers polyps are hamartomas that come with lip and buccal pigmentation
  4. 19-year-old man is seen for follow-up of familial adenomatous polyposis Annual colonoscopy since age 11 2 weeks of rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL · low ferritin consistent with iron deficiency → Colectomy now → bleeding is an any-age indication, so the operation planned for the teens to early 20s happens now. Polypectomy with iron treats the symptom and leaves a colon that adenomas carpet, and repeating colonoscopy in a year delays a trigger that is already met
  5. 15-year-old boy has 3 months of fatigue, anorexia and weight loss diffuse hyperpigmentation, darkest over the elbows, knees and sun-exposed skin No lip macules; gums normal BP 106/64 mm Hg · hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 88 fL → Addison disease → diffuse pigmentation, worst on pressure and sun-exposed areas, is primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), with an anemia that is usually normocytic if present; the adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation test answers it. Peutz-Jeghers gives discrete brown macules on the lips, buccal mucosa, palms and soles, and lead a blue gingival line with a microcytic anemia
  6. 10-year-old girl is seen for a well visit Her mother has familial adenomatous polyposis the girl has never had genetic testing Asymptomatic; no rectal bleeding Afebrile · growth at the 50th percentile · hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL → APC genetic testing → APC is autosomal dominant, so each child of an affected parent has a one-in-two risk and is tested rather than presumed: a positive result starts annual endoscopic screening, and a negative result for the known family mutation means average-risk screening. Average-risk screening presumes she is not a carrier, and annual fecal immunochemical testing is the wrong pathway for a carrier
  7. 16-year-old girl has 4 months of fatigue dark brown macules on the lips, buccal mucosa and palms Regular menses lasting 5 days; intermittent cramping abdominal pain Afebrile · hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 68 fL · platelets and leukocytes normal → Occult polyp bleeding → the macules mark Peutz-Jeghers, whose hamartomatous polyps bleed slowly and cause iron deficiency. The low MCV separates the bleeding causes from the marrow causes, and normal platelet and leukocyte counts argue against marrow failure, which is usually normocytic; microcytic anemia in an adolescent girl is not automatically menstrual once the macules are seen
  8. 14-year-old boy is seen for follow-up of familial adenomatous polyposis annual colonoscopy shows a few small adenomas, all under 1 cm biopsies show no dysplasia No rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL → Continue annual colonoscopy and plan colectomy for the late teens to early 20s → no immediate trigger is present: no bleeding, no polyp over 1 cm, the polyps are few rather than innumerable, and there is no high-grade dysplasia, so annual surveillance continues toward a planned prophylactic proctocolectomy. Operating now is for a met trigger, and a 5-year interval is not the annual schedule a carrier needs
  9. 15-year-old boy has recurrent cramping abdominal pain ultrasound shows a small-bowel intussusception pigmented macules on the lips, buccal mucosa and palms No vomiting; stools without visible blood Afebrile · HR 96/min · hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL → Peutz-Jeghers syndrome → mucocutaneous macules with hamartomatous polyps that intussuscept is Peutz-Jeghers, autosomal dominant; intussusception in an older child has a lead point until proven otherwise, and a hamartoma can be one. The tell of FAP is hundreds of colonic adenomas, and Addison pigmentation is diffuse, worst on pressure and sun-exposed areas, not discrete macules
  10. 23-year-old woman is seen for follow-up Total proctocolectomy for familial adenomatous polyposis 2 years ago Asymptomatic; eating well; no abdominal mass Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg · HR 72/min · hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL → Upper endoscopy for duodenal and ampullary adenomas → colectomy does not address duodenal and ampullary adenomas, so upper endoscopy surveillance continues; the duodenum and ampulla remain at risk, so stopping surveillance is wrong. A desmoid tumor marks Gardner syndrome, a feature of the variant rather than the surveillance that continues after colectomy, which is upper endoscopy
  11. 14-year-old girl has 2 months of fatigue a blue line along the gingival margin at the teeth No lip or buccal macules; regular 4-day menses Afebrile · hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 66 fL · basophilic stippling on the smear → Lead poisoning → a blue gingival line at the tooth margin with a microcytic anemia and basophilic stippling is lead poisoning: check a blood lead level. Peutz-Jeghers pigment is discrete macules on the lips and buccal mucosa, and menstrual iron deficiency brings no pigment and needs heavy or prolonged menses
  12. 17-year-old girl is seen for follow-up of familial adenomatous polyposis colonoscopy shows innumerable polyps, several over 1 cm biopsy of one polyp shows high-grade dysplasia No rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL → Total proctocolectomy → innumerable polyps, polyps over 1 cm and high-grade dysplasia are each an any-age colectomy trigger. Polypectomy of the largest lesions is not enough once innumerable polyps or dysplasia indicate colectomy, and a segmental resection leaves the rest of a colon that adenomas carpet
  13. 15-year-old girl has fatigue Regular menses every 28 days, lasting 6 days brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa No medications; no visible blood in stool Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 72 fL · platelets normal → Iron and an oral contraceptive → iron and an oral contraceptive treat the anemia but leave the syndrome undiagnosed. Upper and lower endoscopy finds the bleeding hamartomas, the source of the anemia, and adding STK11 testing confirms the syndrome, after which first-degree relatives are tested because inheritance is autosomal dominant
  14. 36-year-old woman has a right-sided colon cancer on colonoscopy 12 polyps elsewhere in the colon Her mother had endometrial cancer at 45; her brother had colon cancer at 42 Afebrile · hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL · no mucocutaneous pigmentation → Lynch syndrome → early right-sided colon cancer with few polyps and an endometrial cancer in the pedigree is Lynch syndrome, a mismatch-repair mutation: test the tumor for mismatch repair. FAP brings hundreds to thousands of adenomas, and Peutz-Jeghers brings hamartomas with lip and buccal pigmentation
  15. 20-year-old woman is seen for follow-up of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome STK11 mutation confirmed at age 14 Asymptomatic; her lip macules have faded Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 70/min · hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL → Periodic upper and lower endoscopy with small-bowel examination → surveillance is lifelong, upper and lower endoscopy and small-bowel examination every 2 to 3 years from about 18, plus breast and genital tract cancer screening, because the risk includes gastrointestinal, pancreatic, breast and genital tract (ovary, cervix) cancers, plus testicular Sertoli cell tumors; faded macules do not end the polyp risk. Prophylactic proctocolectomy is the FAP pathway, and the age-40 schedule belongs to sporadic family history
Common wrong answers Colonoscopy at 40: the sporadic family-history schedule; an APC carrier is scoped annually from puberty. Polypectomy of the largest lesions: not enough once innumerable polyps or dysplasia indicate colectomy. Stopping surveillance after colectomy: the duodenum and ampulla remain at risk. Iron with an oral contraceptive: an adolescent girl with menses and microcytic anemia looks like menstrual iron deficiency until the oral macules are noted. ACTH stimulation or a lead level: Addison disease and lead also cause pigmentation, but in a different distribution.
Pairs with Part I Abnormal Uterine Bleeding lists Lynch syndrome among the endometrial cancer risk factors; Lynch syndrome and its colorectal screening intervals are not covered on this page.
Transferable rule

Identify the hereditary syndrome first: start age, interval and operation all depend on it, and sporadic family-history numbers do not apply to a known carrier. When one finding does not fit an otherwise ordinary explanation, that finding usually determines the diagnosis.
