Feeding an Infant or Toddler

the feeding ladder by age · the toddler who refuses food · eosinophilic esophagitisIs the child well and due for the next age-gated step, or refusing a texture, a food group, or eating altogether?

Feeding by ageFood refusalManagementPractice
Bottom line

A well infant: read the age first; each feeding step has an age gate.

A child who refuses food: name the pattern before choosing a test.

  • Texture: every solid refused, purees only past 12 months. The esophagus (dysphagia).
  • Food group (bread and pasta: gluten): celiac disease or IgE (immunoglobulin E) allergy.
  • Appetite changed (lost, or increased with poor gain): systemic or metabolic disease.

Atopic toddler, purees only, normal swallow study: endoscopy with esophageal biopsy.

Feeding by age
The feeding ladder
AgeFeedAdvance when
0 to 6 monthsExclusive breast milk or formula; if breastfed or partially breastfed, vitamin D 400 IU (international units) daily; if breastfed, iron 1 mg/kg daily from 4 monthsAbout 6 months, readiness signs
About 6 monthsIron first (fortified cereal, pureed meats), then pureed vegetables and fruit, one new food every 3 to 5 days; stop supplemental iron once iron-rich foods are establishedSits independently; pincer grasp at 8 to 9 months
8 to 9 monthsSoft finger foods, lumpier textures, self-feeding, a cupTurns 12 months
12 monthsWhole cow's milk, limited to about 16 to 24 oz daily; table foods; off the bottleAge 2: reduced-fat milk
Defining criteria Readiness – sits with support, head control, no extrusion reflex, interest in food · Why 6 months – fetal iron stores deplete at 4 to 6 months; breast milk no longer meets iron and zinc needs · Pincer grasp – emerges at 8 to 9 months; the gate for finger foods · Vitamin D – continues through the first year · Whole milk to age 2 – fat is required for myelination in the second year
Not before 12 months Whole cow's milk – iron deficiency (low content, occult blood loss, poor absorption); later, cap at 16 to 24 oz · Honey – infant botulism · Fruit juice – none · Allergens – no delay; severe eczema or egg allergy: peanut at 4 to 6 months after evaluation
The toddler who refuses food
Defining findings Eosinophilic esophagitis – T helper type 2 (Th2) response to food antigen; most are atopic; 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, other causes, such as achalasia and infection, excluded · By age – toddler: refuses solids; school age: pain and vomiting; adolescent: dysphagia, impaction · Normal swallow study – excludes oropharyngeal dysfunction and aspiration
The toddler who stops advancing his diet
CauseThe tell
Celiac diseaseDiarrhea or constipation, pain, distension; avoids gluten foods only
Oropharyngeal dysphagiaCoughing and choking with feeds; abnormal video swallow study
Anatomic obstruction (stricture, ring, vascular ring)Abrupt onset, or a caustic or reflux history; esophagram or endoscopy shows it
Behavioral feeding disorderDevelopmental delay or autism spectrum; a normal endoscopy
Hyperthyroidism; abdominal massBig appetite, tachycardia, goiter; anorexia, palpable mass
Management
By diagnosis Eosinophilic esophagitis – a proton pump inhibitor, a swallowed topical glucocorticoid or dietary elimination are first-line options; feeding therapy for learned avoidance · Food impaction – urgent endoscopy · Allergy testing – only after biopsy confirms the diagnosis, to guide the elimination diet; tests may have limited accuracy for food triggers · Normal endoscopy – feeding therapy
Practice
  1. 18-month-old boy takes only purees and refuses every solid food weight fell from the 25th to the 5th percentile height steady at the 30th Eczema; always a picky eater; development normal Afebrile · stools soft and daily · swallow study normal → Endoscopy with esophageal biopsy → a texture refusal in an atopic toddler with a normal swallow study points below the pharynx: biopsy, where 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field is diagnostic
  2. 2-year-old boy was diagnosed with eosinophilic esophagitis last week biopsy showed 30 eosinophils per high-power field takes purees, refuses solids Eczema; parents ask about first-line treatment Afebrile · weight at the 10th percentile · examination normal → Dietary elimination → a proton pump inhibitor, a swallowed topical glucocorticoid or dietary elimination are first-line options; systemic prednisone and dilation are not
  3. 16-year-old boy has had meat stuck in his chest for 3 hours now drooling, cannot swallow saliva was diagnosed with eosinophilic esophagitis at age 12 Breathing comfortably, no stridor HR 104/min · oxygen saturation 98% · afebrile → Urgent endoscopy → food impaction is the adolescent presentation of eosinophilic esophagitis: urgent endoscopy
  4. 8-year-old girl has had abdominal pain and vomiting for 6 months asthma and allergic rhinitis esophageal biopsies show 25 eosinophils per high-power field No diarrhea or weight loss Afebrile · abdomen soft and nontender → Eosinophilic esophagitis → abdominal pain and vomiting in an atopic child is the school-age presentation; 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, with other causes excluded, makes the diagnosis
  5. 3-year-old girl has poor weight gain and chronic diarrhea abdomen distended refuses bread and pasta but eats other solids Weight fell from the 50th to the 10th percentile Afebrile · development normal → Tissue transglutaminase IgA with a total IgA level → a food-group refusal with diarrhea and distension points to gluten: celiac serology, sent with a total IgA level
  6. 14-month-old boy coughs and chokes during most feeds two prior pneumonias weight at the 10th percentile No eczema, asthma or diarrhea T 37.0 °C · respiratory rate 30/min · lungs clear · abdomen soft → Video swallow study → coughing and choking with feeds and aspiration pneumonias are oropharyngeal dysfunction: a video swallow study
  7. 20-month-old girl takes only purees and gags on solids eczema and asthma weight down to the 5th percentile Normal swallow study; eosinophilic inflammation of the esophagus is suspected Afebrile · development normal · stools soft → Allergy skin testing → skin testing shows IgE sensitization only; it diagnoses IgE-mediated allergy, not this, and guides the elimination diet after biopsy
  8. 2-year-old boy has poor weight gain and eats only a few soft foods development normal, no eczema or asthma swallow study normal Endoscopy and esophageal biopsies normal Afebrile · stools soft and daily · weight at the 5th percentile → Feeding therapy for a behavioral feeding disorder → the scope has excluded the organ: a behavioral feeding disorder, treated with feeding therapy
  9. 9-year-old boy was diagnosed with eosinophilic esophagitis after months of vomiting eczema, allergic rhinitis and a peanut allergy biopsy: 40 eosinophils per high-power field Parents ask what drives the inflammation Afebrile · growth normal → A Th2-mediated response to food antigen → a T helper type 2 response to food antigen; comorbid atopy is the clinical correlate; the peanut allergy is IgE-mediated, the esophageal lesion is not
  10. 6-year-old girl was diagnosed with eosinophilic esophagitis by biopsy last month eczema and seasonal allergic rhinitis starting dietary elimination Parents ask whether allergy skin testing still has a role Afebrile · growth at the 40th percentile → To guide dietary elimination given frequent concomitant IgE sensitivities → after the diagnosis, never instead of it: skin testing may guide which foods to eliminate, though its accuracy for food triggers is limited
  11. 6-month-old girl is seen for a well visit born at term takes breast milk, formula and iron-fortified cereal Weight 75th, length 60th percentile Afebrile · examination normal · good head control · sits with support → Begin pureed vegetables and fruit, one new food every few days → the iron source is already in: next comes variety, one new single-ingredient food every 3 to 5 days
  12. 9-month-old boy is seen for a well visit sits independently, brings food to his mouth pincer grasp emerging Tolerating purees of cereal, meats, vegetables and fruit Afebrile · weight 50th percentile · examination normal → Offer soft finger foods → an emerging pincer grasp at 8 to 9 months is the gate for soft finger foods and self-feeding
  13. 12-month-old girl is seen for a well visit healthy, tracking the 50th percentile still taking formula from a bottle Eats table foods with the family Afebrile · hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL · examination normal → Whole cow's milk, about 16 to 24 oz daily → at 12 months, whole cow's milk capped at 16 to 24 oz daily and a move from bottle to cup; reduced-fat milk waits until age 2
  14. 14-month-old boy is pale and irritable drinks 40 oz of whole milk daily eats little else No bleeding, no dark stools Afebrile · HR 128/min · hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 68 fL → Limit milk under 24 oz daily and start oral iron → excess cow's milk causes iron deficiency (low iron content, occult blood loss, impaired absorption): cap the milk and give oral iron
  15. 6-month-old girl is seen for a well visit parents ask about giving fruit juice takes breast milk and iron-fortified cereal Started pureed vegetables last week Afebrile · weight 50th percentile · examination normal → Give no fruit juice before 12 months → no fruit juice before 12 months; offer water in a cup with meals
  16. 4-month-old boy is seen for a well visit exclusively breastfed, born at term already receiving vitamin D No complementary foods started yet; parents ask about supplements Afebrile · weight 50th percentile · examination normal → Oral iron 1 mg/kg daily → a breastfed infant gets iron 1 mg/kg daily from 4 months until iron-rich complementary foods are established
  17. 3-day-old girl is seen for her first newborn visit exclusively breastfed, latching well born at term after an uncomplicated delivery Parents ask which supplements she needs Afebrile · weight 4% below birth weight · examination normal → Vitamin D 400 IU daily → every breastfed or partially breastfed infant gets vitamin D 400 IU daily from the first days through the first year
  18. 5-month-old boy is seen for a well visit severe eczema since 2 months known egg allergy Parents ask when peanut can safely be started Afebrile · weight 40th percentile · examination otherwise normal → Introduce peanut-containing food early, after evaluation → delaying allergens is obsolete: with severe eczema or egg allergy, introduce peanut at 4 to 6 months after evaluation
  19. 8-month-old girl is seen for a well visit grandmother asks which foods to hold until the first birthday eats purees of cereal, meat and vegetables Started soft finger foods this week Afebrile · examination normal → Honey → honey before 12 months risks infant botulism; peanut is introduced early and iron-fortified cereal is a first food
Decoys Always a picky eater: suggests a behavioral cause, but development is normal. Eczema in the past history: easy to overlook. Allergy skin testing: diagnoses IgE-mediated allergy (acute urticaria, angioedema). Finger foods, whole milk: right steps, wrong age; exclusive breastfeeding runs through 6 months, not beyond.
Pairs with Abnormal Growth in a Child: refusing food, or simply failing to grow? Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth: is the curve crossing lines? Stool Changes in a Well Infant: cow's-milk protein before 12 months.
Transferable rule

When the child is well and every option is reasonable, choose by age. When the child refuses food, name the pattern (texture, food group, appetite) before choosing a test.

Hip and Thigh Pain and Numbness

groin vs lateral vs buttock · tendon vs nerve · which nerves have motor fibers · when to imageWhere is the pain, and is there tenderness, weakness or only numbness?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Sort by location, then trust findings over descriptors:

  • Groin: the joint itself (osteoarthritis, avascular necrosis, fracture, labral tear).
  • Lateral hip: trochanter and its tendons, greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS), or the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.
  • Buttock: spine, sacroiliac joint or piriformis.

Point tenderness over the trochanter with a normal neurologic exam is GTPS, however burning the pain sounds.

The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is purely sensory: a numb upper lateral thigh with normal strength is meralgia paresthetica, and normal strength confirms it.

Diagnosis
Defining findings GTPS – overuse tendinopathy of gluteus medius and minimus at the greater trochanter (trochanteric bursitis is a misnomer); point tenderness, normal range of motion; worse lying on that side, stairs, uphill, getting out of a car; age 50 or more, women, obesity, lower-limb or low-back disorders · Meralgia paresthetica – lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, from the L2 (second lumbar) and L3 (third lumbar) roots, compressed under the inguinal ligament near the ASIS (anterior superior iliac spine); upper lateral thigh patch, no bony tenderness, no motor loss; tight belts, straining, obesity, pregnancy
Hip and thigh: the mimics
DiagnosisWhere and whatThe tell
Hip osteoarthritis (OA)Groin or medial, to thigh or knee; internal rotation reduced, groin pain on FABER (flexion, abduction, external rotation)Crepitus; morning stiffness under 30 minutes
Femoral neck stress fractureGroin or anterior; pain with hopping and log-rollRunner or recruit; female athlete triad: MRI
Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral headGroin; motion reduced in all planesSteroids, alcohol, sickle cell: MRI
Gluteal tendon tearLateral hip; abductor weakness, Trendelenburg gaitSevere end of GTPS: MRI
Osteoid osteomaProximal femur; often no focal finding in adultsNight pain dramatically relieved by an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug); children and young adults
Iliotibial (IT) band syndromeLateral knee at the femoral condyle; Noble testA knee diagnosis, not a hip one
L2 to L3 radiculopathyDermatomal with back pain; hip flexion weaknessFemoral stretch test positive
Femoral neuropathyAnterior thigh and medial leg; quadriceps weaknessReduced patellar reflex
Diabetic amyotrophyProximal weakness, wasting; asymmetricSevere pain and weight loss
Piriformis syndromeButtock, down the back of the thigh; worse sittingPiriformis tenderness, normal neurologic exam
Diabetic polyneuropathyStocking-glove, feet first; motor lateBilateral, symmetric; vibration lost first
Management and treatment
Management ladder: GTPS
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Activity modification, an NSAID and physical therapy (abductor strengthening)Refractory
2Corticosteroid injectionRefractory to injection: refer to investigate the underlying cause
Any tierAbductor weakness or Trendelenburg gaitMRI for a gluteal tendon tear
By diagnosis Meralgia paresthetica – weight loss, loosen restrictive belts; conservative care resolves over 90% · Metformin neuropathy – vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency over years gives a distal symmetric neuropathy, never a focal thigh patch · Peroneal palsy – foot drop after leg-crossing or rapid weight loss, at the fibular head · Other sensory-only nerves – sural (lateral foot), superficial peroneal (foot dorsum), saphenous (medial leg), digital (Morton neuroma, third interspace between the third and fourth toes, Mulder click)
Practice
  1. 54-year-old woman has 3 months of lateral hip pain she calls burning worse lying on that side and on stairs point tenderness over the greater trochanter Hip range of motion full; neurologic exam normal Afebrile · body mass index 33 → Greater trochanteric pain syndrome → tenderness over the trochanter with a normal neurologic exam outweighs the word burning: greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS); activity modification, an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) and physical therapy
  2. 58-year-old woman was diagnosed with greater trochanteric pain syndrome 2 months ago still tender over the trochanter 8 weeks of an NSAID and abductor-strengthening therapy No weakness or limp Afebrile · hip range of motion full → Corticosteroid injection → refractory to an NSAID and physical therapy: corticosteroid injection; MRI is for suspected tendon tear
  3. 66-year-old woman has 6 months of lateral hip pain weak hip abduction Trendelenburg gait Tender over the greater trochanter; worse lying on that side Afebrile · no back pain · sensation and reflexes normal · hip internal rotation full → Gluteus medius tendon tear → abductor weakness with a Trendelenburg gait is the severe end of the GTPS spectrum, a gluteus medius tendon tear: MRI; weakness separates a tear from uncomplicated GTPS, which has normal strength
  4. 67-year-old man has 2 years of groin pain pain radiates to the knee, worse after walking internal rotation reduced, with crepitus Morning stiffness under 30 minutes Afebrile · body mass index 29 · no trochanteric tenderness → Hip OA → groin pain with reduced internal rotation and crepitus is the joint itself, hip osteoarthritis: radiograph
  5. 26-year-old woman training for a marathon has groin pain pain when she hops on that leg log-roll of the leg reproduces the groin pain Hip radiograph normal; irregular periods Afebrile · body mass index 18 → Femoral neck stress fracture → groin pain on hopping in a runner with a normal film is a femoral neck stress fracture: MRI; irregular periods and low weight suggest the female athlete triad
  6. 30-year-old man, a cyclist, has lateral knee pain tender over the lateral femoral condyle Noble test reproduces it Hip examination normal; rides 200 km a week Afebrile · BP 118/70 mm Hg · no knee effusion → IT band syndrome → lateral knee pain at the femoral condyle with a positive Noble test is iliotibial (IT) band syndrome, a knee diagnosis, not a hip one
  7. 40-year-old man has numbness over the upper lateral thigh a patch that burns when he wears a tight belt no tenderness over the trochanter; no back pain Strength normal; reflexes normal Afebrile · body mass index 36 → Meralgia paresthetica → a sensory-only patch on the upper lateral thigh with normal strength is meralgia paresthetica; a radiculopathy usually brings back pain, a dermatomal pattern or weakness
  8. 16-year-old boy has 3 months of thigh pain pain wakes him at night ibuprofen relieves it dramatically No trauma; no weight loss Afebrile · radiograph: small lucency with sclerosis in the proximal femur → Osteoid osteoma → night pain dramatically relieved by NSAIDs in a young patient is an osteoid osteoma; CT (computed tomography) shows the nidus
  9. 45-year-old man on prednisone for 2 years has progressive groin pain drinks heavily range of motion reduced in all planes Hip radiograph normal; no trauma Afebrile · BP 124/78 mm Hg · hemoglobin normal → AVN → steroids or alcohol with groin pain and a normal film is avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)
  10. 38-year-old woman has 2 months of right buttock pain pain runs down the back of the thigh worse sitting, tender over the piriformis No back pain; straight-leg raise negative Afebrile · strength, reflexes and sensation normal → Piriformis syndrome → buttock pain sorts to the spine, sacroiliac joint or piriformis; worse sitting with piriformis tenderness and a normal neurologic exam fits piriformis syndrome
  11. 44-year-old man, obese, has burning numbness over the upper lateral thigh wears a tight work belt every day no back pain Strength 5/5 throughout Afebrile · BP 136/86 mm Hg · reflexes normal · body mass index 37 → Meralgia paresthetica → the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is purely sensory, so full strength confirms meralgia paresthetica: weight loss and loosening restrictive belts
  12. 44-year-old man has numbness over the anterior thigh and medial leg weak knee extension reduced patellar reflex Began after a long procedure in the lithotomy position; no back pain Afebrile · BP 128/80 mm Hg → Femoral neuropathy → anterior thigh and medial leg numbness with quadriceps weakness and a reduced patellar reflex is a femoral neuropathy
  13. 44-year-old man has 2 months of lateral thigh numbness back pain radiating to the knee reduced patellar reflex, weak hip flexion Femoral stretch test positive; no bladder symptoms Afebrile · BP 132/84 mm Hg → L2–L3 radiculopathy → back pain with weakness, a reduced reflex and a positive femoral stretch test is an L2 to L3 radiculopathy; meralgia has no motor or reflex loss
  14. 56-year-old woman has 2 months of lateral hip pain point tenderness over the greater trochanter no numbness Worse lying on that side and climbing stairs Afebrile · strength normal · knee examination normal → Trochanteric bursitis → trochanteric tenderness without numbness is trochanteric bursitis, the older, misnamed label for greater trochanteric pain syndrome; the exam may still use it
  15. 60-year-old man with diabetes has severe right thigh pain proximal leg weakness and thigh wasting lost 7 kg in 2 months Asymmetric; the left leg is spared Afebrile · hemoglobin A1c 9.1% → Diabetic amyotrophy → severe asymmetric thigh pain, proximal weakness and weight loss in diabetes is diabetic amyotrophy; polyneuropathy is symmetric and starts in the feet
  16. 44-year-old man has burning numbness over the upper lateral thigh since he started wearing a tool belt strength and reflexes normal No back pain Afebrile · sensory loss in a patch on the upper lateral thigh → No testing; it is a clinical diagnosis → meralgia paresthetica is a clinical diagnosis; no imaging or electrodiagnostic testing is needed
Transferable rule

When the pain quality and the findings disagree, rely on the findings. A nerve's motor content sets what its lesion can look like: if it has no motor fibers, a normal motor exam confirms rather than refutes.

Oral Lesions in a Child

vesicles vs exudate · front of the mouth or back · herpangina vs herpetic gingivostomatitis · the palm and sole rashAre the lesions vesicles or exudate, and do they sit at the front of the mouth or the back?

Source vignette Pt — 5 yo M, 3 days of fever with 2 days of throat pain and poor intake; T 38.3, HR 108 · Exam — scattered 1 mm vesicles on the anterior palatine pillars with gray shallow ulcers on the soft palate and uvula; tongue, lips and buccal mucosa spared; no rash · Q — the most likely associated pathogen; options spanned adenovirus, coxsackievirus, Epstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex virus and Streptococcus pyogenes
The decision point

The lesions are vesicles and ulcers, not exudate. This removes every bacterial and mononucleosis-type pharyngitis. Adenovirus, EBV (Epstein-Barr virus) and S. pyogenes all produce tonsillar exudate, and none produces oral vesicles. The lesions are posterior (soft palate, uvula, anterior palatine pillars), with the tongue, lips and buccal mucosa explicitly spared. Herpangina, from coxsackievirus A, affects the back of the mouth. In herpetic gingivostomatitis, lesions affect the front, with red swollen gums. The spared structures are exactly those HSV (herpes simplex virus) would involve.

Defining criteria Herpangina — coxsackievirus A; ages 3 to 10; late summer and early fall; fever and pharyngitis with gray vesicles progressing to fibrin-coated ulcers on the posterior oropharynx, and no rash; treatment is supportive · Herpetic gingivostomatitis — HSV-1; 6 months to 5 years; no seasonality; clusters of vesicles on the anterior oral mucosa and lips with erythematous, edematous gingiva; treated with oral acyclovir · Hand-foot-and-mouth disease — also coxsackievirus, but anterior oral lesions plus vesicles on palms and soles; herpangina's defining negative is the absent rash
Pertinent positives & negatives Vesicles and ulcers, not exudate — excludes adenovirus, EBV and group A streptococcus in one move · Soft palate, uvula and palatine pillars involved — the posterior distribution, herpangina territory · Tongue, lips and buccal mucosa spared — a stated negative that excludes HSV gingivostomatitis, whose distribution is precisely those structures · No rash — separates herpangina from hand-foot-and-mouth disease · No gingival erythema or edema described — a second strike against HSV, whose gingivitis is near-universal · Age 5, starting the fall term in 2 weeks — age 3 to 10 and late summer, both epidemiological features; the school detail is dating the season, not flagging exposure · No adenopathy or splenomegaly — nothing to support mononucleosis
Oral lesions in a child — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Herpangina (coxsackievirus A)3 to 10 yrs, late summer and early fall, abrupt high feverPosterior gray vesicles becoming ulcers: soft palate, uvula, pillars; no rash— (the answer)
Herpetic gingivostomatitis (HSV-1)6 months to 5 years, any season; drooling, refuses to drinkAnterior clusters on buccal mucosa, tongue and lips; swollen red gingivaThose exact sites are stated as spared
Hand-foot-and-mouth diseaseSame virus family, same seasonAnterior oral lesions plus palms and solesThe skin has no rash
Streptococcal pharyngitisFever, sore throat, no coughTonsillar exudate, tender anterior nodes, palatal petechiaeVesicles and ulcers rather than exudate
Infectious mononucleosisAdolescent with prolonged fatigueExudate plus posterior cervical nodes plus splenomegalyNo exudate, no adenopathy, no splenomegaly
Adenoviral tonsillitisFever, cough, sore throat, sometimes conjunctivitisExudate without vesiclesVesicular lesions are not its picture
Decision spine Vesicles and ulcers, or exudate? — Vesicles means a viral enanthem, and the bacterial and EBV options fall · Front of the mouth or back? — Back means herpangina · Are the gums red and swollen? — Not described, which argues against HSV · Is there a rash on palms and soles? — No, so not hand-foot-and-mouth · Age and season? — Five years in late summer corroborates · So what is the management? — Supportive; it self-resolves within a week
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M, 3 days of fever with throat pain, 1 mm vesicles on the anterior palatine pillars and gray shallow ulcers on the soft palate and uvula, tongue and lips and buccal mucosa spared, no rash → Coxsackievirus A → herpangina
  2. 2 yo with fever, drooling and refusal to drink; clusters of vesicles on the gingiva, tongue and lips with erythematous edematous gums → Herpetic gingivostomatitis → oral acyclovir
  3. 3 yo with fever, oral ulcers and vesicles on the palms and soles → Hand-foot-and-mouth disease → supportive care
  4. 5 yo with posterior oral vesicles and ulcers, drinking less but with moist mucous membranes and normal vital signs → Cold non-acidic fluids with analgesia → herpangina resolves within a week
  5. 8 yo with fever, tonsillar exudate and tender anterior cervical nodes, without cough or oral vesicles → Group A streptococcal pharyngitis → rapid antigen testing before treating
  6. 16 yo with 2 weeks of fatigue, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly → Epstein-Barr virus infection → avoid contact sports
  7. 5 yo with gray vesicles and ulcers confined to the soft palate and uvula, no rash, well hydrated → Oral acyclovir → herpangina is an enteroviral illness, not a herpesvirus one
  8. 4 yo with herpangina now refusing all fluids, with dry mucous membranes and no urine output for 10 hours → Intravenous rehydration → dehydration is the principal complication
  9. 5 yo in late summer with abrupt fever and sore throat; gray vesicles and shallow ulcers on the soft palate, uvula and anterior pillars; gums, lips and tongue normal; no rash → Herpangina → coxsackievirus A; supportive care
Pearls Anterior is herpes, posterior is coxsackie — both diseases otherwise present with fever, sore throat and a miserable child · Vesicles and ulcers exclude exudate-producing pathogens wholesale: strep, EBV and adenovirus make exudate, not blisters · Herpangina has no rash; hand-foot-and-mouth does — same virus family, separated by the skin · Red swollen gingiva is the HSV signature, and its absence is as informative as any positive finding · Starting the fall term in two weeks is dating the season, not describing an exposure · The virus can stay in stool for weeks after infection, so hand hygiene is the public-health answer
Pairs with Part I Respiratory Infection in a Child covers the exudative pharyngitis fork and the Centor rule; this brief covers vesicular lesions. Ask: are the lesions exudate or vesicles, and are they front or back? Part II Fever and Rash in a Child sorts hand-foot-and-mouth disease among the other rashes with fever.
Transferable rule When two diseases share a lesion type, the discriminating attribute is usually anatomical, not clinical. Ask where the lesions are before asking what they are. Treat a stated spared structure as an active exclusion, not as background.
Unchecked attributeHerpes simplex virus: oral vesicles in a child retrieves HSV automatically, but HSV is anterior and those sites are explicitly spared, with no gingival swelling.
Class-vs-memberAdenovirus: a common cause of pediatric fever with sore throat, but it produces exudative tonsillitis, not vesicles or ulcers.
Class-vs-memberStreptococcus pyogenes: exudate with tender anterior nodes; vesicles and ulcers argue against it.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpstein-Barr virus: exudate, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and adolescent age; none present.

Hypertension in an Adult

baseline panel · end-organ injury starts the drug · comorbidity picks it · secondary causes and how renin separates themIs there end-organ injury or a comorbidity that picks the drug, and is the patient resistant, young or hypokalemic?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Confirmed hypertension gets one baseline panel: it looks for end-organ injury and the comorbidity that picks the drug.

  • End-organ injury, such as LVH (left ventricular hypertrophy) on ECG (electrocardiogram): start treatment at that visit; echo or stress testing never delays it.
  • No comorbidity: an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor, ARB (angiotensin receptor blocker), thiazide or dihydropyridine CCB (calcium channel blocker), interchangeable first-line.
  • A comorbidity: match the drug to it. Gout takes losartan (mildly uricosuric); thiazides are avoided because they raise urate.
  • Resistant, young or hypokalemic: hunt a secondary cause. In a young patient, hypertension with hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis and normal renal function is mineralocorticoid excess.
  • Renin separates the look-alikes: suppressed in primary hyperaldosteronism, high in renal artery stenosis.
Diagnosis
Secondary hypertension: what to test for
DiagnosisThe stem showsFirst testConfirms, then
Primary hyperaldosteronismHypokalemia and alkalosisAldosterone-to-renin ratioAldosterone fails to suppress with salt loading; then adrenal CT (computed tomography) and adrenal venous sampling to lateralize
Fibromuscular dysplasia (“string of beads”, media of the artery)Young woman, abdominal bruitRenal artery duplex or CT angiographyCT or MR (magnetic resonance) angiography; catheter angiography is the reference standard
PheochromocytomaEpisodic hypertension, headache, sweatingPlasma or urine metanephrinesMetanephrines several-fold high; then adrenal CT or MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) to locate the tumor
Obstructive sleep apneaSnoring, obesity, daytime sleepinessPolysomnographyPolysomnography is itself confirmatory; a home study can screen
Coarctation of the aortaWeak femoral pulses, rib notchingEcho or CTArm-leg pressure gradient first at the bedside; CT or MR angiography defines the narrowing
Cushing syndromeStriae, moon facies, hyperglycemiaLow-dose dexamethasone or 24-hour cortisolA second, different screening test abnormal (late-night salivary cortisol, 24-hour urine cortisol, 1 mg dexamethasone); then ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone) to localize
Mechanism Aldosterone – raises ENaC (epithelial sodium channel) in the collecting duct; sodium reabsorption leaves the lumen electronegative, which drives potassium and hydrogen ion secretion: hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis · Aldosterone escape – through ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide) and pressure natriuresis, sodium plateaus and there is no edema; a normal sodium does not argue against the diagnosis · Bilateral renal artery stenosis – classically flash pulmonary edema with severe hypertension in an elderly patient with vascular disease
Management and treatment
Antihypertensive choice by comorbidity
ComorbidityPreferred agents
Coronary diseaseAngina: β-blocker, CCB; after myocardial infarction: ACE inhibitor or ARB plus β-blocker
Heart failure with reduced ejection fractionACE inhibitor or ARB, β-blocker, diuretic, aldosterone antagonist
Atrial fibrillation or flutterβ-blocker, nondihydropyridine CCB
Chronic kidney diseaseACE inhibitor or ARB
GoutLosartan, other ARB, CCB; avoid diuretics
OsteoporosisThiazide diuretic
Migraineβ-blocker, CCB
Calcium kidney stonesThiazide diuretic
By situation Two drugs – stage 2 hypertension (BP 140/90 mm Hg or more): most adults start two first-line drugs from different classes, preferably as one single-pill combination · LVH – regresses on an ARB or ACE inhibitor · Atrial fibrillation – a β-blocker or a nondihydropyridine CCB controls rate and treats the pressure; avoid combining them (bradycardia, heart block, depressed contractility) · Bilateral renal artery stenosis – when severe, an ACE inhibitor can cause AKI (acute kidney injury): the efferent arteriole needs angiotensin II to maintain GFR (glomerular filtration rate)
Practice
  1. 48-year-old man has hypertension confirmed on 3 separate visits gout, no flares in a year on allopurinol ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy No chest pain or dyspnea BP 136/86 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · uric acid 8.4 mg/dL → Losartan → gout picks losartan, which is mildly uricosuric; a thiazide raises urate, and stopping allopurinol treats neither the pressure nor the hypertrophy and invites a flare
  2. 62-year-old woman has hypertension on repeated office readings osteoporosis, with a hip T-score of -2.7 BP unchanged after 6 months of lifestyle changes No gout, kidney disease or migraine BP 134/84 mm Hg · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → Thiazide diuretic → a thiazide reduces urinary calcium loss, so one drug treats both the pressure and the osteoporosis; losartan and a dihydropyridine CCB treat only the pressure
  3. 60-year-old man has hypertension on repeated readings chronic kidney disease, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 420 mg/g No diabetes, gout or heart failure; takes no medications BP 138/86 mm Hg · potassium 4.6 mEq/L → ACE inhibitor → albuminuric chronic kidney disease takes an ACE inhibitor or ARB; a thiazide or a nondihydropyridine CCB treats only the pressure
  4. 45-year-old woman has hypertension on repeated readings migraine headaches 6 times a month BP unchanged after 6 months of lifestyle changes No gout, kidney disease or osteoporosis BP 136/84 mm Hg · HR 78/min → Beta-blocker → a beta-blocker treats both the pressure and the migraine, one drug for both diagnoses; a thiazide treats only the pressure, and hydralazine is not a first-line class
  5. 58-year-old man has hypertension on repeated readings 3 calcium kidney stones in 4 years urine calcium high on a 24-hour collection No gout or kidney disease BP 134/86 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL → Thiazide diuretic → a thiazide reduces urinary calcium and treats both; a loop diuretic increases urinary calcium, and losartan treats only the pressure
  6. 55-year-old man has hypertension newly confirmed on home readings ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy no chest pain, exertional dyspnea or syncope Baseline electrolytes, creatinine and urinalysis normal BP 138/88 mm Hg · HR 72/min → Start an antihypertensive now → left ventricular hypertrophy is end-organ injury, the treatment gate; echo or stress testing only characterizes it and never delays the first drug
  7. 29-year-old man has hypertension found at a work physical potassium 2.8 mEq/L bicarbonate 32 mEq/L, metabolic alkalosis No headaches, sweating or abdominal bruit BP 168/102 mm Hg · sodium 142 mEq/L · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Aldosterone-to-renin ratio → hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis with normal renal function are mineralocorticoid excess; a suppressed renin separates primary hyperaldosteronism from renovascular disease, and a normal sodium (aldosterone escape) does not argue against it. Duplex fits a bruit, metanephrines fit spells
  8. 32-year-old woman has new hypertension found at a routine visit abdominal bruit lateral to the umbilicus plasma renin activity elevated Femoral pulses normal and equal to radial pulses BP 166/102 mm Hg · potassium 4.0 mEq/L · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → Fibromuscular dysplasia → a young woman with an abdominal bruit and high renin has fibromuscular dysplasia (“string of beads”, a disease of the media): CT angiography. Primary hyperaldosteronism suppresses renin; coarctation weakens the femoral pulses
  9. 38-year-old man has spells of pounding headache palpitations and drenching sweats during spells hypertension during spells, normal pressure between Thyroid-stimulating hormone normal BP 188/110 mm Hg during a spell · HR 124/min → Pheochromocytoma → episodic hypertension with headache, palpitations and sweating is pheochromocytoma: plasma free metanephrines, several-fold high, then adrenal CT or MRI. A normal thyroid-stimulating hormone argues against hyperthyroidism, and panic disorder is not diagnosed when another condition better explains the spells
  10. 16-year-old boy has headaches and hypertension at a sports physical weak, delayed femoral pulses chest radiograph shows rib notching No palpitations, sweating or snoring right arm BP 162/94 mm Hg · leg BP 118/70 mm Hg → Coarctation of the aorta → weak femoral pulses, rib notching and an arm-leg pressure gradient are coarctation of the aorta; CT or MR angiography defines the narrowing. The arm-leg gradient places the narrowing in the aorta
  11. 48-year-old man has hypertension resistant to 3 medications loud snoring and daytime sleepiness body mass index 38 kg/m², obese No striae; neck circumference 46 cm BP 158/98 mm Hg · potassium 4.3 mEq/L → Obstructive sleep apnea → snoring, daytime sleepiness and obesity with resistant hypertension are obstructive sleep apnea: polysomnography, itself the confirmatory test. Snoring, sleepiness and a thick neck point to the airway first, and there are no striae to suggest Cushing syndrome
  12. 42-year-old woman has new hypertension and 6 months of weight gain wide purple abdominal striae round, full face Snoring absent; no episodic headache, palpitations or sweating BP 158/96 mm Hg · fasting glucose 168 mg/dL → Cushing syndrome → striae, moon facies and hyperglycemia are Cushing syndrome: an overnight dexamethasone suppression test, then a second, different screening test, then ACTH to localize
  13. 44-year-old woman has hypertension and potassium 3.0 mEq/L was diagnosed with primary hyperaldosteronism after salt loading CT shows a 1.5-cm left adrenal nodule She is willing to undergo surgery BP 162/98 mm Hg · renin suppressed → Adrenal venous sampling → bilateral adrenal hyperplasia is more common than adenoma, so adrenal venous sampling lateralizes before any adrenalectomy; another CT shows the anatomy again, not which gland secretes
  14. 74-year-old man has severe hypertension peripheral vascular disease with claudication was diagnosed with bilateral renal artery stenosis on CT angiography A new antihypertensive is being chosen BP 186/104 mm Hg · creatinine 1.4 mg/dL → An ACE inhibitor → the efferent arteriole needs angiotensin II to maintain GFR, so with bilateral lesions an ACE inhibitor is contraindicated: it can cause AKI; a calcium channel blocker and a thiazide are effective at controlling pressure in renal artery stenosis
  15. 66-year-old man has hypertension that has worsened over a year abdominal bruit and high plasma renin CT angiography: 80% narrowing of the left renal artery BP 174/100 mm Hg · potassium 3.3 mEq/L · creatinine 1.2 mg/dL → Angiotensin II → renin initiates the cascade and aldosterone causes the hypokalemia, but angiotensin II directly mediates the vasoconstriction
Common wrong answers Discontinue the allopurinol: the uric acid level baits it, but it lowers nothing that matters; it treats neither the pressure nor the LVH and invites a flare. Echo or stress testing first: characterization never delays treatment.
Pairs with Part I Inherited Tumor Syndromes: the hypertension is one organ in a heritable pattern. Part II Stroke in a Child or Adolescent: fibromuscular dysplasia versus Takayasu arteritis, the inflammatory cause of renal artery stenosis in a young patient. Part II Hypokalemia and Acid-Base Disorders in a Child: low potassium without hypertension, sorted by acid-base status.
Transferable rule

Store the pairings, never a favorite drug: the same agent is preferred with one comorbidity and avoided with another. Name what the evidence proves: labs prove the physiology (hyperaldosteronism), imaging or pathology proves the lesion (adrenal adenoma).

edits.html:
Hypoxemia

five mechanisms · A-a gradient · response to oxygen · shunt vs ventilation-perfusion mismatch · saturation gapIs the A-a gradient widened, and does the hypoxemia correct when inspired oxygen rises?

Source vignette Pt — 28 wk preterm, 1 hour old, cyanosis with grunting and increased work of breathing, bilaterally decreased breath sounds · Q — the mechanism of the hypoxemia; options spanned five mechanisms — intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, hypoventilation, diffusion limitation and low inspired oxygen
The decision point

Grunting with bilaterally decreased breath sounds at one hour of life in a 28-weeker indicates diffuse alveolar collapse. Surfactant deficiency raises alveolar surface tension, and the alveoli close. Those units stay perfused while their ventilation falls to zero, so blood crossing them reaches the left heart unoxygenated. This is intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt. Of the five mechanisms listed, it is the only one that produces cyanosis with increased work of breathing and bilaterally reduced air entry.

Defining criteria A-a gradient — alveolar minus arterial PO2 (partial pressure of oxygen). Widened in shunt, V/Q mismatch, and diffusion limitation; normal in hypoventilation and in low inspired PO2. Normal value approximately (age/4) + 4 · Shunt vs V/Q mismatch — shunt is the limiting case of mismatch (V/Q = 0). The gate is the oxygen response: mismatch corrects with modest supplemental oxygen; true shunt barely moves, because blood bypassing ventilated alveoli never sees the higher FiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen) · Saturation gap — pulse oximetry (SpO2) far below what the measured PaO2 (arterial partial pressure of oxygen) predicts → the hemoglobin is the problem (methemoglobin levels near 30% to 35% give a reading of about 85%, and the reading often stays low even on supplemental oxygen; carboxyhemoglobin is read as oxygenated, so the pulse oximeter is falsely reassuring)
Pertinent positives & negatives Grunting with bilaterally decreased breath sounds — auto-PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) against closed alveoli; locates the lesion in the parenchyma and excludes both cardiac shunt and central hypoventilation · Increased work of breathing at 1 hour — excludes apnea of prematurity, which appears days later with apnea and bradycardia and no respiratory effort · No murmur, regular rhythm — does not by itself exclude cyanotic heart disease, but with loud parenchymal findings it makes an intracardiac cause the second explanation, not the first · Normal CBC (complete blood count) — no anemia to lower content, no leukocytosis. The sepsis workup already running does not explain the hypoxemia; the CBC is typically normal in RDS (respiratory distress syndrome) · Still hypoxemic on 30% oxygen by CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) — the shunt fraction is large enough that a modest FiO2 cannot overcome it; recruit alveoli rather than raise the oxygen concentration
Hypoxemia: sorting by A-a gradient and oxygen response
MechanismIllness script + buzzwordsThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt (V/Q = 0)Alveoli perfused but unventilated: RDS, lobar atelectasis/mucus plug, pneumonia, ARDS (acute respiratory distress syndrome), pulmonary edemaWidened A-a, hypoxemia refractory to raising FiO2, corrected by recruitment (CPAP, PEEP, surfactant)(the answer)
V/Q mismatch (low but non-zero)Asthma, COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), early pneumonia, atelectasis in evolutionWidened A-a that corrects on a few liters of oxygen; the commonest mechanism in adult medicineThe question keys the extreme: collapsed alveoli with zero ventilation
Right-to-left shunt outside the lungCyanotic CHD (congenital heart disease); hepatopulmonary syndrome; PFO (patent foramen ovale) opened by high right-sided pressuresNo rise in PaO2 on 100% oxygen; lungs clear, work of breathing normal or minimalGrunting and bilaterally decreased breath sounds: the lungs are abnormal
Dead space (ventilated, not perfused)Pulmonary embolism, low cardiac outputSudden dyspnea with a clear chest; hypercapnia is the primary consequenceBilateral decreased breath sounds; PE (pulmonary embolism) is vanishingly rare in young children
Normal-A-a hypoxemia: hypoventilation or low inspired PO2Opioids, neuromuscular disease, obesity hypoventilation, apnea of prematurity · altitude, hypoxic gas mixtureNormal A-a gradient; hypoventilation adds a high PaCO2 (arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide), altitude does not; both fully correct with a little oxygenTachypnea and grunting: effort is increased, not depressed; he is already receiving 30% oxygen
Abnormal hemoglobin affinity or carryingCO (carbon monoxide) poisoning, methemoglobinemia, fetal hemoglobinNormal PaO2 with cyanosis or a saturation gap; cyanosis unmoved by oxygenNormal Hb (hemoglobin), no exposure; fetal hemoglobin's left shift is physiologic and does not cause distress
Management, in one line Diffusion limitation is a seventh category and has no row in the table. It is a chronic, exertional finding (interstitial disease, emphysema) with a low DLCO (diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide). The resting saturation is often normal. The typical patient desaturates only on the walk down the hall. Shunt from collapsed alveoli is treated by reopening them with surfactant plus CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure), not by turning the oxygen up.
Decision spine Is the PaO2 low, or only the saturation? — Saturation-only → hemoglobin problem (carbon monoxide, methemoglobin) · Is the A-a gradient normal? — Normal → hypoventilation (high PaCO2) or low inspired PO2 (normal PaCO2) · Widened: what happens on oxygen? — Corrects → V/Q mismatch. Refractory → shunt · Shunt: are the lungs abnormal? — Grunting, decreased breath sounds, infiltrate → intrapulmonary. Clear lungs, no distress → intracardiac or intravascular · Any reason to think dead space? — Sudden onset, clear chest, risk factors; without them, embolus is unlikely
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to

Co-oximetryConfirmsMethemoglobin or carboxyhemoglobin raisedMethemoglobinemia or carbon monoxide poisoning
A-a gradient from the blood gasNextNormal gradientHypoventilation if PaCO2 high; low inspired PO2 if PaCO2 low
Response to supplemental oxygenBy branchWidened gradient that corrects on modest oxygenV/Q mismatch; little change means shunt
Chest X-rayBy branchClear lungs with oxygen-refractory hypoxemiaIntracardiac shunt or embolism: echocardiogram or CT (computed tomography) angiography
DLCO with a walk testBy branchLow DLCO, desaturation only on exertionDiffusion limitation: interstitial disease or emphysema
Pulse oximetry alone in suspected CO poisoningSkipReads falsely normalCarboxyhemoglobin is counted as oxygenated; get co-oximetry
Scenario bank
  1. 27 wk preterm M, 3 h old, grunting, ground-glass film with air bronchograms, SpO2 85% on CPAP FiO2 0.6 and rising → Intubate and give intratracheal surfactant → Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
  2. 24 yo M, POD 1, RR 6, pinpoint pupils, PaO2 55, PaCO2 68, normal A-a gradient → Naloxone → Opioid-induced hypoventilation
  3. 4 mo F, cyanosis after topical teething gel, chocolate-brown blood, SpO2 fixed at 85% on 100% oxygen, PaO2 96 → Methylene blue IV → Methemoglobinemia
  4. 34 yo F and two housemates with headache and nausea after a furnace failure, COHb (carboxyhemoglobin) 18%, no syncope, normal neurologic exam → High-flow 100% oxygen by nonrebreather → Carbon monoxide poisoning
  5. 58 yo M with ARDS, PaO2 58 on FiO2 0.8 with PEEP 8, diffuse bilateral opacities → Increase PEEP → Refractory intrapulmonary shunt
  6. 68 yo M, COPD exacerbation, baseline PaCO2 62, now receiving oxygen → Titrating oxygen to a saturation of 100% → Oxygen-induced hypercapnia
  7. 62 yo F, 8 months of exertional dyspnea, resting SpO2 96% falling to 86% with ambulation, clear lungs, normal chest film → Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide → Diffusion limitation
  8. 44 yo F, POD 5 from knee arthroplasty, sudden dyspnea, clear lungs, normal film, widened A-a gradient → CT pulmonary angiography → Pulmonary embolism
  9. 29 yo M trekker at 4,500 m, dyspnea with SpO2 84%, clear lungs, PaCO2 30, normal A-a gradient → Reduced inspired oxygen tension → Descent; acetazolamide
  10. 72 yo F, POD 2 laparotomy, febrile, SpO2 88%, absent breath sounds at the left base, film shows left lower lobe collapse → Intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt → Incentive spirometry and mobilization
Decoy note The umbilical line and the started antibiotics reflect a sepsis workup. They do not explain the hypoxemia: the CBC (complete blood count) is normal and no fever or instability is reported. Apgar 7 at both marks argues against perinatal depression, which would present as hypoventilation. The absent murmur does not exclude cyanotic heart disease on its own; the parenchymal findings do.
Pearls Normal A-a means hypoventilation or low inspired oxygen; widened and oxygen-responsive means V/Q mismatch; widened and oxygen-refractory means shunt. · Shunt is the hypoxemia that oxygen will not fix. When the FiO2 goes up and the saturation does not follow, stop titrating and start recruiting. Recruit with PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure), CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure), surfactant, drainage, or a diuretic for the edema behind it. · RDS (respiratory distress syndrome) hypoxemia is clinically responsive to oxygen administration. The reason is that partially collapsed alveoli are recruitable by the CPAP delivering that oxygen, not that shunted blood responds to FiO2. · Hypoventilation is the one hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient and a high PaCO2; low inspired PO2 is the one with a normal gradient and a low PaCO2 from the compensatory hyperventilation. · A normal or high PaO2 in a cyanotic patient means the hemoglobin cannot carry or release oxygen. Causes are methemoglobin, carbon monoxide, or cyanide (where the tissue, not the blood, is the problem). · Boundary: refractory hypoxemia with clear lungs and no cardiac history can still be an embolus. If it raises right-sided pressures enough to open a PFO (patent foramen ovale), a dead-space disease presents as a right-to-left shunt. Look for the cause of the raised pressure, not just the shunt.
Pairs with Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant covers the parenchymal differential by chest film (ground glass and air bronchograms versus retained fluid, meconium, or air leak). Congenital Heart Disease covers the lesions themselves. Cyanosis in the Newborn covers sorting at-rest physiology in the delivery room. This brief covers the mechanism categories above all three. Ask: is the A-a gradient widened, and does the hypoxemia respond to oxygen?
Transferable rule Treat hypoxemia as a physiology question. Compute the A-a gradient, then check what happens on supplemental oxygen. Those two answers name the mechanism before the illness is named.
True-fact-wrong-slotUnderdeveloped medullary respiratory center: Apnea of prematurity appears days later as apnea with bradycardia and no respiratory effort; this infant is grunting and tachypneic at one hour
Salient decoyObstructed pulmonary arterial blood flow: Obstruction creates dead space, not bilaterally reduced breath sounds; embolus is nearly nonexistent in neonates
True-fact-wrong-slotGreater red blood cell oxygen affinity: It is the normal neonatal state; it is physiologic and does not cause respiratory distress
Class-vs-memberIncreased intracardiac left-to-right shunting: Left-to-right recirculates already-oxygenated blood; systemic saturation is unaffected, so it cannot desaturate a newborn

Lymphadenopathy

tempo and laterality sort every neck node · acute and unilateral is bacterial · covering staph, strep, anaerobesHow fast did the node appear, on one side or both, and which organisms must the drug cover?

Source vignette Pt — 3 yo M, lump on the right neck noticed yesterday, today red, painful and larger; cough, rhinorrhea and low-grade fever a week ago, resolved; family reunion in eastern Arkansas with several cousins also coryzal · Exam — T 38.6, HR 98; 5 cm tender, warm, poorly mobile anterior cervical node with overlying erythema; no hepatosplenomegaly · Q — the most appropriate treatment; options spanned azithromycin, cefdinir, clindamycin, itraconazole, oseltamivir and supportive care only
The decision point

Sort the node by tempo and laterality. A node that appeared yesterday and is bigger, red and tender today is acute. A single inflamed node on one side is unilateral. Acute unilateral cervical lymphadenitis in a child under five is a bacterial infection of the node itself. The organisms are Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, with anaerobes when there is periodontal disease. Empiric therapy has to cover gram-positives including MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) plus anaerobes. Among the offered agents, only clindamycin does all three. The preceding viral illness is the portal of entry, not the cause, and it has already resolved.

Defining criteria Acute unilateral cervical lymphadenitis — child under 5; a 3 to 6 cm node, markedly tender, warm and erythematous, with or without fever; the child is usually well-appearing and the diagnosis is clinical · Empiric coverage required — S. aureus including MRSA, S. pyogenes, and anaerobes, which is clindamycin; amoxicillin-clavulanate is reasonable where community MRSA is low, a first-generation cephalosporin where periodontal disease is unlikely · Suppuration — fluctuance on examination signals abscess and adds incision and drainage · Observation gate — supportive care alone is defensible only in an afebrile child with minimal tenderness and minimal enlargement
Pertinent positives & negatives Onset yesterday, larger today — acute; excludes cat-scratch disease and nontuberculous mycobacterial disease, both of which build over weeks · Unilateral — a node infection, not reactive adenopathy, which is bilateral · Tender, warm, erythematous — inflammatory; mycobacterial nodes are nontender and violaceous · T 38.6 — opens the antibiotic gate that observation would otherwise satisfy · 5 cm — large enough to risk suppuration; size is part of the treatment gate · Poorly mobile with overlying erythema — tethering from inflammation; malignancy is painless and not erythematous · URI (upper respiratory infection) a week ago, now resolved — the portal of entry, not the active illness · No hepatosplenomegaly or diffuse adenopathy — excludes disseminated histoplasmosis and mononucleosis
The inflamed cervical node — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Acute bacterial lymphadenitisUnder 5, after a URI; S. aureus and S. pyogenesAcute, unilateral, tender, warm, erythematous, with or without fever— (the answer)
Cat-scratch diseaseCat or kitten scratch or bite, or flea bite; Bartonella henselae; the inoculation papule is often small and not reportedTender regional node proximal to the scratch, arising over weeks, sometimes suppurative; fails antibiotics aimed at S. aureus and S. pyogenes; fever in someOnset yesterday; no animal exposure
Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitisAlso under 5, indolent courseChronic, violaceous, nontender; treated by excisionAcute, tender, erythematous and febrile
Reactive viral adenopathyConcurrent URI or influenzaBilateral, small, mobile, mildly tenderUnilateral and 5 cm; the URI has resolved
Disseminated histoplasmosisMississippi and Ohio River ValleysPulmonary disease with mediastinal adenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly with diffuse adenopathyIsolated neck node; no organomegaly or lung findings
Infected branchial cleft cystCongenital second-arch remnant that declares itself after a URI, often in later childhoodCystic lateral mass with a draining pit anterior to the sternocleidomastoidA solid tender node with no pit or sinus tract
The node pattern names the cause Acute, unilateral, tender, warm node — pyogenic: S. aureus or S. pyogenes; clindamycin · Tender regional node proximal to a scratch, failing antistaphylococcal antibiotics — Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease): ask about cats and kittens, send Bartonella serology; azithromycin speeds recovery · Chronic, single, nontender cervical node — mycobacterial: tuberculosis in an adolescent or adult with TB risk (interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test, then biopsy); nontuberculous mycobacteria in a child under 5, violaceous, excised · Generalized, painless adenopathy — systemic: HIV (antigen/antibody test), EBV (Epstein-Barr virus) with pharyngitis and splenomegaly, disseminated histoplasmosis in the immunosuppressed · Bilateral, symmetric, nontender nodes with cat exposure — toxoplasmosis; Toxoplasma serology · Bilateral, small, mildly tender nodes with a current URI — reactive viral adenopathy; supportive care
Decision spine Acute or chronic? — Days means bacterial; weeks means Bartonella or mycobacterial · Unilateral or bilateral? — Unilateral is a node infection; bilateral is reactive · Tender and erythematous, or violaceous and painless? — Tender means pyogenic · Febrile? Large? — Both means antibiotics, not observation · Fluctuant? — If yes, drain as well · Which agent covers S. aureus including MRSA, S. pyogenes and anaerobes? — Clindamycin
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsAcute, unilateral, tender, warm node in a child under 5Bacterial lymphadenitis; treat empirically; tests are for mimics and abscess
Neck ultrasoundBy branchFluctuance or no response by 48 hours: abscessIncision and drainage with continued antibiotics
Gram stain and culture of drained pusCauseGram-positive cocci in clustersS. aureus; identifies MRSA and narrows therapy
Bartonella henselae serologyBy branchTender regional node proximal to a scratch, not responding to antistaphylococcal antibiotics: positiveCat-scratch disease; the diagnosis is often clinical, serology confirms
Excisional biopsyBy branchChronic violaceous nontender node: granulomas, acid-fast bacilliNontuberculous mycobacteria; excision is also the treatment
Interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin testBy branchChronic, single, nontender cervical node with TB risk: positiveTuberculous lymphadenitis; confirm by node biopsy or aspirate with acid-fast culture
HIV antigen/antibody testBy branchGeneralized painless adenopathy: positiveHIV; a single tender regional node is not its pattern
Histoplasma testingSkipA single hot node is not histoplasmosisThe Arkansas geography is a decoy
Scenario bank
  1. 3 yo M with a 5 cm tender, warm, erythematous, poorly mobile right anterior cervical node appearing over 2 days, T 38.6, with a resolved upper respiratory illness a week earlier → Clindamycin → covers MRSA, S. pyogenes and anaerobes
  2. 4 yo with a 2 cm mildly tender unilateral cervical node, afebrile, well-appearing, no overlying erythema → Supportive care with reassessment → observation is appropriate below the treatment gate
  3. 3 yo who has taken clindamycin for 48 hours whose node is now fluctuant with spreading erythema → Incision and drainage with continued antibiotics → suppuration has developed
  4. 8 yo with a 3-week history of a slowly enlarging tender axillary node and a papule where a kitten scratched him → Cat-scratch disease → azithromycin
  5. 3 yo with a 6-week painless violaceous submandibular node, afebrile and otherwise well → Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis → surgical excision
  6. 3 yo with acute unilateral bacterial cervical lymphadenitis in a community with high MRSA prevalence → Cefdinir → no coverage of Staphylococcus aureus or anaerobes
  7. 5 yo from the Mississippi River Valley with cough, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and diffuse adenopathy → Disseminated histoplasmosis → itraconazole
  8. 2 yo with fever, cough and rhinorrhea with bilateral small mobile mildly tender cervical nodes → Reactive viral adenopathy → supportive care
  9. 4 year old with 1 day of fever and a red, tender, fluctuant 2 cm anterior cervical node; normal dentition, no animal contact, no rash → Staphylococcus aureus → With Streptococcus pyogenes — acute, unilateral, suppurative
  10. Child with acute unilateral cervical adenitis and extensive dental caries → Anaerobic oral flora → Prevotella and relatives follow periodontal disease
  11. Child with acute unilateral cervical adenitis after skinning a rabbit → Francisella tularensis → The exposure names the organism
  12. Child with bilateral tender cervical nodes, coryza and pharyngitis for 3 days → Acute viral adenitis → Bilateral and acute points at adenovirus and its relatives
  13. 3 yo with cough and rhinorrhea last week, now resolved, and a single neck node noticed yesterday that is 4 cm, tender, warm and red today; T 38.5 → Acute bacterial lymphadenitis → empiric clindamycin
  14. 12 yo M with a painful left neck lump a week after a febrile URI, now cystic, with a small pit anterior to the sternocleidomastoid draining mucopurulent fluid → Branchial cleft cyst → second-arch remnant infected after a URI; resect cyst and tract
  15. 8 yo with a tender midline neck cyst after a cold that rises when she sticks out her tongue → Thyroglossal duct cyst → follows the path of thyroid descent from the foramen cecum
  16. Adult trumpet player with a soft lateral neck swelling that enlarges when he bears down → Laryngocele → laryngeal mucosa pouching through the thyrohyoid membrane, inflated by pressure
  17. 16 yo F with a tender red lump at the left elbow 5 days ago, diagnosed as lymphadenitis and treated with clindamycin taken as prescribed; now fever and increasing swelling in the left armpit; T 38.3; a 1 cm tender mobile epitrochlear node and several 2 to 3 cm tender left axillary nodes; no other enlarged nodes → Bartonella henselae serology → cat-scratch disease; ask about cats; azithromycin speeds recovery
  18. 24 yo F who adopted a stray cat 2 months ago, with 3 weeks of fatigue and low-grade fever; 1 to 2 cm nontender, mobile posterior cervical nodes on both sides, symmetric; no pharyngitis, no splenomegaly, no skin lesions; heterophile antibody test negative → Toxoplasmosis → Toxoplasma serology; self-limited in an immunocompetent adult
  19. 26 yo M who moved from the Philippines 2 years ago, with a single firm, nontender, 3 cm right cervical node that has enlarged slowly over 2 months; no pain, no overlying warmth, no animal exposure; other node regions normal → Tuberculous lymphadenitis → interferon-gamma release assay, then node biopsy with acid-fast culture
Decoy note The location, eastern Arkansas, is genuinely endemic for histoplasmosis. Mentioned beside the sick contacts, it reads as an exposure history. It is not one: the cousins explain the resolved URI. The location explains nothing, because histoplasmosis does not present as a single hot node.
Congenital neck masses, sorted by location Midline, moves with swallowing or tongue protrusion — thyroglossal duct cyst, often found after a URI · Midline, does not move with the tongue — dermoid cyst, along an embryologic fusion plane · Lateral, anterior to the sternocleidomastoid, below the mandible — branchial cleft cyst, usually second arch, between the internal and external carotids; cured by resecting the cyst and its tract · Lateral, necrotic node with violaceous skin and a fistula — nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis · Posterior triangle, from birth or on prenatal ultrasound — cystic hygroma · Lateral, enlarges with Valsalva — laryngocele, through the thyrohyoid membrane; glassblowers and trumpet players · Submandibular sinus draining sulfur granules — actinomyces, after dental infection or trauma
Pearls Tempo and laterality sort neck nodes before anything else — acute and unilateral is bacterial, chronic and unilateral is Bartonella or mycobacterial, acute and bilateral is viral · Clindamycin is chosen for its spectrum, not its class — a cephalosporin that misses staphylococci fails · Violaceous and nontender is mycobacterial, and its preferred treatment is surgical excision rather than antibiotics · Fluctuance adds drainage — the drug stays the same · A resolved URI a week earlier is a portal of entry, not a competing diagnosis; a concurrent URI would point at reactive adenopathy instead
Pairs with Part I Respiratory Infection in a Child covers the reactive-adenopathy end of this spectrum and the exudative pharyngitis fork. Ask: how fast did it appear, and is it one node or many?
How NBME framed it Scratches from a pet cat were planted beside a cat-scratch disease option, but acute midline pain that worsens with swallowing or tongue protrusion names an infected thyroglossal duct cyst.
Transferable rule When every option is a drug, name the organisms you must cover, then find the single agent that covers all of them. A geographic detail matters only when the syndrome matches the endemic disease, not merely the location.
Unchecked attributeSupportive care only: the observation gate requires an afebrile child with a small, minimally tender node; this is 38.6 with a 5 cm inflamed node at risk of abscess.
Unchecked attributeAzithromycin: correct for cat-scratch and part of mycobacterial therapy, but both are chronic and indolent; this appeared yesterday.
Class-vs-memberCefdinir: covers S. pyogenes but not S. aureus or anaerobes, and the two are clinically indistinguishable here.
Salient decoyItraconazole: eastern Arkansas is histoplasmosis country, but histoplasmosis presents with pulmonary or disseminated disease, not an isolated hot node.
True-fact-wrong-slotOseltamivir: influenza adenopathy is bilateral and accompanies active respiratory symptoms, which have resolved.

Heart Failure in a Child

the viral prodrome that is not bronchiolitis · gallop, apical murmur and weak pulses · cardiogenic shock: cautious fluidIs there a gallop or a new murmur, and are the pulses weak with a low pressure?

Source vignette Pt — 2 yo M, 4 days of rhinorrhea, congestion and low-grade fever, now tired with decreased urine output and labored breathing · Exam — T 38.2, HR 155, RR 48, BP 60/40, SpO2 91% on room air; scattered mobile subcentimeter anterior cervical nodes; gallop rhythm with a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex; brachial and femoral pulses 1+; nasal flaring, subcostal retractions and basal rales · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned acute rheumatic fever, bronchiolitis, glomerulonephritis, Kawasaki disease and myocarditis
The decision point

The respiratory findings are real, but every one of them is a consequence of the heart. Three cardiac findings decide the diagnosis: a gallop, a new holosystolic murmur at the apex, and 1+ pulses with a blood pressure of 60/40. A gallop is an S3, from a ventricle taking volume it cannot handle. In this setting, an apical holosystolic murmur is mitral regurgitation from ventricular dilation, not a primary valve lesion. Weak pulses with hypotension in a 2-year-old are shock. With basal rales and oliguria, this is acute left heart failure with pulmonary edema. That is why the lungs sound wet and the saturation is 91%. The viral prodrome is the cause, not a coincidence. The usual agents are coxsackievirus B and adenovirus. Myocyte injury is part direct and part immune-mediated.

Defining criteria Myocarditis — a viral prodrome, upper respiratory or gastrointestinal, then heart failure: respiratory distress, gallop, hepatomegaly, with or without arrhythmia, which is how it causes sudden death · Acute rheumatic fever gate — Jones criteria 2 to 4 weeks after untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis; a concurrent viral URI is the wrong illness at the wrong interval · Kawasaki gate — fever of 5 or more days plus 4 of 5 criteria, with a cervical node over 1.5 cm; four days of fever with no criteria does not open it · Workup — troponin, ECG showing sinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST change, chest film showing cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema, and echocardiography showing diffuse hypokinesis with a reduced ejection fraction
Pertinent positives & negatives Gallop rhythm — an S3, the most specific finding in the stem for ventricular failure · Holosystolic murmur at the apex — functional mitral regurgitation from a dilated ventricle, new in a failing child · BP 60/40 with 1+ pulses — cardiogenic shock, an emergency · Basal rales with hypoxemia — pulmonary edema, not consolidation and not bronchospasm · No wheeze — argues strongly against bronchiolitis, whose classic finding it is · Decreased urine output — hypoperfusion; urine output reflects cardiac output · Subcentimeter mobile nodes — reactive to the viral illness and too small for Kawasaki, which requires over 1.5 cm · Fever 4 days with no rash, conjunctivitis or mucosal change — the Kawasaki gate fails on duration and on criteria count
Respiratory distress after a viral prodrome — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Viral myocarditis Can't missCoxsackie B or adenovirus; prodrome then failureGallop plus new apical holosystolic murmur plus poor perfusion after a URI— (the answer)
BronchiolitisRSV; first or second year, coryza then distressWheeze and hyperinflation; heart sounds normalNo wheeze; gallop and murmur unexplained by it
Acute rheumatic feverGAS pharyngitis, then an immune sequelJones criteria 2 to 4 weeks later; migratory arthritis, choreaConcurrent viral URI and no Jones criteria
Kawasaki diseaseVasculitis of young children; can include myocarditisFever 5 or more days plus 4 criteria; node over 1.5 cmFour days of fever, no criteria, subcentimeter nodes
GlomerulonephritisPost-infectious or IgA; may follow a URIHematuria and Nephritic Syndrome, hypertension and edemaHypotensive rather than hypertensive; no hematuria
Management Treatment is supportive: diuresis, afterload reduction and inotropes. IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) is commonly given, but its benefit in children is not established. Do not treat the shock reflexively. This child's hypotension is cardiogenic, so a rapid large-volume bolus worsens pulmonary edema. Give fluid cautiously and in small aliquots, or not at all, while getting the echocardiogram.
Decision spine Is there a gallop or a new murmur? — Yes means the heart is the failing organ, whatever the lungs are doing · Wheeze or rales? — Rales means edema, not bronchiolitis · What is the blood pressure and what are the pulses? — 60/40 with 1+ means shock · How long has the fever run, and how many Kawasaki criteria? — Four days and none, so the gate is closed · Was the antecedent illness strep pharyngitis 2 to 4 weeks ago? — No, it is concurrent coryza, so not rheumatic fever · So what confirms it? — Echocardiography with troponin, ECG and a chest film
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
ECGFirstSinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST changesSupports myocarditis; watch for arrhythmia, the cause of sudden death
TroponinFirstElevatedMyocyte injury
Chest radiographSupportsCardiomegaly with pulmonary edemaRales are edema, not bronchiolitis or pneumonia
EchocardiographyConfirmsDiffuse hypokinesis with a reduced ejection fractionMyocarditis with heart failure; excludes a structural lesion
Cardiac MRI or endomyocardial biopsyBy branchMyocardial inflammation or lymphocytic infiltrateTissue-level confirmation when the diagnosis remains uncertain
ASO titerSkipNo pharyngitis 2 to 4 weeks earlier, no Jones criteriaConcurrent coryza is the wrong illness at the wrong interval for rheumatic fever
Scenario bank
  1. 2 yo M, 4 days of rhinorrhea and low-grade fever, now tired with decreased urine output; HR 155, RR 48, BP 60/40, gallop rhythm with a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex, 1+ pulses, basal rales → Viral myocarditis → acute decompensated heart failure
  2. 2 yo with a 4-day viral prodrome who now has a gallop, basal rales and poor peripheral perfusion → Echocardiography with troponin and ECG → diffuse hypokinesis with a reduced ejection fraction
  3. 3 yo with suspected myocarditis, hypotensive with a gallop, rales and hepatomegaly → A rapid 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus → the shock is cardiogenic, not hypovolemic
  4. 8 mo, 3 days of coryza, now wheezing with retractions and hyperinflation; heart sounds normal with no murmur → Bronchiolitis → supportive care and suctioning
  5. 6 yo with migratory polyarthritis and a new murmur 3 weeks after an untreated sore throat → Acute rheumatic fever → Jones criteria with an antistreptolysin O titer
  6. 4 yo with 6 days of fever, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked lips, a polymorphous rash and a 2 cm cervical node → Kawasaki disease → IVIG with aspirin
  7. The organisms most commonly responsible for myocarditis in children → Coxsackievirus B and adenovirus → direct viral injury plus immune-mediated myocyte necrosis
  8. 5 yo recovering from biopsy-proven myocarditis who has a syncopal episode and an irregular pulse → Continuous cardiac monitoring → arrhythmia is the mechanism of sudden death
Pearls S3 or new murmur in any child in respiratory distress — heart failure until an echocardiogram says otherwise, however viral the story sounds · A new holosystolic murmur at the apex in a failing ventricle is functional mitral regurgitation — a consequence, not a second disease · Hypotension in myocarditis is cardiogenic: fluid loading fills the lungs and is the commonest management error · Rheumatic fever is defined by its interval, 2 to 4 weeks after pharyngitis; a murmur appearing during a viral illness is myocarditis · Kawasaki's fever requirement is five days, and it is mandatory
Pairs with Part II Shock in Children covers the perfusion categories and the cardiogenic-versus-distributive fork. Part I Acute Rheumatic Fever covers Jones and the post-streptococcal interval. Kawasaki Disease covers the five-day fever requirement. Ask: is there a gallop or a new murmur, and how long has the fever run?
Transferable rule When respiratory findings are prominent and cardiac findings are subtle, read the cardiac findings first. A gallop, a new murmur or weak pulses point to the heart as the failing organ. The lung signs are then a consequence rather than a cause.
Unchecked attributeAcute rheumatic fever: fever with a new murmur after an infection is its exact shape, but the antecedent is coryza not pharyngitis, the interval is concurrent not 2 to 4 weeks, and no Jones criteria are met.
Unchecked attributeKawasaki disease: genuinely causes myocarditis, but fever is 4 days and no criteria are met; the nodes are subcentimeter against a 1.5 cm requirement.
True-fact-wrong-slotGlomerulonephritis: oliguria after a URI (upper respiratory infection) fits, but it presents with hematuria and hypertension, and this child is hypotensive with unexplained cardiac findings.
Salient decoyBronchiolitis: the whole respiratory picture and the age fit, but it explains nothing cardiac and the classic wheeze is absent while rales are present.
