Hair Loss in a Child

the scalp surface and the nodes identify the cause · tinea capitis needs oral therapy · trichotillomania and alopecia areataIs the patch scaly, and are the draining nodes enlarged?

Source vignette Pt — 8 yo, enlarging scaly bald patch with pruritus, tender occipital and postauricular nodes · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned tinea capitis, trichotillomania and alopecia areata
The decision point

Two examination findings, not the history, identify the cause. The patch has overlying scale, which means an inflammatory or infectious process in the skin rather than hair that is simply being pulled or shed. The occipital and posterior auricular nodes are enlarged and tender, which is regional lymphadenopathy draining an infected scalp. Together these findings indicate tinea capitis. Unlike tinea of the body, this dermatophyte invades the hair follicle and shaft. As a result, the hair breaks and the patch expands centrifugally over weeks. The recent school change and the anxiety suggest trichotillomania, but neither scale nor tender nodes occurs in trichotillomania.

Defining criteria Tinea capitis — scaly erythematous patch with hair loss and localized lymphadenopathy, with or without black dots (broken hairs at the follicle) and with or without a tender boggy kerion · Why systemic therapy is required — the organism invades the follicle and shaft, which topical agents penetrate poorly, so oral griseofulvin or terbinafine is needed · Confirmation — the diagnosis is clinical; Potassium hydroxide (KOH) examination of proximal hair shafts or fungal culture confirms it
Pertinent positives & negatives Scale over an enlarging bald patch — an inflammatory or infectious scalp process; scale is what separates infection from every non-inflammatory alopecia · Tender occipital and posterior auricular lymphadenopathy — the nodes that drain the scalp; expected in tinea capitis and absent in traction alopecia and trichotillomania · Frequent scratching — pruritus, an inflammatory feature that argues against a purely mechanical cause · Recent school change with anxiety — a psychosocial cue for hair-pulling, which the scale and the nodes exclude · Age 8, previously healthy — the peak age; tinea capitis is predominantly a disease of children and the immunocompromised
Patchy hair loss in a child: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Tinea capitisTrichophyton or Microsporum acquired from a contact or a fomite (shared comb, hat, pillowcase); invades follicle and shaftScaly patch with hair loss plus regional lymphadenopathy; black dots; kerion(the answer)
Alopecia areataAutoimmune, non-scarring; abrupt, sharply circumscribedRound, smooth patch completely devoid of hair, scale-free, no lymphadenopathy; exclamation-point hairs; nail pittingThe patch is scaly and the nodes are enlarged
TrichotillomaniaRecurrent pulling the patient cannot stop; most common in children and adolescent girls; loss hidden under hats or wigs; swallowed hair can form a trichobezoarIrregular patch with hairs of varying lengths, often sparse eyebrows or eyelashes; no scale, no erythema, nonscarringScale and tender lymphadenopathy
Traction alopeciaProlonged pulling from bands or braidsGeometric loss along the traction sites, most often frontal and temporal or along braids; no scale, no nodes; never thins the eyebrowsNo hairstyle history; scale and nodes present
Telogen effluviumSynchronized shedding a few months after a stressor such as illness, surgery or childbirthDiffuse thinning over the whole scalp, not a patchThe loss is a single patch with scale and nodes
Seborrheic dermatitisScalp scaling, i.e. dandruff, with pruritusScale without hair lossIt cannot explain the alopecia or the nodes
Discoid lupus erythematosusCutaneous lupus; scarring, well-demarcated inflammatory plaquesAdult women, with face and neck lesions, and the alopecia scarsAge 8 and no facial or neck involvement
Trichotillomania: the tells Irregular patch, hairs of different lengths — hairs pulled and regrowing at different times; alopecia areata leaves a round patch that is completely bald · Sparse eyebrows or eyelashes — pulling reaches other sites; traction and tinea stay on the scalp · Hats or wigs — used to hide the loss; even when another reason for them is given, traction does not explain the eyebrows or a parietal patch · No scale, no erythema, no scarring — excludes tinea capitis and discoid lupus · Treatment — cognitive behavioral therapy with habit reversal · Complication — swallowing the hair (trichophagia) can form a gastric trichobezoar
Management, in one line Treatment requires oral griseofulvin or terbinafine, because topical antifungals do not reach the organism inside the hair follicle.
Decision spine Is there scale on the patch? — Yes → an inflammatory or infectious cause, not a pulling one · Are the draining nodes enlarged? — Yes → infection, which excludes trichotillomania and traction alopecia · Are the remaining hairs broken? — Black dots are shafts snapped at the follicle; the fungus is inside the hair · Any traction history or geometric pattern? — No · Confirm and treat — KOH of the proximal shafts; oral, never topical alone
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Scalp exam with a check of the draining nodesFirstScale plus tender occipital and postauricular nodesInfection: tinea capitis; a smooth patch without nodes is not
Close look at the remaining hairsBy branchBroken hairs of varying lengths in an irregular patch, no scale; eyebrows or lashes sparseTrichotillomania; exclamation-point hairs point to alopecia areata
KOH of plucked proximal hair shaftsConfirmsSpores within or around the hair shaftTinea capitis: start oral griseofulvin or terbinafine
Fungal culture of hairs or scaleConfirmsTrichophyton or Microsporum growsTinea capitis; results take weeks, so do not wait to treat
Wood lampSupportsGreen fluorescence only with MicrosporumNegative with Trichophyton tonsurans, the common US cause
Serum fungal antibody titersSkipNo role in dermatophyte infectionKOH or culture of the hair confirms it
Scenario bank
  1. 8 yo with an enlarging scaly bald patch, pruritus, and tender occipital and postauricular nodes → Tinea capitis → Regional lymphadenopathy plus scale
  2. Child with clinically confirmed tinea capitis; appropriate treatment → Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine → Topicals cannot reach the follicle
  3. Child with tinea capitis; which therapy will not clear the infection → Topical antifungal shampoo used alone → Adjunctive at best
  4. 8 yo with a smooth, scale-free, sharply demarcated bald patch, no lymphadenopathy, and nail pitting → Topical or intralesional glucocorticoid → Alopecia areata
  5. 10 yo with irregular patches of broken hairs of varying lengths, no scale, no lymphadenopathy, after a recent stressor → Habit-reversal behavioral therapy → Trichotillomania
  6. 12 yo with symmetric temporal thinning along tightly pulled braids, no scale and no lymphadenopathy → Loosen the hairstyle → Traction alopecia is reversible if caught early
  7. Child on oral antifungal therapy for tinea capitis who develops a boggy tender scalp mass with pustules → Continue systemic antifungal therapy → A kerion is the same infection
  8. Child with a scaly patch of alopecia and regional lymphadenopathy → KOH examination of proximal hair shafts or fungal culture → The diagnosis is otherwise clinical
  9. Why tinea capitis requires oral therapy while tinea corporis responds to topical treatment → It invades the hair follicle and shaft → Body lesions remain in the epidermis
  10. Child newly diagnosed with tinea capitis → Examine close contacts and stop sharing combs, hats and pillowcases → Fomite transmission
  11. 15 yo F cast as the lead in a school play a month ago, wearing hats and wigs to stay in character; her mother noticed bald spots a few days ago; doing well in school, no substance use, regular menses, body mass index 22 kg/m²; a 3 x 5 cm irregular right parietal patch of hair loss bordered by hairs of uneven length, sparse eyebrows, no scale or erythema → Trichotillomania → Cognitive behavioral therapy with habit reversal
  12. 9 yo with a round, sharply bordered bald patch that appeared over 2 weeks; the scalp inside is completely smooth with no scale or erythema; a few short hairs at the margin taper toward the scalp; eyebrows normal; no lymphadenopathy → Alopecia areata → Topical or intralesional glucocorticoid
  13. 16 yo F shedding handfuls of hair in the shower for 3 weeks, 3 months after hospitalization for pneumonia; thinning is spread evenly over the whole scalp with no patches, no scale and normal eyebrows → Telogen effluvium → Reassurance; regrowth over months
  14. 15 yo F with long-standing hair pulling who also chews and swallows the hair, now with early satiety, weight loss, halitosis and a firm, mobile epigastric mass → Gastric trichobezoar → Endoscopic or surgical removal
Decoy note A new school and anxiety about teachers and friends make a complete, plausible causal story. The examination refutes it. "Frequently scratches at the area" seems to support it, since scratching sounds like a behavior. However, scratching reflects pruritus, an inflammatory symptom, and it points the other way. The patch is nontender, which is easy to misread as a general absence of tenderness. The nodes are tender, and that tenderness is the key finding.
Pearls A scaly, enlarging bald patch with tender occipital nodes in a child is tinea capitis, and it needs an oral antifungal. · Scale plus regional lymphadenopathy means infection rather than a simple alopecia; the two pulling alopecias, traction and trichotillomania, have neither. · Tinea capitis invades the follicle and shaft, so it needs an oral antifungal, the single most tested management point on the topic. · Black dots are hair shafts broken at the follicular orifice; a boggy tender mass is a kerion, which is the same infection inflamed, not a bacterial abscess to drain. · Alopecia areata causes a smooth, scale-free, sharply circumscribed patch with no lymphadenopathy, sometimes with nail pitting. · Fomites such as combs, hats and pillowcases carry it, so the household is examined rather than treated blindly. · A scaly scalp plaque that scars, in an adult woman with facial lesions, is discoid lupus rather than tinea.
Pairs with Part I Scaly Rashes covers the scaly-plaque differential of the body. It also covers the rule that a scaly annular lesion needs a KOH preparation rather than a steroid. This brief covers the scalp version, where the follicle changes the therapy. Ask: is there scale, and are the draining nodes enlarged?
Transferable rule In hair loss, the surface of the patch identifies the diagnosis. Scale with regional nodes means infection. A smooth patch means an autoimmune or traction cause. Broken hairs of unequal length mean the hair is being pulled. Examine the scalp before you accept a psychosocial explanation.
Class-vs-memberTraction alopecia: Traction produces geometric loss along the sites of pulling (temporal areas, along braids), with no scale and no lymphadenopathy
Salient decoyTrichotillomania: Hair-pulling leaves broken hairs of varying lengths in an irregular pattern, without scale or nodes
Class-vs-memberCutaneous candidiasis: Candida causes intertrigo in warm moist skinfolds; it does not scale the scalp or take hair
True-fact-wrong-slotSeborrheic dermatitis: It explains only the scale and the pruritus, not the hair loss or the nodes
True-fact-wrong-slotDiscoid lupus erythematosus: It occurs mostly in adult women, involves the face and neck, and scars

Pyelonephritis

home or admit · imaging gates · organism from the urine · complicated vs uncomplicatedCan the patient take oral therapy safely, and what does the urine say about the organism?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Fever, chills, dysuria and costovertebral angle tenderness make pyelonephritis a clinical diagnosis; with a benign abdomen, treat without imaging.

Admit for intravenous (IV) antibiotics when any of these holds:

  • Cannot take oral therapy: vomiting, or only clear fluids for days.
  • Unstable: sepsis or hypotension, read against the baseline (104/68 is low in long-standing hypertension).
  • Anatomy or host: pregnancy, obstruction, stones or a catheter; immunocompromise or extremes of age.
  • Failed outpatient therapy, or no oral agent the organism is sensitive to.

Otherwise a healthy, stable patient tolerating oral intake goes home on oral therapy. Nitrofurantoin treats cystitis, not the kidney.

Diagnosis
Defining criteria Pyelonephritis – fever and chills with flank or costovertebral angle tenderness and urinary symptoms · Complicated UTI (urinary tract infection) – infection beyond the bladder: systemic signs such as fever or bacteremia, a catheter-related infection, or pyelonephritis (IDSA (Infectious Diseases Society of America) 2025); men can have uncomplicated cystitis. Older teaching called every UTI in a man complicated · Duration – every pyelonephritis is a complicated UTI: typically 7 days, oral or IV, switching to oral as soon as the patient improves (IDSA 2025; older teaching 5 to 14 days, by drug)
Which enzyme Nitrate reductase – nitrate to nitrite: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterobacter; not Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Enterococcus or Pseudomonas · Urease – urea to ammonia, alkaline urine, struvite staghorn stones: Proteus, Klebsiella, S. saprophyticus · Catheter, instrumentation, prior antibiotics or hospital – Enterococcus and Pseudomonas (nitrite-negative), Citrobacter, Serratia, Enterobacter; the stem supplies the exposure
Management and treatment
Management ladder: pyelonephritis
TierInterventionEscalate when
OutpatientOral therapy chosen by local resistance: in adults, a fluoroquinolone, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) if the organism is sensitive; in a well child, an oral third-generation cephalosporin; avoid fluoroquinolones in childrenAny admission criterion, or failure of outpatient therapy
AdmitIV antibiotics; switch to oral as soon as the patient improvesNo improvement at 48 to 72 hours: CT for abscess or obstruction
Source controlDrain an abscess or relieve an obstruction; urgent urology for emphysematous pyelonephritisTop rung
By diagnosis Cystitis – no fever, no flank tenderness: nitrofurantoin · Pyelonephritis in pregnancy – admit for IV antibiotics · Benign prostatic hyperplasia – incomplete emptying causes stasis and ascending infection · Struvite stones – a urease organism, usually Proteus
Practice
  1. 28-year-old woman has 2 days of fever, chills and dysuria right costovertebral angle tenderness eating and drinking normally Healthy; not pregnant T 38.6 °C · BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 96/min · abdomen benign → Outpatient oral therapy → a healthy, stable patient who tolerates oral intake is treated at home with oral therapy; nitrofurantoin does not reach the kidney
  2. 28-year-old woman has fever, flank pain and dysuria has taken only clear fluids for 2 days vomits everything, including her tablets Healthy; not pregnant T 39.0 °C · BP 110/70 mm Hg · left costovertebral angle tenderness → Admit for IV antibiotics → a patient who cannot keep oral therapy down is admitted for IV antibiotics; one intramuscular dose does not finish the course
  3. 28-year-old woman has 2 days of dysuria and frequency suprapubic discomfort no flank pain or costovertebral angle tenderness Not pregnant; no vaginal discharge Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg · urinalysis: nitrites positive → Treat as cystitis with nitrofurantoin → no fever and no flank tenderness is cystitis: nitrofurantoin; it does not treat pyelonephritis; a fluoroquinolone is not first line for cystitis, and 14 days is a pyelonephritis-length course
  4. 28-year-old woman at 24 weeks of gestation has fever and flank pain dysuria for 3 days right costovertebral angle tenderness Tolerating fluids; no contractions T 38.8 °C · BP 112/68 mm Hg · fetal heart rate 150/min → Admit for IV antibiotics → pregnancy is on the admission list by itself, even with oral intake intact; nitrofurantoin does not treat the kidney
  5. 28-year-old woman admitted with fever and flank pain is still febrile 72 hours of IV antibiotics matched to the culture flank pain unchanged Blood cultures negative T 39.1 °C · BP 108/70 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL → CT for abscess or obstruction → no improvement at 48 to 72 hours on correct antibiotics: CT for an abscess or obstruction, not broader antibiotics
  6. 28-year-old woman has fever, flank pain and dysuria eating and drinking a past culture grew an organism resistant to every oral agent Not pregnant T 38.7 °C · BP 120/76 mm Hg · left costovertebral angle tenderness → Admit for IV therapy → no oral option means IV therapy, so she is admitted; nitrofurantoin does not reach the kidney
  7. 9-month-old girl has 2 days of fever and fussiness feeding poorly but still drinking well no cough, rash or diarrhea Catheterized urine culture sent; no drug allergies T 39.0 °C · urinalysis: nitrites positive, leukocyte esterase positive → Cefixime → a third-generation cephalosporin such as cefixime covers the gram-negative uropathogens; ciprofloxacin is avoided in children, and clindamycin misses them
  8. 11-month-old boy has a first febrile urinary infection well-appearing, taking fluids pediatrician prescribes cefixime, not trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or amoxicillin-clavulanate Parents ask why the two older drugs were not used T 38.9 °C · urinalysis: nitrites positive → Rising Escherichia coli resistance → rising Escherichia coli resistance; the local resistance pattern drives the empiric choice
  9. 9-month-old girl has a first febrile urinary infection well-appearing, tolerating oral intake culture sensitivities pending No drug allergies; parents ask which drugs are options T 38.8 °C · urinalysis: nitrites positive, leukocyte esterase positive → Ciprofloxacin → fluoroquinolones are avoided in children (cartilage toxicity) and kept for organisms such as Pseudomonas with no alternative; an oral cephalosporin fits
  10. 72-year-old man with an indwelling urinary catheter has fever right flank pain catheter in place for 6 weeks Several antibiotic courses this year T 38.9 °C · BP 128/80 mm Hg · urinalysis: nitrites negative, pyuria → Pseudomonas aeruginosa → a catheter, instrumentation or prior antibiotics widen the organism list beyond Escherichia coli to Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, Serratia and Candida
  11. 58-year-old woman has a third urinary infection this year urine pH 8.5 on every recent urinalysis CT: staghorn calculus filling the left renal pelvis No catheter Afebrile · BP 124/80 mm Hg · urinalysis: nitrites positive → Proteus mirabilis → urease splits urea to ammonia, alkalinizes the urine and builds struvite staghorn stones: Proteus mirabilis; Klebsiella also has urease but is a far less common cause
  12. 22-year-old woman has 2 days of dysuria and frequency sexually active, with a new partner this month culture: gram-positive cocci, coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant No flank pain Afebrile · urinalysis: leukocyte esterase positive, nitrites negative → Staphylococcus saprophyticus → Staphylococcus saprophyticus: young sexually active women, coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant, and nitrite-negative because it lacks nitrate reductase
  13. 26-year-old woman has 1 week of dysuria sexually active, inconsistent condom use pyuria, but the urine culture is sterile No flank pain Afebrile · BP 114/70 mm Hg · urinalysis: nitrites negative → Chlamydial urethritis → sterile pyuria in a sexually active patient is chlamydial urethritis until shown otherwise: nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)
  14. 64-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has fever and flank pain worse despite 2 days of antibiotics CT: gas within the left renal parenchyma Glucose 420 mg/dL T 39.4 °C · BP 96/60 mm Hg · HR 118/min → Emphysematous pyelonephritis → gas in the kidney of a diabetic is emphysematous pyelonephritis: IV antibiotics, glucose control and urgent urology
  15. 45-year-old man has his fourth urinary infection in 2 years every culture grows Proteus mirabilis urine pH 8.0 Imaging shows a large branching calculus in the right renal pelvis Afebrile · BP 126/82 mm Hg → Struvite stones → a urease-splitting organism alkalinizes the urine and precipitates struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate)
Pairs with Urinary Tract Infection in a Child covers febrile infection in children, the imaging that follows it and afebrile recurrences. Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia and Urinary Retention covers the obstruction behind infection in an older man. Ask: is the infection in the bladder or beyond it?
Transferable rule

Treat a clinical diagnosis without imaging, and image only for a named reason. When an organism is ruled out by an enzyme, name the enzyme: urease and nitrate reductase are independent.

Heart Murmurs in an Adult

shape first, then breathing · the click and the second heart sound (S2) decide · a repaired congenital lesion in a young adult is the causeWhat is the shape, which side does breathing point to, and what are the click and S2 doing?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Fix phase and side before you name a valve; the click, S2 and the response to breathing or standing carry the diagnosis.

  • RILE (right inspiration, left expiration): inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure and fills the right heart, so right-sided murmurs grow (as with leg raise or hepatic compression); left-sided on expiration.
  • Pulmonic stenosis: ejection click, crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left 2nd interspace, widened S2 split; usually congenital and isolated (rarely carcinoid or rheumatic), often silent until adult exertional dyspnea.
  • Tricuspid regurgitation: holosystolic at the left lower sternal border, with right heart failure: distended jugular veins with v waves, pulsatile, tender, enlarged liver, ascites, edema, right ventricular heave.
  • Pulmonic regurgitation: decrescendo diastolic off S2, louder on inspiration; classically after tetralogy of Fallot repair (disrupted pulmonic annulus); with a loud P2 (pulmonic component of S2), pulmonary hypertension.
  • Atrial septal defect: wide, fixed S2 split, no click.
  • Functional flow murmur: no click, normal S2, in a high-output state (anemia, fever): treat the cause.
Diagnosis
Murmur Man: the shape places the murmur, breathing names the valve
ShapeTenantsWhat separates them
Diamond head: crescendo-decrescendo ejectionAortic stenosis, pulmonic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathyHypertrophic cardiomyopathy louder with Valsalva and standing, aortic stenosis softer; pulmonic stenosis louder on inspiration
Flat body: holosystolic, S1 (first heart sound) to S2Mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, ventricular septal defectTricuspid louder on inspiration; mitral radiates to the axilla; septal defect harsh at the lower sternal border
Left arm: late diastolic rumble into S1Mitral and tricuspid stenosisTricuspid louder on inspiration; mitral on expiration, with an opening snap at the apex
Right arm: early diastolic decrescendo off S2Aortic and pulmonic regurgitationPulmonic louder on inspiration; aortic on expiration, with a wide pulse pressure
Late systolic with a clickMitral valve prolapseClick moves earlier with standing and Valsalva
Crossing S2Patent ductus arteriosusContinuous, machine-like: runs through S2
Reading S2 Widened, varies – pulmonic stenosis, after an ejection click · Wide, fixed – atrial septal defect: more right-sided flow across a normal pulmonic valve · Narrowed, or paradoxical when severe – aortic stenosis (a bicuspid valve calcifies early, 40s to 50s); paradoxical also in left bundle branch block · Single – severe pulmonic regurgitation, pulmonary atresia, severe aortic stenosis, transposition, truncus · Loud P2 – pulmonary hypertension; with a decrescendo diastolic murmur, Graham Steell
Management
Treatment Congenital pulmonic stenosis – percutaneous balloon valvulotomy preferred, if severe and symptomatic · Pulmonic regurgitation after repair – serial echocardiography; pulmonic valve replacement when severe, with progressive right ventricular dilation and symptoms · Tricuspid regurgitation – usually functional: find the cause · Graham Steell – treat the pulmonary hypertension
After congenital heart repair In a young adult the repair is the etiology, not the background. Tetralogy of Fallot repair: pulmonic regurgitation, right ventricular dilation, ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death; palpitations and syncope: ECG (electrocardiogram), Holter and electrophysiology referral. Aortic valvotomy: aortic regurgitation. Coarctation repair: re-coarctation, persistent hypertension. Fontan: protein-losing enteropathy, arrhythmia. Mustard or Senning: baffle obstruction, systemic right ventricular failure.
Practice
  1. 30-year-old man has exertional dyspnea tetralogy of Fallot repaired at age 3 decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, louder with inspiration single S2; parasternal heave Afebrile · BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 84/min → Pulmonic regurgitation → a decrescendo diastolic murmur off S2 sits on the right arm, and louder on inspiration puts it on the right heart; P2 is lost (single S2), the heave is the dilated right ventricle carrying the volume load, and the repair enlarged the outflow tract and disrupted the pulmonic annulus. Aortic regurgitation is the same arm, wrong side; tricuspid regurgitation is the right side, wrong phase. Next, echocardiography to grade the regurgitation and right ventricular size; severe regurgitation with symptoms and progressive right ventricular dilation goes to valve replacement
  2. 18-year-old woman is evaluated for a murmur ejection click, then a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left 2nd interspace widely split S2 that varies with respiration Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 72/min → Pulmonic valve stenosis → an ejection click and a widened split that varies with breathing are pulmonic stenosis; an atrial septal defect splits S2 wide but fixed, with no click, and the innocent pulmonic flow murmur has no click and a normal S2; confirm with echocardiography
  3. 38-year-old woman is evaluated for a murmur mid-diastolic rumble at the apex with an opening snap loud S1 ECG shows atrial fibrillation Afebrile · BP 118/76 mm Hg · HR 112/min, irregularly irregular → Mitral stenosis → a diastolic rumble into S1 is the left arm, mitral or tricuspid stenosis; the opening snap at the apex marks the mitral valve, while tricuspid stenosis grows louder on inspiration; a myxoma rumble varies with body position
  4. 17-year-old boy is evaluated for a murmur harsh crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left mid-sternal border louder with Valsalva and on standing Family history of sudden death Afebrile · BP 120/74 mm Hg · HR 70/min → Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy → a diamond-shaped murmur that grows with Valsalva and standing (reduced preload) is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a dynamic left ventricular outflow obstruction at the left mid-sternal border; aortic stenosis, bicuspid or not, gets softer, and pulmonic stenosis grows louder on inspiration; confirm with echocardiography
  5. 64-year-old man has leg edema and ascites distended jugular veins with large v waves pulsatile, tender, enlarged liver holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg · HR 88/min → Tricuspid regurgitation → a holosystolic murmur is the flat body; louder on inspiration puts it on the right, and a pulsatile liver with large v waves belongs to tricuspid regurgitation, usually functional from right ventricular dilation. Mitral regurgitation radiates to the axilla; a ventricular septal defect is harsh at the lower sternal border but does not grow on inspiration or bring a pulsatile liver and v waves
  6. 45-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur decrescendo diastolic murmur that decreases with inspiration bounding pulses No history of heart surgery or lung disease Afebrile · BP 158/52 mm Hg, a wide pulse pressure · HR 76/min → Aortic regurgitation → a decrescendo diastolic murmur off S2 is the right arm; softer on inspiration puts it on the left, and a wide pulse pressure with bounding pulses marks aortic regurgitation. Pulmonic regurgitation grows louder on inspiration, and mitral stenosis is a rumble into S1; confirm with echocardiography
  7. 20-year-old woman has 6 months of heavy menstrual periods soft midsystolic murmur normal S2; no click No syncope or chest pain on exertion Afebrile · BP 110/68 mm Hg · HR 96/min · hemoglobin 8 g/dL → Functional flow murmur → no click and a normal S2 exonerate the valve and the septum: a flow murmur of a high-output state, here anemia; treat the anemia. Pulmonic stenosis brings an ejection click and a widened split, and an atrial septal defect a wide, fixed split
  8. 55-year-old woman has dyspnea that changes with body position a plop and a rumble that vary with body position fever and weight loss T 38.1 °C · BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 92/min → Left atrial myxoma → a plop and a rumble that shift with position, with fever and weight loss, are a left atrial myxoma; mitral stenosis gives an apical rumble with an opening snap, and fever with weight loss also fit endocarditis, but a plop and rumble that shift with position point to a mass
  9. 20-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur midsystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border S2 split widely, and fixed with breathing; no click Lungs clear; no edema Afebrile · BP 116/70 mm Hg · HR 70/min → Atrial septal defect → a wide, fixed split with no click is an atrial septal defect, more right-sided flow across a normal pulmonic valve; pulmonic stenosis splits S2 widely but the split varies, after an ejection click, and tricuspid regurgitation is holosystolic at the lower border
  10. 78-year-old man is evaluated after an episode of syncope crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids softer with Valsalva delayed carotid upstroke No family history of sudden death Afebrile · BP 128/84 mm Hg · HR 70/min → Aortic stenosis → a diamond-shaped murmur to the carotids that softens with Valsalva, with a delayed upstroke, is aortic stenosis; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy grows louder with Valsalva, and mitral regurgitation is holosystolic and radiates to the axilla; confirm with echocardiography
  11. 28-year-old man has 2 weeks of palpitations and one episode of syncope repaired tetralogy of Fallot No chest pain, fever or seizure activity Afebrile · BP 116/70 mm Hg · HR 92/min → Ventricular arrhythmia → a repaired lesion is the etiology: tetralogy repair gives pulmonic regurgitation, right ventricular dilation, ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death, and palpitations with syncope point to the arrhythmia: ECG, Holter and electrophysiology referral. Pulmonic regurgitation dilates the right ventricle and sets up the arrhythmia, but by itself brings dyspnea and a heave, not palpitations with syncope; a residual ventricular septal defect is a holosystolic murmur
  12. 30-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border loud P2 echocardiogram shows pulmonary hypertension No prior heart surgery Afebrile · BP 118/76 mm Hg · HR 80/min → Graham Steell murmur → Graham Steell is pulmonic regurgitation from pulmonary hypertension: a loud P2, not the absent one (single S2) after repair, and there was no surgery; aortic regurgitation brings a wide pulse pressure, and this one is normal; treat the pulmonary hypertension
  13. 28-year-old woman is evaluated for a murmur mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur the click moves earlier on standing No family history of sudden death Afebrile · BP 108/68 mm Hg · HR 72/min → Mitral valve prolapse → a click that moves earlier with standing (reduced preload) is mitral valve prolapse; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy also grows louder with reduced preload but is a harsh diamond-shaped murmur, and aortic stenosis has no mid-systolic click and gets softer with reduced preload
  14. 22-year-old woman has exertional dyspnea ejection click and a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left 2nd interspace echocardiogram shows a doming pulmonic valve with a severe gradient Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 84/min → Percutaneous balloon valvulotomy → congenital pulmonic stenosis, often silent until adult exertional dyspnea, now severe and symptomatic: percutaneous balloon valvulotomy is preferred over surgical replacement, and a severe, symptomatic valve is past observation
  15. 52-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur systolic murmur at the right 2nd interspace S2 splits paradoxically ECG shows no bundle branch block Afebrile · BP 134/82 mm Hg · HR 70/min → Aortic stenosis of a bicuspid valve → a right 2nd interspace murmur with a narrowed split, or a paradoxical one when severe, is aortic stenosis; a bicuspid valve calcifies prematurely and presents in the 40s to 50s, the most common congenital defect found in adults. Pulmonic stenosis sits at the left 2nd interspace with a widened split, and a flow murmur keeps a normal S2
  16. 30-year-old man has worsening exertional dyspnea repaired tetralogy of Fallot echocardiogram shows a severely regurgitant pulmonic valve right ventricle more dilated than a year ago Afebrile · BP 118/72 mm Hg · HR 86/min → Pulmonic valve replacement → severe pulmonic regurgitation after repair with progressive right ventricular dilation and symptoms needs pulmonic valve replacement; serial echocardiography is surveillance, and diuretics with a recheck in a year leave the dilating ventricle untreated
Common wrong answers Tricuspid regurgitation: against pulmonic stenosis it also grows on inspiration, so the click and the split decide; against pulmonic regurgitation it is the right side, wrong phase. Aortic regurgitation: the other tenant of the right arm, right shape, wrong side. Atrial septal defect: fixed splitting, when the stem says single. Anemia flow murmur: the benign look-alike; a normal S2 and no click exonerate it.
Pairs with Part I Heart Murmurs in a Child: the innocent pulmonic flow murmur, the benign counterpart of pulmonic stenosis; ask: is there a click, and what is S2 doing? Part II Congenital Heart Disease: when a murmur appears and why; this brief covers what the murmur is.
Transferable rule

Fix phase and side before you name a valve, and check inspiration in every murmur. Then separate look-alikes by the accompanying findings, not the sound.

Right Lower Quadrant Pain

appendix, ileocecum, or neither · Campylobacter and Yersinia · appendix-sparing imaging · when to treat CampylobacterIs there profuse mucoid diarrhea, and is there a sick contact?

Source vignette Pt — 17 yo, migratory periumbilical to right lower quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, sibling with the same illness · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned Campylobacter infection, acute appendicitis and Escherichia coli O157:H7 infection
The decision point

Fever, right lower quadrant tenderness, and a neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis occur in both appendicitis and ileocecitis and do not discriminate. Two findings that appendicitis does not explain are twelve mucus-containing loose stools in 24 hours and a brother with the same illness. Both fit infectious ileocecitis (pseudoappendicitis) from organisms with an ileocecal predilection, Campylobacter jejuni and Yersinia enterocolitica. The migratory periumbilical-to-right-lower-quadrant pain also fits: Campylobacter may infect the jejunum first and then spread to the ileum and cecum.

Defining criteria Infectious ileocecitis (pseudoappendicitis) — right lower quadrant pain from acute ileocecitis caused by organisms with an ileocecal predilection, specifically Yersinia enterocolitica and Campylobacter jejuni · The discriminating symptom — profuse watery or mucoid diarrhea, which acute appendicitis is not classically associated with · The imaging tell — ileocecal inflammation and mesenteric lymphadenopathy with sparing of the appendix · When Campylobacter earns antibiotics — duration beyond 7 days, bloody stools, high fevers, or a patient who is pregnant, immunocompromised, or elderly
Pertinent positives & negatives Twelve mucus-containing stools in 24 hours — profuse mucoid diarrhea, not a feature of appendicitis · A brother with the same illness, now improving — a shared exposure, which appendicitis does not explain; the sibling's course fits a self-limited enteritis · Migratory periumbilical → right lower quadrant pain — classic for appendicitis, but also explained by jejunal-then-ileocecal spread of Campylobacter · Right lower quadrant tenderness without rebound or rigidity — no peritonitis; this argues against an advanced or perforated appendix without excluding an early one · Fever 38.8 °C with WBC (white blood cell count) 13,700 and 80% neutrophils — present in both diagnoses; does not discriminate · Mucus in the stool — argues against norovirus, whose stools are watery without mucus · No hematochezia in the patient, with fever above 38.5 °C — argues against E. coli O157:H7, which usually brings hematochezia within 1–3 days and rarely high fever · Age 17 — diverticulitis is exceedingly rare at this age
Right lower quadrant pain in a young patient: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Infectious ileocecitis (Campylobacter, Yersinia)Undercooked poultry or a sick contact; ileocecal predilection; fever with mucoid or bloody diarrheaProfuse mucoid diarrhea with right lower quadrant pain; imaging spares the appendix(the answer)
Acute appendicitisLuminal obstruction; migratory periumbilical to right lower quadrant pain, anorexia, vomitingLittle or no diarrhea, progressive localized peritonitis, no sick contactsTwelve mucoid stools and an affected sibling
E. coli O157:H7Shiga toxin colitis; undercooked beef or a point-source outbreakHematochezia within 1–3 days and fever above 38.5 °C is rareThe patient has no bloody stools and a temperature of 38.8 °C
NorovirusCommon-source outbreak; prominent vomitingWatery stools without mucus, normal white blood cell countMucoid stools with a neutrophilic leukocytosis
Cecal diverticulitisRight-sided diverticular inflammationRight lower quadrant pain and fever in an adult; mild or no diarrheaExceedingly rare at 17; profuse mucoid diarrhea
Crohn ileitisChronic transmural ileal inflammationChronic, relapsing pain, weight loss, perianal diseaseThree days of illness with a sick contact
Management, in one line Campylobacter is treated supportively because it is usually self-limited within seven days. Antibiotics are reserved for the severe or high-risk cases listed above. In infectious ileocecitis, surgery is not required.
Decision spine Is there diarrhea, and how much? — Twelve mucoid stools → argues against appendicitis · Is there a sick contact? — A brother with the same illness → an infectious exposure, not a luminal obstruction · Are there peritoneal signs? — No rebound, no rigidity → not a surgical abdomen at this moment · What is the stool like? — Mucoid, with or without blood → invasive bacterial rather than viral · Which organisms live at the ileocecum? — Campylobacter and Yersinia
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
CBCFirstNeutrophil-predominant leukocytosisShared by appendicitis and ileocecitis; decides nothing
Ultrasound or CT of the abdomenBy branchIleocecal inflammation with a spared appendixInfectious ileocecitis: supportive care, no surgery
Inflamed appendixAcute appendicitis: surgical consultation
Stool culture or PCRConfirmsCampylobacter or YersiniaNames the organism; a susceptibility panel alone is not a reason to treat
Colonoscopy with ileal intubationBy branchChronic ileal inflammation on biopsyCrohn ileitis: chronic, relapsing pain, weight loss, perianal disease
Diagnostic laparoscopySkipInvasive when imaging can decideImage first when the examination leaves the diagnosis unclear
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo with migratory periumbilical to right lower quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, and a sibling with the same illness → Campylobacter infection → Infectious ileocecitis
  2. A hemodynamically stable 17-year-old with migratory periumbilical-to-right-lower-quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, and a sibling with the same illness has had 3 days of symptoms without bloody stools. → Supportive care with stool studies → Usually self-limited within 7 days
  3. A 17-year-old with migratory periumbilical-to-right-lower-quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, and a sibling with the same illness now presents on day 9 with bloody stools and fever to 39.5 °C. → Start antimicrobial therapy → A high-risk criterion is met
  4. 17 yo with right lower quadrant pain, anorexia and vomiting but no diarrhea, with rebound tenderness → Surgical consultation for appendectomy → The classic script without the stool
  5. 17 yo with right lower quadrant pain and diarrhea in whom the diagnosis remains unclear after examination → Cross-sectional imaging of the abdomen → Ileocecal inflammation with a spared appendix
  6. 16 yo with months of right lower quadrant pain, weight loss and a perianal fistula → Colonoscopy with ileal intubation → Crohn ileitis
  7. 6 yo with severe crampy abdominal pain and grossly bloody stools, temperature 37.6 C, after a family cookout → Escherichia coli O157:H7 infection → Hematochezia early, high fever rare
  8. That 6 year old with suspected Shiga toxin producing E coli; which intervention should be withheld → Empiric antibiotics → Risk of precipitating hemolytic uremic syndrome
  9. Three weeks after a Campylobacter enteritis, ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia → Guillain-Barre syndrome → The classic post-infectious sequela
  10. Two weeks after a Campylobacter enteritis, asymmetric oligoarthritis with conjunctivitis and urethritis → Reactive arthritis → The second named sequela
  11. 5 yo M, 4 days of mucoid diarrhea after a low-grade fever that has resolved, still 5 or 6 stools a day, well hydrated, afebrile, guaiac negative; stool culture grows Campylobacter coli, ciprofloxacin resistant, ampicillin and tetracycline sensitive → Symptomatic care only → mild and self-limited; the susceptibility panel is not an indication
  12. 6 yo with Campylobacter coli enteritis now on day 9 with bloody stools; ciprofloxacin resistant, erythromycin intermediate, ampicillin and tetracycline sensitive → Amoxicillin → sensitive, and safe under 8
  13. 4 yo in day care with high fever, bloody diarrhea and a brief generalized seizure; stool grows Shigella → Azithromycin → treating shortens illness and spread
Decoy note The brother's illness supports an infectious cause, but his bloody stools may prompt a diagnosis of Shiga toxin E. coli in a patient with no blood in his own stool. A contact's findings describe the exposure, not this patient's phenotype. The migratory pain is also explained by Campylobacter spread, so it does not confirm appendicitis.
Bacterial diarrhea: who gets antibiotics Campylobacter — self-limited within about a week; supportive care. Treat only for symptoms beyond 7 days, bloody stools, high fever, or pregnancy, immunocompromise or old age; choose by susceptibility · Stool culture — a positive culture with a susceptibility panel is not an indication. Culture is for protracted or severe illness and for outbreak control in day care and nursing homes · Shiga toxin-producing E. coli — bloody diarrhea with little fever; never give antibiotics, which can raise the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome · Shigella — high fever, bloody diarrhea, sometimes a febrile seizure; antibiotics (azithromycin) shorten illness and spread · Nontyphoidal Salmonella — supportive in a healthy child; treat infants under 3 months, sickle cell disease, immunocompromise or bacteremia, because treatment otherwise prolongs carriage · Yersinia — pseudoappendicitis like Campylobacter; supportive unless bacteremic or immunocompromised · Clostridioides difficile — recent antibiotics; oral vancomycin or fidaximicin · Doxycycline under 8 — avoided when another agent covers the organism, because of tooth staining
Pearls Appendicitis does not cause twelve mucoid stools or a sick sibling; ileocecal Campylobacter or Yersinia explains both. · Profuse watery-then-mucoid diarrhea or a sick contact alone should prompt reconsideration of appendicitis before surgery. · Campylobacter and Yersinia have an ileocecal predilection and mimic appendicitis; imaging shows ileocecal inflammation and mesenteric adenopathy with a normal appendix. · Campylobacter may infect the jejunum before the ileum and cecum, so the pain can migrate as in appendicitis. · The two tested sequelae of Campylobacter are Guillain-Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis. · For Campylobacter, antibiotics are for illness beyond seven days, bloody stools, high fevers, or pregnancy, immunocompromise, or advanced age; otherwise the treatment is supportive. · Antibiotics are withheld for Shiga toxin E. coli.
Pairs with Part II Acute Kidney Injury in a Child has the Shiga toxin and hemolytic uremic syndrome row from the renal side, where the E. coli O157:H7 branch of this differential ends. Ask: whose stool was bloody, and how many days into the illness? Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers hemolytic uremic syndrome, which follows Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, not Campylobacter. Part II Infectious Diarrhea covers the organism by exposure: what did the patient eat, and when?
Transferable rule When a presentation fits a textbook script, look for the finding the script cannot explain, such as a symptom the disease does not produce or an exposure it cannot have.
Salient decoyAcute appendicitis is not associated with profuse watery then mucoid diarrhea and cannot explain a sibling with the same illness. There are no peritoneal signs.
True-fact-wrong-slotE. coli O157:H7 causes hematochezia in the patient within 1–3 days, and fever above 38.5 °C rarely occurs. The bloody stools are the brother's, not this patient's.
Class-vs-memberNorovirus gives watery stools without mucus, a normal white blood cell count, and prominent vomiting
Unchecked attributeCecal diverticulitis is exceedingly rare in children and adolescents and does not produce profuse mucoid diarrhea.
Test-overrides-findingsA susceptibility panel invites treatment, but a mild, improving, afebrile child is treated by the clinical picture, not the culture report.

Tick-Borne Illness

treat suspected rickettsiosis before confirming it · a rash from the extremities inward · the platelet, sodium and liver triadWhere did the rash start, and what did the platelets, sodium and transaminases do?

Source vignette Pt — 12 yo M, 3 days of fever, abdominal pain, body aches and headache with an unremarkable emergency department workup, now back with confusion and worse pain; lives by a lake surrounded by woods · Exam — T 39, BP 90/60, HR 120; new maculopapular rash on arms and legs, generalized abdominal tenderness without rebound, no neck stiffness, nonfocal neurologically · Labs — leukocytes 4,600, platelets 46,000, ALT (alanine aminotransferase) 158, AST (aspartate aminotransferase) 202, creatinine 1.1 · Imaging — abdominal CT (computed tomography) normal · Q — the most appropriate next step in management; options spanned amoxicillin, doxycycline, laparoscopy, prednisone, serum ceruloplasmin and stool ova and parasites
Source vignette · NBME Pediatrics CMS Pt — 6 yo F, previously healthy, seen in June with 4 days of persistent fever and severe headache and 1 day of a rash on the hands; lives in a rural area and is often bitten by mosquitoes; took corticosteroids for poison ivy a month ago; appears ill · Exam — T 39 C, HR 110, RR 22; bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge; scattered petechiae on the palms and distal arms · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned dengue fever, erysipelas, erythema infectiosum, exanthema subitum, Kawasaki disease, measles, meningococcemia, Rocky Mountain spotted fever and typhoid fever
The decision point

The picture is three to four days of undifferentiated fever, headache and myalgia, then a rash on the extremities, in a child with wooded exposure. With the laboratory triad of thrombocytopenia, transaminitis and hyponatremia, this is Rocky Mountain spotted fever. The management is empiric doxycycline started now. Diagnosis is made retrospectively by serology, and the disease progresses to vascular collapse and death if you wait for it. The abdominal pain is not a second problem: severe abdominal pain is part of RMSF (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) in children. It is the specific reason this boy got a CT rather than an antibiotic on his first visit.

Defining criteria Rocky Mountain spotted fever — Rickettsia rickettsii, a gram-negative obligate intracellular organism transmitted by tick bite, peaking in late spring and summer, most often in the southeastern and south-central United States despite the name; incubation 2 to 14 days; many patients never recall the bite, so its absence proves nothing · The rash — begins maculopapular on the wrists and ankles, spreads centrally, involves palms and soles, and evolves to petechiae · The laboratory triad — thrombocytopenia from intravascular platelet destruction, hyponatremia, and raised AST and ALT from hepatic endothelial injury · Treatment gate — doxycycline empirically on suspicion, in all patients including young children; a study found no staining of permanent teeth after short courses (5 to 10 days)
Pertinent positives & negatives Three days of nonspecific fever then a rash — the rickettsial tempo; the rash appears late, which is why the first visit was unremarkable · Rash on arms and legs — extremity onset, spreading centrally · Platelets 46,000 with raised transaminases — the vascular-injury signature, belonging to no isolated abdominal process · Lives near woods — the exposure; no recalled bite is typical, not exculpatory · Severe abdominal pain with a normal CT — the pediatric RMSF mimic of appendicitis; the negative scan closes the surgical option rather than opening a new one · Confusion with a nonfocal examination and no neck stiffness — early encephalitic involvement, not meningitis · BP 90/60 with HR 120 — early vascular compromise, and the reason waiting is dangerous · No adenopathy, clear oropharynx — argues against the viral exanthems and mononucleosis
Fever and rash after outdoor exposure — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Rocky Mountain spotted fever Can't missSummer, wooded exposure; R. rickettsiiExtremity rash spreading centrally, palms and soles; low platelets, low sodium, high transaminases— (the answer)
Lyme diseaseSame season and habitat; Borrelia burgdorferiErythema migrans — a single expanding annular lesion with central clearingMaculopapular extremity rash; cytopenias and transaminitis atypical
Ehrlichiosis / anaplasmosisSame tick exposure, similar prodromeSame labs, usually no rash; morulae in leukocytesA prominent rash is present
Dengue feverAedes mosquito; travel to or residence in the tropicsRetro-orbital pain, severe bone and muscle pain; leukopenia, low platelets; bleeding in severe casesNo tropical travel; mosquito bites at home in the US do not transmit it
MeningococcemiaNeisseria meningitidis; any seasonHours from fever to petechiae, purpura, shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation; meningismus in someDays of fever before the rash; rash began distally and spread inward
Kawasaki diseaseVasculitis of young childrenFever for 5 days or more plus 4 of 5: nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked lips or strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, hand and foot redness or swelling, cervical node; platelets risePetechial palm rash, low platelets; conjunctival injection alone does not make it
MeaslesUnvaccinated child; paramyxovirusCough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots; rash starts at the hairline and spreads down, sparing palms and solesRash began on the hands and wrists; no cough or coryza
Roseola (exanthema subitum)Human herpesvirus 6; under age 2Days of high fever in a well infant, then a blanching truncal rash as the fever breaksIll school-age child; petechial rash during the fever
Immune thrombocytopeniaPost-viral, otherwise well childIsolated thrombocytopenia, normal liver, afebrileFever, rash, transaminitis and hypotension
Wilson diseaseGenetic copper transport defectKayser-Fleischer rings; hepatic and neuropsychiatric disease over monthsAn acute febrile illness with a rash over days
AmebiasisFever, abdominal pain, liver abscessBloody diarrhea; abscess on imagingCT normal, no diarrhea, rash unexplained
Decision spine How long has the fever run and when did the rash appear? — Three to four days, then rash, the rickettsial tempo · Where did the rash start? — Wrists and ankles, spreading inward · What did the platelets, sodium and transaminases do? — Low, low, high, the triad · Any outdoor or wooded exposure? — Yes, and a recalled bite is not required · Is there abdominal pain? — In a child that is part of the disease, not a second one · So when do you treat? — Now; serology is retrospective and untreated disease kills
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
CBCFirstPlatelets low, white count normal or lowEndothelial injury; fits RMSF, not a surgical abdomen
Basic metabolic panel and liver enzymesFirstHyponatremia with raised AST and ALTCompletes the rickettsial triad; start doxycycline now
Peripheral smearBy branchMorulae in leukocytes, usually no rashEhrlichiosis or anaplasmosis; doxycycline treats it too
Rickettsia rickettsii serology, acute and convalescentConfirmsFourfold rise in IgG titerRMSF, in retrospect; never delay treatment for it
Abdominal CTSkipNormalSevere abdominal pain is part of RMSF in children
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo M, 3 days of fever, headache and abdominal pain, now confused with a maculopapular rash on the arms and legs; platelets 46,000, AST 202, ALT 158; lives near woods; abdominal CT normal → Doxycycline → empiric treatment for Rocky Mountain spotted fever
  2. 10 yo with fever, an extremity rash, thrombocytopenia and transaminitis after wooded exposure; serology has been sent → Withholding antibiotics until serology returns → untreated disease progresses to vascular collapse
  3. 9 yo seen 10 days after a hike with a single expanding annular lesion showing central clearing and mild fatigue → Lyme disease → erythema migrans
  4. 4 yo with suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever whose parents decline doxycycline over concerns about dental staining → Give doxycycline → a study found no staining of permanent teeth after short courses (5 to 10 days)
  5. 40 yo with summer tick exposure, fever, headache, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases, with no rash → Ehrlichiosis → doxycycline treats it as well
  6. The mechanism of thrombocytopenia in Rocky Mountain spotted fever → Intravascular platelet destruction from infection of vascular endothelium → small-vessel vasculitis
  7. 12 yo with severe abdominal pain and fever, a maculopapular rash on the wrists and ankles, and a normal abdominal CT → Rocky Mountain spotted fever → abdominal pain in children mimics appendicitis
  8. Child already started on doxycycline for suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever → Rickettsia serology → confirmation is retrospective and never delays therapy
  9. 6 yo F, previously healthy, seen in June with 4 days of high fever and severe headache and 1 day of a rash on the hands; lives in a rural area, often bitten by mosquitoes; finished a steroid course for poison ivy a month ago; appears ill; T 39 C; bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge; scattered petechiae on the palms and distal arms → Rocky Mountain spotted fever → doxycycline now, without waiting for serology
  10. 10 yo F, 5 days after returning from 2 weeks in the Dominican Republic, with fever to 39.5 C, severe headache with pain behind the eyes, and severe bone and muscle pain; diffuse macular rash on the trunk; no outdoor or wooded exposure in the US; WBC (white blood cell count) 2,800, platelets 90,000, sodium normal → Dengue fever → supportive care with fluids; avoid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
  11. 4 yo M on a farm in Tennessee, seen in July with 4 days of fever and headache; bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge; blanching macules on the wrists and ankles that became petechial and now reach the palms, soles and trunk; no cracked lips or hand swelling; platelets 85,000, sodium 130, AST 140 → Start doxycycline → Rocky Mountain spotted fever; any age, treat on suspicion
Decoy note Two details suggest abdominal and hepatic causes. Worsening abdominal pain with a normal CT is the classic pediatric RMSF presentation that gets children taken to the operating room. Once the scan is negative, stop pursuing an abdominal cause. Confusion with transaminitis suggests Wilson disease, but confusion in RMSF is early encephalitis arriving over hours, not over months.
Decoy note: no tick in the stem No tick — most RMSF stems never mention one; the clue is season (late spring to summer), rural or outdoor life, days of fever and severe headache, then a rash that starts on the wrists, ankles, palms or soles and spreads inward, turning petechial · Mosquito bites — point to dengue only with tropical travel, and dengue brings retro-orbital pain and severe bone and muscle pain · Conjunctival injection — occurs in RMSF too; Kawasaki disease needs 5 days of fever plus its criteria, and measles needs cough, coryza and a rash from the hairline down · Steroids for poison ivy a month ago — irrelevant; they explain none of the fever, headache or petechiae
Pearls Treat on suspicion, confirm retrospectively — doxycycline treats the patient; serology only documents the diagnosis · Doxycycline is given to children of any age for RMSF — the staining concern applies to prolonged courses, and withholding it is the dangerous choice · Low platelets plus transaminitis plus hyponatremia after outdoor exposure — a rickettsial fingerprint the viral exanthems do not produce · The rash moves inward — extremity onset spreading centrally with palms and soles is a short differential: RMSF, secondary syphilis, coxsackie hand-foot-and-mouth · No recalled tick bite — does not lower suspicion; the exposure history is habitat, not bite · Abdominal pain in a febrile child with a rash is part of the illness — a normal CT should redirect you to a systemic diagnosis, not a more invasive abdominal one
Pairs with Part I Skin and Soft Tissue Infection covers the febrile-rash differential. Fever and Rash in a Child covers measles and roseola, and Kawasaki Disease covers the 5-day fever with red eyes. Related conditions without their own brief: Lyme disease and ehrlichiosis. Ask: where did the rash start, and what did the platelets and transaminases do?
How NBME framed it Kawasaki disease appeared under its formal name, mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, as a decoy for a child with 4 days of fever, red eyes and a petechial rash on the palms.
Transferable rule When the confirmatory test is retrospective and the untreated disease is lethal, treat on the clinical picture. Let the serology arrive whenever it arrives. A pending test is not a reason to wait; treatment should already have started.
Salient decoyStool for ova and parasites: fever with abdominal pain and liver enzymes fits amebiasis, but that causes bloody diarrhea and a liver abscess and explains no rash.
Treat-the-numberPrednisone: platelets of 46,000 invite ITP (immune thrombocytopenia), but ITP is isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child, not fever with rash, transaminitis and hypotension.
True-fact-wrong-slotAmoxicillin: correct for Lyme, same season and habitat, but Lyme rash is a single expanding annular lesion and it spares the platelets and liver.
Salient decoySerum ceruloplasmin: liver enzymes plus confusion reads as Wilson disease, a chronic disorder with Kayser-Fleischer rings, not four days of fever with a rash.
Sequencing trapLaparoscopy: the abdominal CT is already normal, which answers the surgical question.
Salient decoyDengue fever: mosquito bites suggest it, but without tropical travel dengue is not on the table. It brings retro-orbital and bone pain rather than a rash spreading in from the wrists.
Unchecked attributeKawasaki disease: red eyes fit, but fever has run 4 days, not 5, and the rash is petechial on the palms, not polymorphous with swollen hands.
Salient decoyMeasles: conjunctivitis tempts, but measles rash starts at the hairline, spares the palms and soles, and follows cough and coryza.

Hot Joint or Bursa in an Adult

septic arthritis, crystal arthritis and septic bursitis · synovial fluid thresholds · prosthetic joint and gonococcal branches · post-injection flareIs joint motion preserved, and has the fluid been sampled before any treatment?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Aspirate before you treat. Nothing on exam excludes infection, and a missed septic joint destroys cartilage in days.

Passive range of motion picks the space:

  • Preserved, swelling over the bursa: the bursa is aspirated when infection is plausible (redness, warmth, fever, or pain worsening days after an injection).
  • Pain with any passive motion, diffuse effusion: the joint is aspirated.

No antibiotics, colchicine, steroid or repeat injection before the fluid is sampled.

Diabetes and joint space narrowing raise septic risk even when the history suggests gout.

Diagnosis
Defining findings Septic bursitis – localized bursal swelling with redness and warmth, joint motion preserved; fever in only about 40% and absent in most patients 65 or older; usually Staphylococcus aureus, also Streptococcus pyogenes · Septic arthritis – hot, swollen joint, severe pain on passive motion, fever; joint fluid white cells over 50,000 (over 100,000 is more specific), neutrophils over 75% · Gout – negatively birefringent needles (monosodium urate) · Pseudogout – positively birefringent rhomboids of CPPD (calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate), chondrocalcinosis on radiograph · Post-injection steroid flare – starts within hours and settles within 48 hours; infection worsens over several days; timing separates them, not severity
Risk factors Bursa – cellulitis, abrasions, penetrating trauma, bursal injection or instrumentation; diabetes and immunocompromise · Joint – diabetes; preexisting joint disease (joint space narrowing on radiograph)
Synovial fluid
FluidWhite cells/mm³Neutrophils
Noninflammatory (osteoarthritis)200 to 2,000Under 25%
Inflammatory (crystal, rheumatoid arthritis)2,000 to 100,000Over 50%
SepticOver 50,000; over 100,000 is more specificOver 75%
Prosthetic joint infectionAbout 3,000Over 70%
Management and treatment
Management ladder: the hot joint
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Arthrocentesis: cell count and differential, Gram stain, culture, crystals; through clean skin or image-guided, never through cellulitisAlways, for any acute hot joint
2Empiric intravenous antibiotics after cultures: vancomycin with or without ceftriaxone or cefepime; add Salmonella coverage in sickle cell diseasePurulent fluid or white cells over 50,000; do not wait for culture
3Joint drainage: serial aspiration, arthroscopic or open washoutConfirmed septic arthritis
By diagnosis Septic bursitis – systemic antibiotics; incision and drainage if not improving after about 2 days · Gout – NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) or colchicine, once infection is excluded · Suspected infection – no corticosteroid injection, into a joint or a bursa · Subacromial bursa – can communicate with the glenohumeral joint, so its infection can become septic arthritis
Practice
  1. 54-year-old woman has 1 day of a hot, swollen, red right knee severe pain on passive range of motion obesity, hypertension and diabetes Radiograph: joint space narrowing T 38.5 °C · HR 102/min · no rash → Arthrocentesis → nothing on exam excludes infection, and diabetes and joint space narrowing are risk factors for it: aspirate before any treatment
  2. 47-year-old woman has 2 days of a hot, swollen left knee pain with any passive motion aspirate: 68,000 white cells/mm³, 85% neutrophils No crystals seen under polarized light T 38.6 °C · Gram stain pending → Septic arthritis → over 50,000 white cells with over 75% neutrophils and no crystals is septic arthritis: vancomycin after cultures, then drainage
  3. 55-year-old man woke with severe pain at the base of the big toe red, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint began after a steak dinner Aspirate: 12,000 white cells/mm³ T 37.6 °C · negatively birefringent needles → Gout → an inflammatory count with negatively birefringent needles is gout: an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) or colchicine
  4. 47-year-old woman has 2 days of a hot, swollen right knee aspirate shows negatively birefringent needle crystals and 60,000 white cells/mm³ Gram stain shows no organisms T 38.2 °C · culture pending → Treat as septic → crystals do not exclude coexisting infection: over 50,000 white cells is treated as septic until culture says otherwise
  5. 72-year-old woman has 1 day of a hot, swollen right knee radiograph shows chondrocalcinosis aspirate: positively birefringent rhomboid crystals Gram stain shows no organisms T 37.8 °C · aspirate 18,000 white cells/mm³ → Pseudogout → positively birefringent rhomboids with chondrocalcinosis are calcium pyrophosphate crystals: pseudogout
  6. 68-year-old man has 3 weeks of right knee pain had a knee replacement 2 years ago aspirate: 3,200 white cells/mm³, 82% neutrophils No crystals seen T 37.4 °C · radiograph: no loosening seen → Prosthetic joint infection → around a prosthesis the 50,000 threshold does not apply: about 3,000 white cells with over 70% neutrophils is prosthetic joint infection
  7. 24-year-old woman has 4 days of joint pain moving from knee to wrist tenosynovitis over the wrist extensors a few pustules on the hands Sexually active, inconsistent condom use T 38.1 °C · no back pain or conjunctivitis → Disseminated gonococcal infection → migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis and pustules are disseminated gonococcal infection: NAAT and cultures of cervix, urethra, pharynx and rectum
  8. 47-year-old woman has a hot, swollen left knee and fever red, warm cellulitis over the front of the knee the joint must be sampled Diabetes, on metformin T 38.4 °C · pain with passive motion · knee effusion → Arthrocentesis straight through the cellulitis → a needle through cellulitis seeds the joint: aspirate through clean skin or under image guidance
  9. 60-year-old man with sickle cell disease has a hot, swollen left knee pain with any passive motion aspirate cloudy, cultures drawn Empiric antibiotics are being chosen T 38.7 °C · aspirate 90,000 white cells/mm³ → Add Salmonella to coverage → sickle cell disease adds Salmonella to the organisms to cover
  10. 70-year-old man has 2 days of a diffusely swollen right knee severe pain with any passive motion fever and chills No swelling localized over the kneecap T 38.8 °C · large knee effusion → Septic arthritis → pain with any passive motion and a diffuse effusion is the joint, not the bursa: aspirate the joint
  11. 52-year-old man has a red, hot, tender swelling over the kneecap fever since yesterday full, painless passive knee motion Kneels on concrete at work T 38.6 °C · no knee effusion → Septic prepatellar bursitis → preserved joint motion with swelling over the bursa is extraarticular: septic prepatellar bursitis, aspirate the bursa
  12. 45-year-old man, a floor installer, has 3 days of knee swelling boggy swelling over the kneecap, red and warm knee range of motion intact Serum uric acid not yet drawn T 37.4 °C · no knee effusion → Aspirate the bursal fluid → redness and warmth make infection plausible: aspirate the bursal fluid before presuming crystals or overuse
  13. 49-year-old man was diagnosed with septic prepatellar bursitis no improvement after 3 days of antibiotics swelling and redness unchanged Culture grew Staphylococcus aureus T 38.0 °C · knee motion still full → Incision and drainage of the bursa → failure to improve after about 2 days of antibiotics is the drainage gate: incision and drainage of the bursa
  14. 58-year-old woman has worsening right shoulder pain began 4 days after a subacromial corticosteroid injection fever and myalgias Pain was mild the day after the injection T 38.4 °C · white cells 14,000/mm³ → Image-guided aspiration of the bursa → pain worsening days after an injection is iatrogenic inoculation of skin flora: image-guided aspiration of the deep bursa
  15. 60-year-old man has severe right shoulder pain began 6 hours after a corticosteroid injection already easing by the next morning No chills or redness at the injection site Afebrile · white cells normal · no swelling → Post-injection steroid flare → pain within hours that settles within 48 hours is a post-injection steroid flare; infection worsens over days
Distractors Naproxen: skips a tier; treats a diagnosis not yet made and delays drainage. Serum uric acid: wrong parameter; neither rules gout in nor infection out.
Pairs with Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child: in adults every acute hot joint is aspirated at tier 1; only in children does tier 1 depend on toxicity and inflammatory signs, not on the presence of fluid.
Transferable rule

When a test is both diagnostic and therapeutic and the disease it excludes is time-destructive, the test comes before every treatment, even one right for the more likely diagnosis. Aspirate the space that is infected, because infection cannot be excluded.

Tics and Tic Disorders

classify the movement first · motor and vocal tics · Tourette criteria · tic vs compulsion · habit reversal, then medicationIs the behavior involuntary, or is it neutralizing an obsession?

Source vignette Pt — 7 yo M, behavioral concerns at school; repeats exactly what other children say, and last year raised his hand repeatedly then said he was just stretching when called on; plays alone to avoid bullying, prefers books and jigsaw puzzles; says he tries not to be bad but sometimes cannot help it · History — father has obsessive-compulsive disorder; growth tracking at the 60th percentile · Exam — frequent head turning and shoulder shrugging; remorseful and anxious on mental status examination · Q — the most appropriate next step in management; options spanned atomoxetine, exposure and response prevention, fluoxetine, methylphenidate, parent management training and risperidone
The decision point

Three of the described behaviors are tics. Head turning and shoulder shrugging are motor tics. Repeating exactly what other children say is echolalia, a vocal tic. The hand-raising, explained away afterward, is a motor tic he covered for; this is how school-age children manage tics. Multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic, present over a year with onset before 18, is Tourette syndrome. Among the offered options, the therapy that targets tics is the antidopaminergic risperidone. It is a second-generation antipsychotic, preferred over first-generation agents for its adverse-effect profile.

Defining criteria Tourette syndrome — multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, not necessarily concurrent, present over 1 year, with onset before age 18; more common in boys, typically presenting age 6 to 15 · Motor tics — facial grimacing, blinking, head or neck jerking, shoulder shrugging, tongue protrusion · Vocal tics — grunting, sniffing, snorting, throat clearing, barking, yelling, echolalia, coprolalia · Compulsion — the mimic's gate: a repetitive behavior performed in response to an obsession to reduce anxiety; absent an obsession, a repetitive movement is a tic · Treatment tiers — habit reversal training is behavioral and first-line; antidopaminergic agents when tics impair function, meaning second-generation antipsychotics, dopamine depleters such as tetrabenazine, or alpha-2 agonists such as guanfacine and clonidine
Pertinent positives & negatives Head turning and shoulder shrugging — two motor tics, the examination finding that names the disorder · Echolalia — the required vocal tic; without it this is a chronic motor tic disorder, not Tourette · Symptoms over more than a year — meets the duration criterion, and the waxing and waning course is itself characteristic · Reads books, completes jigsaw puzzles, plays alone quietly — sustained attention, which argues against ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) despite the classroom referral · Remorseful, says he cannot help it — insight and distress consistent with tics, not oppositional defiance · No obsessional thoughts described — closes OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder), and with it both exposure therapy and fluoxetine · Bullied and avoiding peers — functional impairment, the gate that licenses pharmacotherapy · Father with OCD — a family-history decoy; OCD and Tourette are comorbid and heritable together, which is why it is plausible and why it is not diagnostic
Repetitive behavior in a school-age child — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Tourette syndromeBoys 6 to 15; waxing and waning; comorbid ADHD and OCDMultiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic over 1 year— (the answer)
Obsessive-compulsive disorderObsessions driving compulsions that relieve anxietyA named obsession; the behavior neutralizes itNo obsessional thought anywhere in the stem
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorderInattention or hyperactivity across settingsFidgetiness, cannot sustain attention, impairment in two or more settingsReads and completes puzzles alone; behavior is school-confined
Oppositional defiant disorderAngry mood, defiance and vindictiveness toward authorityDeliberate defiance without remorseHe is remorseful and distressed by the behavior
Provisional tic disorderTics present less than 1 yearSame movements, shorter durationSymptoms span more than a year
Management, and the option list that was not offered Behavioral therapy with habit reversal training is first-line and is the choice whenever it is offered. When tics impair function, add an antidopaminergic or an alpha-2 agonist. Clonidine and guanfacine are both guideline-supported for tics and ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) together. Guanfacine is often preferred first for its milder sedation profile; this is clinical practice, not a guideline ranking. When the guideline first-line treatment is not on the option list, choose the best offered treatment for the diagnosis you made. Do not change the diagnosis to fit an offered drug.
Decision spine Describe the movements. — Head turning, shrugging, hand-raising are motor tics · Is there a sound? — Echolalia is a vocal tic · How long? — Over a year and waxing and waning, so Tourette rather than provisional · Is any behavior neutralizing an obsession? — No, so not OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder), and the exposure therapy and fluoxetine options fall · Can he sustain attention? — Books and puzzles, so not ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder), and the stimulants fall · Is function impaired? — Bullied and isolated, so pharmacotherapy is licensed
Scenario bank
  1. 7 yo M with head turning, shoulder shrugging and repetition of classmates' words for over a year, now bullied and socially isolated → Risperidone → Tourette syndrome with functional impairment
  2. 8 yo M with mild motor and vocal tics who is performing well academically and has friends → Habit reversal training → behavioral therapy precedes medication when tics are mild
  3. 9 yo M with motor tics who also describes intrusive thoughts of contamination relieved only by repeated handwashing → Comorbid obsessive-compulsive disorder → exposure and response prevention
  4. 7 yo M with head jerking and eye blinking for 8 months and no vocal tic → Provisional tic disorder → duration under 1 year with no vocal tic
  5. How antipsychotic agents suppress tics in Tourette syndrome → Dopamine receptor blockade → tetrabenazine instead depletes presynaptic dopamine
  6. 8 yo with Tourette syndrome and inattention impairing him at home and at school → A stimulant for the comorbid ADHD → stimulants are not contraindicated in Tourette — methylphenidate reduces ADHD symptoms without worsening tics (American Academy of Neurology (AAN) 2019)
  7. 7 yo with Tourette syndrome whose parents request medication to reduce the tics → Fluoxetine → an SSRI treats comorbid OCD, not tics
  8. 10 yo with moderate impairing tics whose parents decline an antipsychotic because of weight-gain concerns → Guanfacine → alpha-2 agonists are an accepted alternative
Decoy note Family history of obsessive-compulsive disorder in the father is the strongest decoy. It is true in a way that makes it worse: obsessive-compulsive disorder and Tourette syndrome are comorbid and co-heritable. So this history is consistent with Tourette syndrome while pointing toward obsessive-compulsive disorder. The child's own words describe the involuntariness of a tic, not the anxiety relief of a compulsion.
Pearls Describe the movement before you name the disorder — a family history does not change what a movement is · A compulsion requires an obsession; with no obsessional thought, a repetitive behavior is a tic and exposure therapy is the wrong tool · Echolalia is a vocal tic, and it upgrades a chronic motor tic disorder to Tourette syndrome. It is the criterion most often missed, because repeating words does not seem like a vocal tic · tics wax and wane, so a behavior that stopped last year and was replaced by a new one is natural history, not improvement · stimulants for comorbid ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) are not contraindicated in Tourette, despite older teaching
Pairs with Part II School Difficulty in a Child is the nearest relative. It shares the same referral route, a school behavior complaint. The resolution is opposite: there the private interview reveals a learning disorder, and here the examination reveals tics. Ask: what exactly is the child doing, and is it involuntary?
Transferable rule A family history raises the prior probability, but the phenomenology decides. When a relative's diagnosis and a child's behavior are both given, first describe the behavior in neutral terms. If the behavior is involuntary and stereotyped, it is a tic, whatever the family carries.
Salient decoyExposure and response prevention: the father's OCD and the anxious remorseful affect sell it, but exposure therapy treats compulsions driven by obsessions and no obsession is described.
True-fact-wrong-slotFluoxetine: first-line for pediatric OCD and depression, but the same category error, and an SSRI does not suppress tics.
Class-vs-memberParent management training: targets oppositional defiant disorder; he is remorseful rather than defiant, and it does nothing for tics.
Class-vs-memberMethylphenidate and atomoxetine: ADHD is genuinely comorbid with Tourette, but these behaviors are tics and sustained attention on books and puzzles argues against ADHD.
