Transfusion Reactions

onset and company · urticarial vs anaphylactic · hemolytic and bacterial emergencies · when to resume · most need nothingWhat are the vitals, and what else is on the skin besides hives?

Source vignette Pt — 12 yo F with idiopathic aplastic anemia, new petechiae and bruising over a week; during a platelet transfusion a chest rash spreads over the body · Labs — absolute neutrophil count 420, platelets 7,000 · Exam — T 37.2 °C, blood pressure (BP) 110/82 mm Hg, heart rate (HR) 90/min, respiratory rate (RR) 18/min, saturation 98%; oropharynx normal, lungs clear; diffuse urticarial rash on trunk and limbs plus pinpoint nonblanching macules and bruises at the extremities · Q — the best next step in evaluation of the reaction; options spanned culture of the product, direct Coombs test, no additional evaluation, peripheral smear and coagulation studies
The decision point

Blood pressure is normal, there is no wheeze, the lungs are clear and the oropharynx is normal. This is isolated urticaria in a hemodynamically stable patient. The rash improved after an antihistamine, with an hour of stable observation. It is an urticarial transfusion reaction, caused by preformed IgE reacting against a soluble allergen in the donated plasma, or the reverse. Management is what has already been done: stop the transfusion, give an antihistamine and observe. Improvement with the antihistamine confirms the diagnosis, and the transfusion may be resumed without additional evaluation.

Defining criteria Urticarial reaction — hives and itching only, onset hours into the transfusion, from preformed IgE against a soluble plasma allergen; stop, antihistamine, resume if otherwise asymptomatic, no workup · Anaphylactic reaction — onset seconds to minutes, from anti-IgA antibodies in an IgA-deficient recipient reacting to donor IgA; respiratory distress or wheeze, angioedema, hypotension; epinephrine, and washed products thereafter · Acute hemolytic reaction — ABO incompatibility from clerical error; fever, flank pain, hypotension, hemoglobinuria, direct Coombs positive · Transfusion-transmitted bacterial infection — fever, chills, hypotension, most common with platelets; culture both the recipient and the product
Transfusion reactions: timing, company and the movethe vitals sort them faster than the rash does
ReactionOnsetThe company it keepsWhat to do
UrticarialHoursHives and itching, nothing else; vitals normalStop, antihistamine, resume; no workup
Anaphylactic EmergencySeconds to minutesWheeze, angioedema, hypotension; IgA-deficient recipientEpinephrine; future transfusions washed
Acute hemolytic EmergencyMinutes to hoursFever, flank pain, hypotension, dark urineStop; direct Coombs, smear, prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT); supportive
Bacterial contamination EmergencyMinutes to hoursFever, rigors, hypotension; platelets most oftenCulture recipient and product; empiric antibiotics
Febrile nonhemolyticDuring or within 4 hFever and chills without hemolysisStop, antipyretic; leukoreduction reduces its incidence
TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload) / TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury)TRALI within 6 h; TACO within 12 hRespiratory distress: volume overload vs noncardiogenic edemaStop; diuretic for TACO, supportive care for TRALI
Pertinent positives & negatives BP 110/82 mm Hg, HR 90/min, saturation 98% — hemodynamically stable, which excludes anaphylaxis, hemolysis and sepsis · Lungs clear, oropharynx normal — no bronchospasm, no angioedema; the two findings that would make this anaphylaxis · Afebrile at 37.2 °C — excludes both a febrile reaction and bacterial contamination · Rash improved with diphenhydramine and stayed stable for an hour — confirms the diagnosis · Petechiae and bruises were present before the transfusion — they reflect a platelet count of 7,000 from aplastic anemia, not a new consumptive process · No flank pain, no dark urine — the findings of a hemolytic reaction are absent · It was a platelet transfusion — platelets are the product most associated with bacterial contamination; without fever, culture is not indicated
Decision spine What is the blood pressure and the saturation? — Normal → the dangerous reactions are out · Is there a fever? — No → not hemolytic, not bacterial, not febrile · Wheeze, angioedema or hypotension? — None → urticaria is isolated, so not anaphylaxis · How fast did it start? — Late, not in the first minutes → urticarial · Did it respond to the antihistamine? — Yes → that is the confirmation · So what is needed? — Nothing further; the transfusion may be resumed
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Vital signs, lung and airway examFirstNormal vitals, clear lungs, hives onlyThe dangerous reactions are excluded
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsHives improve with an antihistamine, vitals stay stableUrticarial reaction; resume the transfusion, no tests
Direct Coombs test, smear, PT and PTTBy branchFever, flank pain, dark urine: Coombs positiveAcute hemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility
Blood cultures of the recipient and the productBy branchFever, rigors, hypotension: growth in bothBacterial contamination, most often a platelet unit
Serum IgA levelBy branchAfter anaphylaxis: IgA absentAnti-IgA anaphylaxis; wash future products
Coombs test or product culture for hives aloneSkipAfebrile and stable: no indicationNothing to find; pre-existing petechiae come from the low platelets
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo F with aplastic anemia developing a diffuse urticarial rash late in a platelet transfusion; BP 110/82 mm Hg, saturation 98%, afebrile, lungs clear; rash improves after diphenhydramine and vitals stay stable for an hour → No additional evaluation is indicated → urticarial reaction; the transfusion may be resumed
  2. 30 yo F who develops wheezing, facial angioedema and a blood pressure of 70/40 mm Hg two minutes into a red cell transfusion → Intramuscular epinephrine → anaphylactic transfusion reaction
  3. Patient with selective IgA deficiency and a history of transfusion anaphylaxis who now requires red blood cells → Transfuse washed red blood cells → washing removes donor plasma IgA
  4. 45 yo who develops fever, flank pain, hypotension and dark urine 20 minutes into a red cell transfusion → Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction → ABO incompatibility from a clerical error
  5. 60 yo M who develops fever to 39 °C with rigors and hypotension 30 minutes into a platelet transfusion → Culture the recipient and the transfused product and start empiric antibiotics → bacterial contamination, most common with platelets
  6. The mechanism of an isolated urticarial transfusion reaction → Preformed IgE reacting against a soluble allergen in donor plasma → or donor IgE against a recipient allergen
  7. 12 yo with aplastic anemia and platelets of 7,000 who develops hives during transfusion; pinpoint nonblanching macules were documented on her limbs before the transfusion began → Pre-existing thrombocytopenia → the petechiae are not part of the reaction
  8. IgA-deficient patient with prior transfusion anaphylaxis who urgently requires red blood cells → Standard unwashed packed red blood cells → residual donor plasma IgA triggers anaphylaxis
Decoy note The petechiae and ecchymoses look like a new hemorrhagic complication, and they appear in the skin examination beside the urticaria as though they arrived together. They were present before the transfusion: she had bruising a week ago, and her platelet count is 7,000. A finding documented before the intervention cannot be a reaction to it.
Pearls Vital signs: normal blood pressure, no fever and no hypoxia eliminate anaphylaxis, hemolysis, bacterial contamination and TRALI · Isolated urticaria is the only reaction in which the transfusion may continue: stop, give an antihistamine, observe, then resume the same unit · Timing separates the two allergic reactions: seconds to minutes with wheeze and hypotension is anaphylaxis; hours with hives alone is urticarial · Anaphylaxis to blood suggests IgA deficiency; the long-term fix is washed products · Platelets carry the bacterial risk because they are stored at room temperature; fever and rigors during a platelet transfusion call for cultures
Pairs with Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers selective IgA deficiency and already keys washed red cells; this brief covers the same topic from the transfusion side. Ask: what are the vitals, and what else is on the skin besides hives?
Transferable rule When a treatment has already been given and the response is reported, the response serves as the diagnostic test, and usually nothing further is needed. Check the reported response before ordering anything.
Redundant workupDirect Coombs test: answers "is this hemolysis?", already excluded by normal vitals, no fever, no flank pain and no dark urine.
Salient decoyPT and PTT: indicated only for hemolysis complicated by disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC); her bruising is thrombocytopenic and predates the transfusion.
Redundant workupPeripheral smear: would show schistocytes if microangiopathy were present; there is no hemolysis to look for.
Unchecked attributeCulture of the product: platelets do carry the bacterial risk, but culture requires fever, chills or hypotension; she is afebrile and stable.
